title: 众安航空与亿维特达成战略合作，携手共拓低空应用新生态 - NE时代
content:
众安航空与亿维特达成战略合作，携手共拓低空应用新生态
9月23日，第五届全球数字贸易博览会现场，众安航空与亿维特正式举行产业合作签约仪式，双方宣布达成战略合作关系。此次签约不仅是展会期间的“高光时刻”，更是双方深化产业协同、推动低空经济迈向规模化应用的重要起点。
第五届全球数字贸易博览会现场
众安航空 × 亿维特
战略合作正式达成
在第五届全球数字贸易博览会现场，众安航空与亿维特举行产业合作签约仪式，双方正式建立战略合作关系。
众安航空与亿维特产业合作签约仪式
此次合作，不只是一次展会期间的签约，更是双方围绕低空产业应用建立长期协同关系的重要起点。
低空经济正在由技术验证逐步迈向规模化应用。对于一架飞行器而言，真正创造产业价值，并不只取决于“能不能飞”，更重要的是能否进入真实场景、形成稳定运营，并最终转化为持续可用的服务。
这意味着，低空产业未来的竞争不只是单一产品的竞争，也将是技术、运营、场景与生态协同能力的竞争。
基于这一产业趋势，众安航空与亿维特将发挥各自在低空航空器、运营服务、场景拓展及产业资源等方面的优势，持续探索低空技术与实际需求之间更加高效的连接方式。
从航空器到运营场景
让双方优势形成协同
亿维特深耕eVTOL航空器研发与产业化，持续推进低空飞行器产品及技术能力建设。
众安航空则立足低空运营，持续探索低空文旅、空中交通及多元化低空应用场景，并通过运营体系、场景资源和产业协同，推动低空飞行从产品能力进一步走向实际服务。
亿维特ET9 eVTOL
一端，是航空器技术与产品；另一端，是运营体系、真实场景与市场需求。此次合作，正是双方能力进一步连接的开始。
对于低空经济而言，从一架航空器走向一项成熟服务，中间还需要跨越场景适配、运营组织、市场需求、基础设施以及商业模式等多个环节。航空器解决的是“飞什么”，场景回答的是“在哪里飞、为谁而飞”，而运营能力决定的，则是这些产品和技术能否真正形成长期、稳定、可持续的服务。
众安航空所持续关注的，正是其中“连接”与“运营”的价值。
通过此次合作，双方有望进一步推动航空器产品与运营场景之间形成更紧密的协同，让先进低空技术从展台走向真实应用，让飞行器从产品逐步走向服务。
从技术创新到产业落地

签约仪式前，新农都集团领导一行实地参观众安航空eVTOL，详细了解机型性能、技术特点、应用场景及低空经济产业发展情况。工作人员围绕eVTOL垂直起降、低碳高效、点对点运输等优势介绍了其应用前景。来访领导对众安航空在低空经济领域的产业布局和运营探索给予肯定。
双方在座谈会上交流
座谈交流环节，双方围绕合作基础、技术支撑、场景落地和执行保障等内容深入交换意见。
新农都团队率先发言，结合农产品流通、社区配送等实际业务，系统阐述了低空应用的合作需求与场景设想。
新农都集团董事长 沈金潮 在交流中指出，新农都长期深耕农产品流通和民生服务领域，拥有覆盖广泛的供应链网络、市场资源和应用场景。此次与众安航空合作，是推动民生服务向高效化、智能化升级的重要探索。希望双方以签约为起点，加快推动低空载人服务、农产品低空运输、社区即时配送等场景落地，让低空经济发展成果更好服务民生。

中国新城市集团总裁 施南路 结合众安航空业务布局，阐述了合作落地的技术路径与场景规划。他表示，众安航空聚焦低空经济赛道，在eVTOL运营、场景开发和产业协同方面具备专业优势。针对双方合作优势与合作方向，众安航空将提供定制化低空运载方案，优先选择成熟场景开展试点，逐步形成可复制、可推广的合作模式。
滑动图集：众安航空与会团队
双方一致认为，低空经济作为战略性新兴产业，正成为培育新质生产力、推动高质量发展的重要方向。新农都集团的应用场景与众安航空的技术优势高度契合，双方将以此次签约为契机，推动低空经济与民生服务深度融合，打通技术、场景与服务闭环。
在双方与会人员共同见证下，沈金潮与施南路代表双方签署战略合作协议，根据协议，双方将建立常态化沟通机制，加快推动合作事项落地，以具体项目为牵引，打造低空经济赋能民生服务的示范样板。
双方代表签署战略合作协议
随后，全体与会人员合影留念，记录双方战略合作的重要时刻。
双方与会人员合影留念
此次签约是双方顺应低空经济发展趋势、推动民生服务提质增效的重要举措，也是众安航空拓展低空应用场景、新农都提升供应链服务能力的具体实践。下一步，双方将充分发挥各自优势，深化资源共享和协同联动，实现互利共赢、共同发展。

title: 动力电池包热管理集成创新之路！ - NE时代
content:
动力电池包热管理集成创新之路！
动力电池包热管理和箱体结构集成方案是动力电池系统结构与热管理结合的关键技术，同时承担结构承载、电池散热、水路密封多重功能，集成方案的选型直接影响PACK的快充性能、安全可靠性、轻量化水平以及制造成本。 随着动力电池技术方案的进化、迭代及创新，当前行业已形成铆钉连接集成、搅拌摩擦焊集成、FDS连接集成三大主流方案，不同工艺依托自身特性及成本应用于各车型。
铆钉连接集成方案
独立液冷板通过大量铆钉与箱体底部固定，冷板与箱体间涂覆密封结构胶进行密封。所用连接件均为拉铆螺母或抽芯铆钉等标准件，成本可控，配合对应拉铆工具即可生产，设备投入低，量产周期短。此外，该方案中冷板与箱体完全独立，可拆解维修，整体成本可控，主要适用于钣金箱体及辊压钢箱体结构。
图1 铆钉连接集成
FDS热融自攻钉连接集成方案
FDS集成方案通过专用设备将热融自攻螺钉穿透冷板与箱体底板，利用高速摩擦使接触区域材料局部软化，实现螺钉攻丝与机械锁合。该方案需在箱体底板密封区域均匀涂布结构密封胶，对工艺要求严格，气密管控难度较高。由于FDS产线柔性较强，对场地及设备投入相对较少；同时对零部件和箱体尺寸公差要求较低，降低了零部件质量管控成本，支持多车型平台共线生产，量产节拍稳定，中、大规模量产具备一定的经济优势。
图2&3 FDS热融自攻钉连接集成
搅拌摩擦焊（FSW）一体化集成方案
搅拌摩擦焊是当前铝型材电池包箱体的主流技术路线。其工艺方案是将冷板与箱体边框预装配，利用搅拌头沿拼接缝匀速行进，通过高速旋转摩擦产热使铝材达到塑性软化状态，实现材料熔合与冷板集成。该方案对冷板与箱体的配合尺寸要求较高，焊接前需保证配合间隙在较小公差范围内，同时大尺寸箱体需通过分段焊接、辅助工装等措施控制焊接变形。焊接所用搅拌头属易损件，需定期更换。该方案焊接强度高，焊缝密封性能优异，轻量化效果突出，适用于大尺寸电池包及热管理性能要求较高的车型。
图4&5 搅拌摩擦焊（FSW）
零跑自研CTC集成冷板一体化技术方案
此外，零跑自研的CTC集成冷板一体化技术方案，通过结构设计创新，直接在箱体壳体上集成流道结构，从而省去了传统箱体总成中的独立液冷板，同时满足热管理性能及整车轻量化需求。该方案通过结构简化，在减少箱体零部件的同时，避免了传统箱体与独立冷板集成过程中存在的整包气密性风险，实现了整车减重需求与密封可靠性的提升。
图6 零跑自研CTC集成冷板一体化
冷板与箱体各类集成方案在不同的产品都有应用，需要结合快充指标、产品定位、售后维修策略、量产成本综合选择不同的工艺路线；随着电池包的不断迭代，未来多工艺复合集成设计将成为主流，兼顾散热性能、安全可靠性、维修便利性和生产成本。

title: 华力创通以1.5亿知识产权出资，设立3亿合资公司布局低空经济 - NE时代
content:
华力创通以1.5亿知识产权出资，设立3亿合资公司布局低空经济
9月28日，创业板上市公司华力创通发布公告，拟与全资子公司北京怡嘉行科技有限公司，及达州市智飞科技有限公司、四川三州圆科技开发有限公司共同投资设立四川空驭智航科技有限公司，注册资本3亿元。
值得关注的是出资方式：华力创通以知识产权作价出资1.5亿元，持有合资公司50% 股权；怡嘉行以现金出资7000万元，持股23.33%；智飞科技现金出资7500万元，持股25%；三州圆现金出资500万元，持股1.67%。
从“研发设计”向“制造运营”延伸
华力创通的主营业务包括卫星应用、雷达信号处理、航空电子、无人系统和仿真测试，是国内少数同时掌握卫星通信与卫星导航核心技术的企业，参与了北斗卫星导航、天通卫星通信两大国家空间基础设施的建设。
在低空经济领域，公司已规划并迭代研制了系列化垂直起降固定翼无人机、小型多旋翼无人机集群、无人靶机等产品，其中靶机业务已实现规模化订单。2025年年报显示，公司全年实现营业收入7.82亿元，同比增长42.91%，明确将低空经济列为重点拓展方向。
此次设立合资公司，核心目的是推动业务链条由研发设计向加工制造、运营服务环节延伸。合资公司将落地四川达州东部经济开发区，围绕无人机制造、低空智能管控、综合服务等方向统筹布局，依托地方产业政策与应用场景开拓西南地区市场。
行业信号：上市公司以“技术入股”切入低空制造
这笔投资的看点不在于金额——3亿元注册资本在低空经济领域并不算大。真正的信号在于出资结构：华力创通以知识产权作价1.5亿元换取50%股权，而合作方以现金出资。
这种“技术换股权”的模式，反映了一个正在发生的趋势：拥有核心技术积累的上市公司，正在以更低现金消耗的方式进入低空经济制造环节。对于华力创通而言，它在卫星导航、无人系统、仿真测试领域的技术积累，正是低空飞行器制造和管控平台所需要的底层能力；对于地方合作方而言，引入一家有技术背书的上市公司，比从零培育本土企业更快见效。
需要说明的是，合资公司目前尚未完成工商设立登记，后续运营存在不及预期的风险。

title: 卫蓝新能源半固态电芯助力张家口赤城100MW/400MWh混合型储能电站项目加速建设 - NE时代
content:
卫蓝新能源半固态电芯助力张家口赤城100MW/400MWh混合型储能电站项目加速建设
近日，张家口赤城县100MW/400MWh混合型储能电站项目进入设备集中交付与现场安装阶段。卫蓝新能源作为项目半固态储能电芯供应方，为项目半固态储能系统提供核心电芯产品支持。多批储能设备已陆续运抵项目现场，基础施工、设备吊装、定位及安装等工作正有序推进。
按照当前项目建设进度，项目预计于2026年9月至10月期间推进并网及相关验收工作，最终并网时间以项目实际建设及电网验收进度为准。
张家口赤城县100MW/400MWh混合型储能电站项目位于河北省张家口市赤城县经济开发区东区。根据项目公开EPC招标信息，项目总投资约5亿元，规划占地约40亩，建设规模为100MW/400MWh，采用“超级电容+半固态电池”的混合储能技术路线，并配套建设一座110kV变电站及附属输变电工程。项目招标人及业主为中八（河北）能源有限公司。中八（河北）能源有限公司为中东（河北）能源有限公司全资子公司，中东（河北）能源有限公司由河北冀能售电有限公司控股。EPC招标阶段披露的计划工期为150个日历天。
混合储能通过不同储能技术的优势互补，兼顾快速功率响应与长时能量支撑需求。在项目建设过程中，卫蓝新能源以半固态储能电芯产品参与其中，为大型储能项目的安全、高效运行提供核心电芯支持，也进一步推动半固态电池技术在百兆瓦级储能场景中的工程化应用。
从产品交付到现场安装，项目建设正按计划持续推进。现场照片显示，多批储能设备已完成运输进场，并按照项目规划分区开展基础施工及设备安装。随着储能系统、配套电气设备和现场工程逐步衔接，项目已进入建设实施的关键阶段。
卫蓝新能源持续与项目业主、系统集成及产业链合作伙伴协同推进项目落地，从电芯产品交付到后续项目配合，为项目建设和并网调试提供稳定支持。
除技术与工程建设持续推进外，本项目在融资模式方面同步形成了清晰的项目融资安排。根据项目业主及相关方提供并确认的融资资料，项目公司中八（河北）能源有限公司作为承租人，与江苏金融租赁股份有限公司于2026年3月11日正式签署《融资租赁合同》，由江苏金融租赁股份有限公司为项目提供融资租赁金融服务。
本项目采用无追索权项目融资安排。根据相关融资文件及项目相关方确认，融资项下的抵押、担保及追索范围仅限于张家口赤城县100MW/400MWh混合型储能电站项目本身，不涉及项目范围以外的额外抵押物，亦不向项目公司股东或母公司资产负债表追偿。融资责任边界与项目资产、设备及项目自身经营安排相匹配，为项目建设提供了金融支持。
技术、工程与金融资源的协同，是大型新型储能项目实现规模化落地的重要支撑。此次项目融资安排，也为先进储能技术与市场化金融工具的结合提供了新的实践场景。
从电芯研发制造，到储能系统交付和百兆瓦级项目现场应用，卫蓝新能源正持续推动半固态电池技术走向更多真实能源场景。张家口赤城项目的持续推进，也进一步拓展了半固态电池在大型电网侧储能中的应用实践。
未来，卫蓝新能源将继续聚焦半固态及固态电池技术创新，深化在电网侧储能、新能源配储、工商业储能及海外储能市场的应用，并与业主、系统集成商、金融机构及产业链伙伴持续协同，为新型电力系统建设和全球能源绿色转型提供更加安全、可靠的电池解决方案。

title: 安森美RCP方案重塑车载电子架构，实现“去MCU化”功能控制 - NE时代
content:
安森美RCP方案重塑车载电子架构，实现“去MCU化”功能控制
随着汽车电子电气架构（EEA）从分布式向域控制器和区域架构演进，传统分布式ECU模式面临成本高昂、线束复杂等系统性难题，且难以满足算力集中化、功能可扩展及高效通信的行业需求。
安森美（onsemi）
推出的RCP（Remote Control Protocol，远程控制协议）技术及oncp全套解决方案，可由中央控制单元直接管控边缘节点，从而帮助在特定场景下省去边缘端微控制器（MCU）。
本文深度解析RCP技术核心价值，阐述安森美RCP芯片与软件方案如何助力车企加速迈入软件定义汽车（SDV）时代。
市场分析：分布式ECU弊端与架构升级趋势
在迈向软件定义汽车的进程中，车企正面临架构迭代的全新挑战。传统分布式电子架构下，车灯模组、车门控制、车载音频等各类功能模块，均需配备独立MCU及外围配套电路。这种设计模式虽逻辑简单，但随着汽车智能化等级持续提升，逐渐暴露出硬件成本高、整车布线繁琐、网络通信效率受限等突出问题。
硬件成本痛点十分直观。按行业常规估算，单颗边缘应用MCU成本约1美元，单车搭载20个边缘功能节点，仅MCU物料成本就达20美元；协议转换网关成本更高，单台网关约45美元，单车平均配备4个网关，架构升级后仅此一项即可节省180美元物料清单成本。
软件研发成本同样不容忽视。分布式ECU架构中，每个MCU都需配套专属开发软件，ECU供应商需搭建专业软件工程团队。据行业测算，即便是结构简单的LIN总线附属开关组，其配套软件开发也需耗费数百小时。
与此同时，分布式ECU架构导致CAN、LIN等多种总线协议并存，车载网络（In-Vehicle Network, IVN）拓扑复杂度，已成为智能汽车架构设计的核心瓶颈。以车载照明系统为例，传统架构采用“ECU-CAN总线-MCU-LED驱动”分布式链路，受限于CAN总线传输带宽与链路层级冗余，通信效率难以提升。当全车各类终端均沿用此类架构，整车线束布局、重量管控及后期维护都会陷入困境。
诸多行业痛点倒逼汽车电子电气架构加速升级。一方面，架构从分散式ECU向中央域控制器集中演进，边缘节点控制逻辑逐步与车身域、自动驾驶域深度融合；另一方面，软件定义汽车成为行业主流设计理念，其本质是数据定义汽车（Data Define Vehicle）。这使得车载通信正从传统CAN总线向车载以太网加速迁移，以此提升大数据传输效率，节点级以太网标准10BASE-T1S也因此获得越来越多关注。
破局之道：RCP技术架构与核心优势
为充分释放集中式架构与10BASE-T1S的技术潜力，作为一种轻量化车载通信协议，RCP技术直击传统边缘设备必须搭载MCU的行业痛点。RCP方案依托10BASE-T1S车载以太网，将分散在各边缘节点的计算、控制逻辑统一收敛至区域控制器（Zonal Controller），可替代传统“MCU+网关”组合架构，打造“域控制器-10BASE-T1S-RCP芯片-终端驱动”的扁平化极简架构。
如上所述，RCP的核心设计思路是将边缘节点MCU的协议转换、逻辑处理功能，上移集成至区域控制器ZCU乃至中央控制器Central ECU。一方面，域控/区域控制器无需依赖边缘MCU，可通过RCP指令直接向终端设备下发控制命令；另一方面，借助以太网骨干网与RCP芯片协同，传感器原始数据可直传中央计算平台，大幅减少中间处理环节带来的时延与信号失真，实现架构、成本、效率多重优化。
RCP应用示意图
性能层面，RCP基于10BASE-T1S以太网搭建，网络传输速率可达10Mbps，远超高速CAN、CAN FD总线传输能力，为车载高频数据交互、实时指令调度筑牢基础。实测数据显示，RCP边缘节点至域控制器传输时延极低，即便经过整车主干网网关转发、跨域传输，整体时延仍可控制在10毫秒以内，能够满足自动驾驶场景对实时性的严苛要求。
系统设计层面，10BASE-T1S节点可通过单对双绞线以多点总线形式实现共享通信，非屏蔽双绞线最长支持25米车载布线，单链路可接入8至40个终端节点；搭配PoDL双线共供技术，同一双绞线同时完成供电与通信，线束综合成本降幅超50%，整车架构复杂度显著降低。同时，RCP方案可大幅压缩车型功能迭代周期，以车灯系统为例，某豪华车型灯光功能迭代周期从传统3个月缩短至2周，开发效率大幅提升。
系统可靠性层面，安森美在第二代RCP芯片中集成专利PLCA协调器冗余技术。该技术通过将备用跟随节点的最大节点数配置为略高于主协调器，赋予其冗余接管能力：正常工作状态下，备用节点检测到主协调器信标后自动重置计数；一旦主协调器失效，备用节点仅延迟一个TO时隙即可主动接管网络、发送替换信标，实现PLCA通信周期无缝接续，防止车载网络降级回退。PLCA通过循环时序调度保障各节点拥有确定性传输时隙，有助于避免物理信号冲突，显著提升多节点组网下的有效吞吐量，有效强化车载以太网通信可靠性。
凭借上述核心优势，RCP方案可推动汽车EEA从分布式ECU，平稳过渡至域控+区域控制器混合架构，并最终向中央计算平台+区域网关的终极架构演进。
安森美RCP全栈解决方案：oncp
安森美完整RCP生态解决方案命名为oncp，涵盖MAC-PHY物理层芯片、专用RCP控制芯片及全套配套软件栈。
T30HM1TS2500是安森美推出的符合IEEE 802.3cg标准的高性能MAC-PHY芯片，搭载CSMA/CD MAC协议与具备物理层冲突避免（PLCA）功能的PHY层，可通过SPI接口对接通用低成本标准MCU，帮助车企低成本、快速升级至10BASE-T1S车载以太网总线。实际应用中，T30HM1TS2500支持直连车载电池供电，集成休眠/唤醒控制逻辑，可有效降低待机功耗；内置高精度时间戳模块，满足整车时间同步需求。同时，芯片搭载多项可靠性增强特性，包括专利PLCA协调器冗余、增强型信号质量指数（SQI+）、增强抗干扰功能（ENI）及线束故障检测（HDD）等，目前已实现量产交付。
T30HM1TS2500应用框图
T30HM1TS2500低功耗特性
安森美还开发了入门级RCP专用芯片，同样符合IEEE 802.3cg以太网标准，已于2026年第一季度向客户送样测试。该芯片原生支持GPIO、SPI、UART、I2C、I2S、PDM、TDM、PWM、LIN、外部ADC、SENT等丰富外设接口，内部集成10BASE-T1S完整MAC、PHY及RCP协议引擎，可通过专用RCP指令完成参数配置，实现边缘设备无MCU、无专属底层软件运行。
oncp软件栈提供从图形化配置到指令执行的全流程开发工具链。图形化配置环节，客户可通过安森美配套GUI可视化配置设备IO映射（如定义Pin2为I2S时钟、Pin5为I2S数据）及网络拓扑参数，配置完成后工具可自动生成配置文件并一键烧录至RCP终端设备。
oncp完整软件栈
硬件抽象层（HAL）适配层面，特斯拉、现代起亚、奥迪、沃尔沃、雷诺、Stellantis等车企已规范地采用Protobuf实现序列化网络数据，可与oncp实现原生无缝对接，无需额外开发适配；未部署Protobuf的车企，也可通过简易封装层（Wrapper）快速将HAL控制指令映射为标准RCP协议指令，适配门槛极低。
Wrapper的指令转化
技术价值最终落地于车载场景。安森美通过多套功能Demo，有效验证了RCP技术商用成熟度，涵盖高精度车载音频传输、150米超长线缆通信、RCP与电感式位置传感器联动、PLCA协调器冗余容错、模块化车门控制等典型应用场景。
以无MCU车灯控制方案为例，传统车灯模组需内置独立MCU，负责解析CAN总线指令、运行逻辑算法并驱动LED光源；采用安森美RCP方案后，中央区域控制器通过10BASE-T1S网络直接下发指令，控制车灯模块LED驱动器工作。不仅节约单灯MCU和网关等物料成本，还大幅简化车灯PCB硬件设计、缩减模组体积。
传统车灯控制链路
基于RCP的车灯控制链路
同时，车灯智能控制逻辑集中上移至中央计算单元，依托域控制器、中央ECU的强大算力，可灵活落地软件定义照明功能。除自适应远光、车道精准照明等基础智能功能外，还可实现流水灯、呼吸灯等动态灯光特效，支持用户通过车机大屏、手机APP自定义灯光模式，成为车企打造车型品牌辨识度的重要差异化抓手。
综上，落地应用RCP技术，是车企迈向软件定义汽车终极架构进程中，兼具务实价值与战略远见的关键布局。

title: 月销7万台创历史新高：欣旺达动力BDU从部件到系统的三级跳 - NE时代
content:
月销7万台创历史新高：欣旺达动力BDU从部件到系统的三级跳
BDU（电池断开单元），是动力电池系统中最为关键的安全部件之一。
它承担着高压回路的通断控制、故障保护、预充电等核心功能——车辆启动、充电、故障断电，每一个高压动作的安全执行，均有赖于BDU的可靠运作。称BDU为动力电池的"安全闸门"，实至名归。
欣旺达动力汽车电子业务（以下简称"欣捷安"）隶属于欣旺达动力科技股份有限公司，致力于成为拥有前沿科技和值得信赖的汽车电子解决方案提供商，核心产品覆盖BMS、BDU、ZCU、车身控制器等关键部件，为全球汽车行业提供稳定、可靠的电子系统解决方案，助力推动未来汽车变革。
2026年1—7月，欣捷安自产BDU累计出货量已突破35万台；其中7月单月出货突破7万台，创下历史新高。
35万台意味着什么？对照2026年同期国内新能源乘用车上险数据，若以车企集团新能源车上险总量计，可跻身行业前三。
规模只是起点。欣捷安布局BDU的底层逻辑，从一开始便与传统厂商迥异——同行做的是"一个部件"，欣捷安做的是"电池系统整体解决方案"。
35万台的成色：BDU实现全场景验证与规模化交付
据NE时代上险数据库统计，2026年1—7月国内新能源乘用车车企集团维度排名中，第一名销量为120万辆，第二名67万辆，第三名35万辆。欣捷安1—7月自产BDU出货超35万台，已迈入大规模交付阶段。
然而数字只是表象。真正拉开差距的，是这35万台背后的"成色"——
欣捷安35万台配套项目，覆盖HEV混动与新能源两大技术路线、400V/800V双电压平台，客户矩阵涵盖头部自主车企、新势力及海外车企，业务版图遍及国内与海外市场，实现了全场景交付能力。
35万台背后还有一个常被忽视的维度——稳定交付能力。BDU行业有一个共识："能做出来"与"能稳定交付几十万台"是两个截然不同的命题。从样件验证到SOP量产，再到月产7万台的稳定爬坡，每一步都考验着企业的供应链管理、制造工艺与质量控制能力。
从单品BDU到智能BDU
35万台代表的是当下。欣捷安真正在布局的，是下一代智能BDU。
传统BDU是"被动执行器"，仅负责通断，不感知状态。智能BDU则通过集成传感与诊断能力，实时监测接触器状态、回路温度、绝缘电阻，并结合BMS数据进行故障预判与寿命评估，实现了BDU产品的控制闭环。
智能BDU的核心，并非简单叠加传感器，而是对电池系统的深度理解。没有BMS的技术积累、不懂电池机理，传感器堆砌再多，也做不出真正有价值的诊断与预测。这恰恰是欣捷安的护城河所在。
早在消费电池业务阶段，欣旺达便已启动BMS自研；切入动力电池赛道后，更积累了丰富的控制算法与高压安全技术经验。据SNE Research数据，2026年上半年欣旺达动力电池装机量达14.5GWh，市占率2.4%，位列全球第十；2026年1—7月，欣捷安BMS出货量超过65万套。
智能BDU并非从零起步，而是水到渠成。
能量域：BDU只是系统中的一个节点
比智能BDU更宏大的棋局，是能量域。
在传统架构下，BMS、BDU、DCDC、OBC各自独立、分散部署，难以实现深度协同。能量域的思路，是将这些模块统一集成，由一个域控制器集中管理——硬件集成化、软件统一化、通信内部化。
BDU在这一新架构中扮演什么角色？它是高压能量的总开关，也是安全保护的最后一道防线。没有BDU的深度参与，能量域便无从谈起。
据欣捷安测算，能量域系统的高度集成，可使线束减少70%以上，系统级降本空间达10%—20%。更为关键的是，能量域能够为高阶自动驾驶提供能源安全保障——电池分区、双路供电、系统安全冗余、400微秒以内的故障切换，确保关键系统持续供电不中断。
35万台，印证了欣捷安BDU的硬实力。
但欣捷安的布局远不止于此。从智能BDU到能量域，欣捷安走的是一条从"做部件"到"做系统"的进阶之路——不只是将BDU推向市场，更是要参与定义下一代整车能源架构。

知行科技正式设立日本分公司，体系化出海加速
Smart Mobility For Everyone
9月28日，知行科技日本分公司在日本东京品川正式设立。这是继德国慕尼黑研发服务中心、马来西亚生产基地之后，知行科技推进全球化战略的又一关键落子，将推动公司对接、融入全球汽车供应链。
知行科技坚定海外扩张战略：全力为中国OEM的海外业务提供技术与服务支持，同时积极开拓国际本土客户，产品及解决方案已跟随海内外客户扩展至欧洲、东南亚、韩国、日本等多个国家和地区，积累了丰富的海外场景应用经验与本地化服务能力。
今年上半年，公司首次成功获得海外直供客户定点及中国台湾地区客户订单，实现了客户覆盖范围的进一步突破。此次落子东京，知行科技日本分公司将构建日本相关领域与中国业务的沟通桥梁，拓展与日本整车厂的长期业务合作，强化知行科技的全球品牌影响力。
从产品出海到体系出海，知行科技的全球化交付闭环正加速形成。公司在马来西亚的合营公司已顺利完成试生产，预计将于2026年第三季度正式投产并向客户进行量产交付。
未来，知行科技将持续强化全球销售、生产与服务网络，依托海外公司与生产基地，结合技术适配、生态合作及数据合规能力的协同优势，加速切入海外车企直供体系。同时，公司将积极借助战略海外股东的资源，拓展新兴海外业务机会，构建更广泛的国际战略联盟，持续为全球汽车产业的智能化转型输出具备强市场竞争力的中国方案。

title: 芯驰科技携手开源硬件领导厂商瑞莎计算机，共推机器人小脑控制器“开箱即用” - NE时代
content:
芯驰科技携手开源硬件领导厂商瑞莎计算机，共推机器人小脑控制器“开箱即用”
9月29日，芯驰科技与瑞莎计算机（Radxa）签署战略合作协议。本次合作以开放硬件生态共建为主线——双方将围绕芯驰D9-Max高性能边缘AI SoC联合设计并正式推出机器人小脑控制器RoboX D9M，并在硬件参考设计、开源软件栈、全球开发者社区三个层面展开协作，让机器人开发者基于开放架构快速搭建产品。
芯驰提供车规级可靠性底座，瑞莎提供开放硬件工程化底座，合力推动具身智能核心控制器从“重复造底板”走向“开箱即用”，让机器人团队回归到运动算法与产品定义本身。
（左起：芯驰科技汽车和具身解决方案资深总监何文、芯驰科技创始人兼董事长仇雨菁、瑞莎计算机创始人兼董事长汤亮、瑞莎计算机联合创始人兼总经理王培瑶）
基于本次合作，芯驰科技以“车规级可靠性+开放硬件生态+开箱即用工程化”的三重底座，帮助机器人公司打造一颗从原型到量产都能用的运动控制核心。
芯驰科技为RoboX D9M提供核心计算平台D9-Max。该SoC配备12核CPU与8 TOPS NPU，内置3对Cortex-R5/R5F，支持LPDDR4X（4266Mbps）与eMMC 5.1（HS400ES），功能安全符合ISO 26262 ASIL-B。
截至目前，芯驰车规芯片累计出货超1400万片，服务70余家汽车品牌、170余款车型。此次将车规级算力下沉至机器人小脑，是芯驰“从汽车芯片到具身智能”战略升级的关键落子。
瑞莎（Radxa）品牌成立于2012年，总部位于深圳，专注于主板、系统级模组、边缘计算平台及网络计算设备的研发与产品化。公司秉持开放与开源理念，为全球开发者、企业客户与生态伙伴提供软硬件产品及技术支持，加速产品开发与部署。瑞莎持续布局边缘AI、机器人与具身智能，为智能设备的感知、推理与控制提供计算平台，致力于成为连接AI与真实世界的智能体硬件平台服务商。RoboX D9M是瑞莎在具身智能领域推出的首款专用运动控制器，面向人形与轮式机器人厂商提供从板卡到SDK的完整方案，让机器人团队无需重复造轮子。
依托瑞莎在硬件设计、嵌入式软件与全球开发者生态方面的深厚积累，RoboX D9M在 100×100mm 紧凑尺寸内原生集成EtherCAT、多路CAN-FD、RS485等工业总线接口，预装Linux 6.12.31、Ubuntu 26.04 LTS、与ROS 2 Lyrical等主流开源机器人软件栈，开箱即可对接人形机器人、四足机器人、协作机械臂等具身智能终端。
RoboX D9M控制器实物 · 100×100mm · 原生集成EtherCAT / CAN-FD / RS485
芯驰科技创始人兼董事长仇雨菁表示：“芯驰启动‘从汽车芯片到具身智能’的战略升级，D9-Max是这一战略落地的核心载体。我们很高兴与瑞莎走到一起。他们用长期技术积淀把国产开源硬件做成了全球开发者的标配语言，这恰恰是具身智能产业最稀缺的工程化能力。芯驰的车规级算力底座叠加上瑞莎的开源工程化能力，为每一家机器人公司提供一颗”拿起来就能用“的运动控制核心，加速具身智能产品从原型到量产落地。”
瑞莎计算机创始人汤亮表示：“瑞莎的使命一直是‘把复杂留给自己、把简单交给开发者’。RoboX D9M把车规级SoC引入具身智能小脑控制器产品线，背后是芯驰多年在汽车功能安全、宽电压、宽温域上的工程积累，也是瑞莎多年来沉淀的开源硬件工程化能力。我们看到国内机器人公司今天最大的痛点不是算力够不够，而是‘从样机到量产’之间的可靠性鸿沟——这恰恰是车规级芯片叠加开源工程化的看家本领。我们非常期待与芯驰一起，让国产机器人小脑控制器走进全球开发者的工作台。”

title: Closing the White Space Gap in Global Supply Chains
content:
Closing the White Space Gap in Global Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Infios is working to close the gap between AI adoption. Credit: Infios
The biggest gap in supply chain technology right now is not at the top of the market or among smaller businesses, but the middle
If you run supply chain execution for a business between US$100m and US$2.5bn in revenue, you know the squeeze. You are carrying enterprise-grade complexity — multiple regions, multiple systems, constant disruption — without an enterprise-sized team or budget to absorb it. You earned that complexity one reasonable decision at a time: a new channel here, a new geography there, B2B and B2C running side by side. Each made sense on its own. Together, they built an operation that looks like a Tier 1 enterprise, but often still runs on a tech stack built for a smaller, simpler company.
That is the white space in supply chain technology: companies large enough to face
enterprise-level execution complexity
, but often underserved by tools built for either the largest enterprises or much smaller businesses. Software gets designed for one end of the revenue spectrum or the other. The middle inherits what is left over.
The gap is not in your planning, but in your execution
Most of the time, you already know something changed. You have the forecast, the alert, the dashboard telling you a shipment is late or a site is short on labor. Detection usually is not the problem. The problem is what happens next: getting from that signal to a coordinated response across execution domains that do not naturally share context.
Orders, warehouse and transportation each run as their own world, with their own data and their own logic. When a carrier slips, it is not only a transportation problem. It is a warehouse labor problem, an inventory problem and a customer-promise problem at the same time. But the signal does not cross those domains on its own. Someone has to carry it by hand: pulling data out of one system and into another, working the phones and deciding who owns the trade off.
That coordination is where the time goes, and where the cost lands.
Supply chains rarely break in planning
. They break in execution: in the handoffs between systems that were never designed to talk to each other. The delay is not that no one saw the disruption. It is how long it takes to coordinate a response across those execution domains and act before it reaches a customer.
Omar Akilah, Senior Vice President, Product & Industry Strategy at Infios
Enterprise complexity, without enterprise resources
Large enterprises absorb those gaps with money and people. They have dedicated teams whose entire job is stitching systems together. In the mid-market, that team often does not exist. What
fills the gap instead
is workaround after workaround: another point solution, a third-party integrator bridging the OMS and ERP, an analyst reconciling numbers across systems that should reconcile themselves. Each fix looks reasonable on its own. Stacked together, they become the problem. The bill arrives quietly through licensing, integration upkeep, manual labor, error rates and decisions made a day too late. The margin you were trying to protect erodes as you grow. Complexity scales, but the cost of managing it scales faster.
The industry is starting to put a number on the gap between the moment a signal changes and the moment the business acts on it. In a 2026 study, Incisiv quantified it at more than five cents on every dollar of revenue, an estimated US$55m a year for a US$1bn business. But you do not need a study to recognise the cost. You have lived it every time a promise that looked safe at 9:00am was gone by lunch.
Infios aims to connect orders across one system. Credit: Infios
What AI actually changes here
For years, coordinated execution across orders, warehouse and transportation was something you could only get by building it yourself, the way Tier 1 enterprises did: with custom integrations and the teams to run them. That is what kept it out of reach for the middle. AI changes the economics of that.
Here is the distinction that matters: AI does not eliminate the need for coordinated execution. It makes coordinated execution more valuable.
First, orders, warehouse and transportation have to work from a shared execution foundation, so data and action are available across the business instead of trapped inside each system. That foundation is real work, and AI does not replace it.
Second, AI changes how the business uses that foundation. It can interpret signals, assemble context across domains, recommend or decide on a response, and orchestrate action within the rules the business has set. The expensive part was rarely the insight alone. It was the manual reconciliation and orchestration in between, and that is the part AI can take on.
That shift has a name: Intelligent Supply Chain Execution. Instead of three execution domains that transact in isolation and reconcile after the fact, orders, warehouse and transportation operate as one coordinated model: sensing a change, deciding on a response, acting across the connected systems, and learning from the outcome, all within the boundaries the business defines. It extends the systems already in place rather than replacing them.
That matters because mid-market leaders do not need to jump straight from manual coordination to full autonomy. Trust in AI is being earned in stages, and the market is moving that way on purpose. In Relex's State of Supply Chain 2026, 67% of leaders say they have grown more confident in AI over the past year, and just 3% report a decline; only about 10% trust it to make a critical decision without a human reviewing it first. Leaders trust AI to inform a decision well before they trust it to make one, and that is exactly the right instinct.
How it works in practice
For mid-market companies, the practical path is not to replace every system. It is to connect the execution workflows that create the most friction and apply intelligence where coordination breaks down.
That is the problem Infios is working to solve. Infios AI powers Intelligent Supply Chain Execution by helping teams sense what is happening across the supply chain, decide the best course of action, act faster and learn from the outcome. Infios Archer is the agentic execution system that turns that intelligence into coordinated decisions and action, using AI
agents that operate
within defined guardrails, inside and across supply chain workflows.
Autonomy is earned, not assumed. You extend it the same way you would with a new hire. It moves in stages: first, agents that recommend an action with a clear rationale; then agents that execute within policies your team has already defined; and eventually, once the trust is there, agents that run a workflow end to end inside guardrails.
You do not hand over the operation on day one. Start with your highest-friction workflow, such as transportation exceptions or order changes, prove the value there and expand from it.
The model is not theoretical. In production, one global apparel brand cut order release from eight hours to eight minutes; a US online retailer reduced backorders by 70%; a logistics provider reached an 83% autonomy rate on automated order entry. In each case, the systems were not replaced. They were made to work as one.
There is a new execution model. Credit: Infios
Coordinated execution becomes the advantage
The next few years will separate the companies that
coordinate execution from the ones
that keep managing around the gap.
The businesses that pull ahead will be the ones that can sense change as it happens, coordinate a response across their systems in real time, and protect both the customer promise and the margin while conditions keep moving. The ones that do not will keep buying workarounds and keep paying for complexity through manual coordination, slower decisions and margin erosion.
Closing the white space gap will not be about adding more software. It will be about making the systems you already run act as one, so the technology finally follows the strategy instead of setting its limits.
About the author
Omar Akilah is SVP, Product & Industry Strategy at Infios, where he helps shape product direction and industry strategy across the company’s supply chain execution portfolio. A proven transformational leader, Omar brings a deep understanding of how  technology, operations and evolving industry needs intersect, and how organisations can apply the principles of Intelligent Supply Chain Execution to turn complexity into business advantage.
Throughout his career, Omar has led innovation across inventory visibility, omnichannel fulfillment, buy-online/pick-up-in-store, ship-from-store, last- mile delivery and operational execution to promise. He has a unique ability to translate tactical challenges into strategic opportunities, identify areas for re-engineering and align cross-functional teams, around scalable capabilities that deliver meaningful customer and business value.
Omar has worked at leading brands, including Apple, Target, Ingram Micro and Yantriks. His expertise spans Product Management, eCommerce, Direct-to-Consumer innovation, Last Mile strategy, global logistics, omnichannel fulfillment, last-mile strategy and 3PL integration. He also has deep experience in OMS, WMS, and TMS and ERP implementations. A strategic and collaborative leader, Omar brings together customer insight, industry expertise and technology strategy to help organizations improve execution focus across retail, logistics, and the broader supply chain ecosystem to prepare them for what comes next.

title: How Accenture and osapiens Prep DS Smith for EUDR
content:
How Accenture and osapiens Prep DS Smith for EUDR
Prioritise Us
on Google
Accenture and osapiens have worked with DS Smit to trace the origin and movement of European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR)-relevant materials across its supply chain. Credit: Getty Images
Matias Pollmann-Larsen, Global Risk lead at Accenture, says DS Smith's supply chain overhaul spans 250 plants in 30 countries
Accenture and osapiens have worked with DS Smith, a leading international sustainable
packaging company
, to trace the origin and movement of European Union Deforestation Regulation of relevant materials across its Europe, Middle East and Africa supply chain.
The programme covers more than 250 plants and facilities in more than 30 countries.
Together, Accenture and osapiens aim to give DS Smith clear, auditable proof of where the materials in its
packaging come from
, ahead of the regulation's enforcement.
Matias Pollmann-Larsen, Global Risk, Resilience and Sustainable Value Chain lead at Accenture, says: “What DS Smith has done with Accenture and osapiens is build the data foundation needed to stay ahead of these challenges, rather than simply responding to the next regulation when it arrives.”
Key facts: DS Smith's EUDR Programme
Accenture and osapiens have partnered with DS Smith to trace EUDR-relevant materials across its supply chain
The programme spans more than 250 plants and facilities in over 30 countries
Nearly 25,000 supply chain workflows are now managed through the osapiens HUB platform
Suppliers are onboarded digitally, with compliance data managed through one centralised system
Wood fibre, DS Smith's principal material, falls within EUDR's scope alongside commodities like cocoa and palm oil
Matias Pollmann-Larsen, Global Risk, Resilience and Sustainable Value Chain lead at Accenture. Credit: Content Publishing
Inside DS Smith's EUDR traceability programme
DS Smith, Accenture and osapiens
reviewed sourcing
, manufacturing, logistics and sales processes across the company's EMEA operations.
Sakis Miliotis, IT director for Paper, Paper Supply Chain, Recycling and Sustainability at DS Smith, says: “Working with Accenture and osapiens, we have built something that works at scale.”
Accenture drove process transformation, supplier enablement, systems integration and programme scaling, while osapiens supplied the technology platform behind the initiative.
Previously separate supply chain systems, onboarding and reporting processes were consolidated onto a single platform, the osapiens HUB.
Nearly 25,000 supply chain workflows are now managed through the osapiens HUB platform.
Suppliers are onboarded digitally, with traceability and
compliance data managed
through one centralised system.
The company can trace EUDR-relevant materials from origin through production and distribution.
The work establishes a foundation for DS Smith to meet future sustainability and product compliance requirements beyond EUDR itself.
Working with Accenture and osapiens, we have built something that works at scale
Sakis Miliotis, IT director for Paper, Paper Supply Chain, Recycling and Sustainability at DS Smith
Deforestation rules and compliance
Under the EU Deforestation Regulation, large and medium operators and traders must comply from 30 December 2026, with most smaller enterprises given until 30 June 2027.
The rules require a Due Diligence Statement for every product batch, submitted through the EU's TRACES system.
Each batch must include GPS-verified geolocation of all plots, supplier documentation and a deforestation
risk assessment
“Nearly 80% of supply chain leaders tell us that uncertain geopolitical regulatory requirements have made operating their businesses more difficult over the past six months. That pressure is not going away,” says Matias.
Meeting these requirements is a key focus for businesses, as non-compliance carries a minimum fine of 4% of a company's annual EU turnover.
Operators sourcing from higher-risk countries face stricter punishments, with authorities required to inspect at least 9% of relevant operators by volume in those cases.
According to Kolvita, around 30% of upstream actors currently have
traceability systems
in place capable of meeting the regulation's plot-level requirements.
Incomplete or inaccurate geolocation data is one of the most common reasons for the rejection of due diligence statements.
DS Smith's own commodity exposure, principally wood fibre for its packaging, sits squarely within EUDR's scope, alongside cocoa, coffee, palm oil, rubber, soya and cattle.

title: M&S and New Look Partner for Circular Textile Value Chains
content:
M&S and New Look Partner for Circular Textile Value Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Leading brands are collaborating to bring greater resilience and sustainability to textile value chains. Credit: Wokephoto17
Lynda Petherick, CEO at New Look, explores how The Circuit is a collaborative opportunity to bring resilience and sustainability to UK textile value chains
The UK fashion and textile industry contributes £62bn (US$82.15bn) to the UK economy, according to Oxford Economics and the UK Fashion and Textile Association (UKFT).
According to the report, it supports 1.3 million jobs and is one of the largest sectors in the country.
However, the industry also has a major environmental impact, which is why some of the major UK retailers are teaming up to
launch a collaborative model designed
to bring greater circularity into the UK’s fashion industry.
An industry concern
As the fashion industry falls under increasing levels of scrutiny for its emissions and global impact, organisations around the world are working to integrate initiatives or collaborative efforts to minimise their impact.
In the UK, approximately 1.4 million tonnes of post-consumer textiles were generated in 2024. Out of this, almost half is non-reusable. This demonstrates a need for greater investment in the infrastructure which can recover, reuse and recycle textile resources.
Consumers are beginning to turn more towards
second-hand clothing items
, rather than buying at full price from the retailer. Circularity is becoming more of a priority for consumers and businesses alike, as it is seen as a more sustainable way of purchasing, as well as a more cost-efficient format.
To transform how waste is managed in the UK, five companies are teaming up to generate new life in fashion.
New Look, M&S, Sainsbury’s and Oxfam have partnered with Circle-8, announcing the launch of The Circuit. This is a new collaborative model, designed to bring together retailers, textile recovery partners, automated sorting, recyclers, digital innovators and manufacturers. The aim is to transform the UK’s generated post-consumer textiles into future circular raw materials, building new circular textile value chains.
“If we want circularity to become a meaningful part of the fashion industry, we need to move beyond ambition and start building the infrastructure and partnerships that can make it work,” Lynda Petherick, CEO at New Look, explains to Supply Chain Digital.
Lynda Petherick, CEO at New Look
“The Circuit partnership is an opportunity to make this work in practice, bringing different parts of the industry together to find new uses for textiles that might
otherwise go to waste
. For New Look, being involved means learning now, and helping to shape solutions that can work at scale, and building greater resilience into our supply chain for the future.”
Textile waste numbers
Every year, the UK discards around 336,000 tonnes of clothing every year (WRAP)
Approximately, 100 billion clothing items are made each year (McKinsey)
The fashion industry contributes an estimated 10% of global carbon emissions (UNEP)
Approximately 92 million tonnes of waste come from the fashion industry every year (UNEP)
Less than 1% of all textiles are recycled around the world (European Parliament)
Developing innovative pathways
Due to the increasing number of synthetic materials being used in clothing, much of it cannot be recycled or re-used. As a result, the initiative is looking to
transform the potential of these waste textiles
and develop them into something new. The first phase of the collaboration will be testing, learning and developing what is needed in order to create operations that can be scaled.
New solutions are needed to recover and recycle these materials, as the systems needed for post-consumer textiles are still emerging.
"The Circuit is an important step forward, bringing together organisations from across the retail industry to help create viable routes for non-reusable textiles and support a more circular future for fashion,” explains Katharine Beacham, Head of Sustainability & Materials in Fashion, Home & Beauty at M&S.
Katharine Beacham, Head of Sustainability & Materials in Fashion, Home & Beauty at M&S
The Circuit is designed to develop new pathways into this recovery process, looking to sort and pre-process discarded textiles. These can be on a small scale, but the collaborative initiative is aiming to develop this significantly.
With large brands involved, alongside companies across the value chain – such as manufacturers, second-hand retailers and recyclers – The Circuit is working towards consistency, scale and supported commercial conditions which can accelerate textile recycling viability.
Ben Smith, Managing Director of Sainsbury's Tu Clothing, adds, "Creating a more circular future for textiles will take collaboration and innovation across the whole industry. The Circuit is an exciting opportunity to work alongside partners from across the value chain to explore how post-consumer textiles generated here in the UK can be given a new life as
valuable raw materials
Ben Smith, Managing Director at Sainsbury's TU
Integrating circularity
Fashion value chains are undergoing a period of transformation, and this initiative will guide it towards a positive one. As more consumers are buying second-hand or thinking more consciously about where their clothing comes from, this responsible process enables buyers to have new clothes with the environmental responsibility of old ones.
The UK economy will see significant benefit from this initiative, as there will be greater job creation and manufacturing opportunities. Alongside this, there will be automated sorting and pre-processing. This will take place close to where the textiles are generated, therefore turning it into feedstock for regional and global supply chains.
Through this initiative, there will be a development of mechanical and chemical recycling processes, which will transform post-consumer textiles into raw materials. This then allows even more innovative production to take place, as manufacturers will have a clean slate for production.
The materials will have increased routes to markets and there will be a heightened number of products from recovered materials.
Rachel Cosgrove-Pearce, Retail Director at Oxfam, explains, “Developing the infrastructure to recover valuable fibres from end-of-use textiles is an important part of building a fashion system that uses fewer virgin resources and creates less environmental harm, and The Circuit brings together the expertise and investment needed to move this forward at scale.”
Rachel Cosgrove-Pearce, Retail Director at Oxfam
Circle-8 is developing the infrastructure, partnerships and commercial frameworks for the initiative, driving a connected network for the project. It is working to connect post-consumer textile recovery with future circular material supply, meaning there will be a feedstock for existing and emerging textile recyclers.
“The retailers who help build circular textile value chains today will be best positioned to influence and benefit from them tomorrow,” adds Cyndi Rhoades, CEO and Co-Founder of Circle-8 Textile Ecosystems.
Cyndi Rhoades, CEO and Co-Founder of Circle-8 Textile Ecosystems
“Through The Circuit, we’re powering the relationships, infrastructure and commercial frameworks needed to make that possible. No one organisation can create a
circular textile value chain
alone, and we look forward to welcoming others to The Circuit.”
The first phase is set to begin in January 2027, with an initial focus on automated textile sorting. It will also develop a framework for traceability reporting, alongside the ability to identify opportunities, new relationships and scalable operational models.
If we want circularity to become a meaningful part of the fashion industry, we need to move beyond ambition and start building the infrastructure and partnerships that can make it work.
Lynda Petherick, CEO at New Look

New Look is a British fast-fashion retailer founded in 1969, targeting young women and men with trend-led, affordable clothing. Operating both physical stores and online, the brand has faced financial challenges in recent years, undergoing restructuring and store closures. Known for accessible prices and quick trend turnaround, New Look competes with brands like H&M and Zara in the value fashion segment.

title: Industrial Accelerator Act: industry may fail to meet battery demand in EU - electrive.com
content:
The EU is currently debating a draft of the 'Industrial Accelerator Act' (IAA), which aims to boost production and competitiveness within the Union. The ACEA has now presented a study examining whether the European battery supply chain would even be capable of meeting the requirements of this legislative package.
Battery production at VW subsidiary PowerCo in Salzgitter.
Image: PowerCo
The European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) commissioned analysts from Mobility Global to conduct a study, which has now resulted in a 19-page executive summary entitled ‘IAA Impact Assessment: European Battery Supply Chain Outlook’. The paper assesses the potential impact on companies in the battery sector and the broader automotive industry if the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) is implemented as proposed by the Commission
in March
. Importantly, the law has not yet been finalised, as negotiations in the European Parliament and Council are still ongoing.
The study’s core message is that stringent localisation requirements for battery production alone are insufficient to guarantee the practical establishment of a battery value chain in Europe. The analysts identify “deeper structural obstacles to localising battery production”, which could take years to overcome.
To break it down: according to the proposed IAA draft, requirements for batteries used in Europe would be introduced in two phases. Six months after the law enters into force (around 2027–2028, according to the study authors), batteries would need to include three EU-sourced components, including battery cells. Three years after adoption (around 2030–2031), this number would increase to five EU-sourced components, including battery cells, battery management systems, and active cathode materials.
Mobility Global examined three scenarios with varying levels of industrial demand for European batteries. The result: in all scenarios, supply cannot keep pace with demand – despite the expected growth of European battery cell production to 306 GWh by 2032. This means that, in the medium term, there will not be enough IAA-compliant batteries to fully supply the electric vehicle industry in the European Union. The study focuses on the next ten years.
ACEA concludes: “Limited supply will remain the key constraint to expanding the number of cars that would be eligible for “made in the EU” incentives. For example, around 3 million cars may be unable to qualify for the associated incentives because of the lack of supply if the IAA enters into force in 2028.” (The so-called “Made in the EU” subsidies are another aspect of the legislative package aimed at ensuring that national programmes primarily subsidise the EU’s own economy.)
ACEA further emphasises that the challenge is even more pronounced for medium- and heavy-duty commercial vehicles than for passenger cars: “The supply-demand gap continues to widen through 2032, reaching 23 GWh, with demand around four times available European supply,” according to a key finding of the study.
The association highlights that the battery value chain in the EU currently has weak structures. The analysts list the following specific issues:
Most planned European gigafactories are focused on NMC batteries, while demand is increasingly shifting towards more cost-effective LFP batteries.
Cells produced in Europe remain significantly more expensive than imported ones.
Announced production capacities are subject to financing, approval, and implementation risks. Announced capacities should therefore not be equated with operational capacities.
Further upstream, Europe continues to face persistent shortages of cathode and anode active materials (CAM/AAM). The analysis suggests that this deficit may only be resolved between 2038 and 2040, even in a low-demand scenario.
ACEA concludes that the results “underline the need for a realistic and economically viable approach to localisation”. The effectiveness of the IAA will ultimately depend not only on the ambition of its requirements but also on “whether Europe can build the upstream capacity, competitive operating conditions and investment framework needed to deliver them in practice”.
The association supplements its assessment with recommendations on how to bridge the gap between ambition and reality. ACEA advises:
Massive upstream investments: To produce CAM and AAM locally and meet demand, substantial investments must be targeted at building foundational upstream components – such as facilities for precursor cathode active material (pCAM) production and graphite purification (AAM).
Shift in policy towards operational support: Policymakers must move beyond merely funding factory construction and begin subsidising ongoing operating costs – particularly high energy costs – while also fast-tracking environmental permits to accelerate project timelines.
Leverage global partnerships and near-shoring: Current EU policy remains highly ambiguous, with unclear “rules of origin” that do not specify whether near-shoring free trade partners like Morocco are treated as equivalent to local EU production. Clarifying these rules to formally include strategic free trade partners is essential; this would enable Europe to avoid high domestic energy costs and utilise international joint ventures to close the material gap.
(Study, PDF)

title: $20.7B US deal boosts AMRAAM missile output to record 1,900 yearly
content: Raytheon is preparing to push AMRAAM production to unprecedented levels after securing a multiyear U.S. defense contract worth up to $20.7 billion.The agreement covers five years of production and includes two option years. It could support annual output of at least 1,900 AMRAAM missiles.The U.S. Department of War awarded the deal Sept. 25 as part of its Arsenal of Freedom initiative. The effort aims to expand American weapons manufacturing and give the military greater access to critical munitions.Raytheon’s production push comes as the United States and its allies seek larger missile inventories. The company nearly doubled AMRAAM output in 2025 compared with 2024.Bigger AMRAAM pipelineAMRAAM has become a central part of the U.S. inventory for beyond-visual-range air combat. The missile also serves as the interceptor used by the NASAMS air-defense system.Raytheon President Phil Jasper said the company is increasing capacity across several parts of its manufacturing operation.“We continue to make significant investments in our workforce, technology, supply chain and facilities,” Jasper said. He pointed to rising demand from the U.S. Air Force, Navy and international customers.Reaching 1,900 missiles each year will put considerable pressure on the production network behind AMRAAM. The missile depends on a broad ecosystem of American suppliers that feed components into the program. RTX says hundreds of small and midsize suppliers already support its operations. The company is also exploring international co-production as demand expands.That industrial network matters because increasing missile output involves more than speeding up final assembly. Suppliers must also expand their own capacity and maintain a steady flow of components.A multiyear order gives those manufacturers a clearer view of future demand. That visibility can make it easier to justify investments in equipment, workers, and additional production capacity.Missile keeps evolvingAMRAAM has reached its fifth generation since entering service. The missile now operates across 14 platforms and serves 44 countries. More than 7,000 successful live fires have taken place during testing and combat. Its continued use reflects the missile’s ability to support different air-combat and air-defense requirements.Newer AMRAAM variants feature upgraded processors that allow engineers to introduce software changes more rapidly. Those updates can help the weapon adapt as threats and electronic-warfare techniques evolve.The missile combines guidance capabilities with electronic protection for operations in contested environments. Its architecture supports engagements where aircraft and weapons face increasingly complex countermeasures.AMRAAM’s ground-based role adds another dimension to the production requirement. NASAMS uses the missile to provide air defense against airborne threats.That means a single missile family supports two distinct operational environments. Fighters can carry AMRAAM for air-to-air engagements, while ground systems can use it for air defense.Pentagon expands missile capacityThe new award fits into a larger U.S. effort to expand domestic weapons production. The Department of War says AMRAAM represents one of several programs supporting that industrial push.“We are working across the defense industry to ramp production and build the Arsenal of Freedom,” said Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael P. Duffey. Duffey said the award will help equip U.S. forces and allied militaries with an established air-to-air weapon.The Air Force, Navy, and Foreign Military Sales partners are participating in the broader procurement effort. The arrangement also relies on congressional authority for multiyear AMRAAM procurement.

title: 3D-printed gas turbine nozzle burns hydrogen, kerosene and natural gas
content: A new 3D-printed injection system created by scientists in Germany could allow compact gas turbines to cleanly burn a wide range of fuels, including hydrogen, kerosene, methanol, natural gas, and other e-fuels. The so-called injection nozzle was built by Fabian Hampp, PhD, a junior research group leader at the University of Stuttgart’s Institute of Combustion Technology for Aerospace Engineering (IVLR), and his team. The system can handle different fuels while limiting emissions and manufacturing costs.To create the gas turbine injector, the team utilized additive manufacturing (or 3D printing). Hampp revealed that the team plans to turn the laboratory-tested tech, which is compatible with fuels with different physical properties, into a prototype and put it through real-world testing. “It is no longer unusual to use additive manufacturing to construct gas turbines,” Hampp said. “However, this has generally not been the case for one of the most important components, the injection systems that spray fuel into the combustion chamber.” Built for different fuelsGas turbines can act as fast-responding backup generators (peaker plants) which stabilize the grid when solar and wind generation drops. However, reducing their carbon footprint could require replacing natural gas with hydrogen, methanol, or other e-fuels.That is a huge challenge, as hydrogen, natural gas, and relatively viscous kerosene behave very differently. These differences make it difficult for a single injector to achieve the fuel-air mixing needed for clean combustion.To address the challenge, the team adapted an injection principle used in aircraft turbines for the new injector. The technology can also tackle soot and nitrogen oxide emissions, which form when fuel and air are not mixed sufficiently. Injection systems therefore need to create a very fine fuel mist and distribute it evenly through the combustion chamber. “However, the special design of our nozzles makes it possible to cleanly burn a wide range of fuels,” Hampp noted.Fixing rough surfacesAccording to the researchers, manufacturing small injection systems using additive manufacturing has historically been difficult because metal 3D printing does not create perfectly smooth surfaces. In laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), a 3D printing method, a laser selectively melts layers of metal powder to form complex internal passages and cavities.The rough surfaces can cause problems when precise amounts of fuel must pass through tiny openings as a fine mist. “The problem is that the surfaces of these printed structures are never completely smooth,” Hans-Christian Möhring, PhD, the director of the university’s Institute for Machine Tools, said in a statement. The new system can work even with these imperfections. Möhring explained that this showed the team that very clean combustion was possible in the lab. Additive manufacturing could also lower production costs. Burners and combustion chambers are already commonly manufactured with the technology, meaning the injection system could potentially be integrated directly into those components. The technology could eventually be used to retrofit older gas turbines. This would enable already existing equipment to operate with different energy sources.The researchers now plan to optimize the additive manufacturing process and nozzle geometry before building a prototype. They also intend to test it with different fuels under real-world conditions.

title: 835 MW US reactor shut in 2019 passes environmental review for restart
content: A US nuclear reactor that stopped generating power in 2019 has passed an environmental review tied to its proposed restart. The Christopher Crane Clean Energy Center in Pennsylvania, formerly known as Three Mile Island unit 1, could return 835 MW of power to the grid in 2027.The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) and the Department of Energy’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing issued an environmental assessment and a finding of no significant impact for proposed federal actions related to reauthorizing power operations. The finding clears an environmental review step, but Constellation Energy still needs NRC approval to resume generation.What the environmental finding coversThe NRC evaluated the reasonably foreseeable environmental effects of the proposed federal actions. It released a draft environmental assessment and draft finding of no significant impact for public comment in June before issuing the final documents.The NRC served as the lead agency for the review, while the Office of Energy Dominance Financing participated as a cooperating agency. The latter closed a $1 billion loan to Constellation Energy Generation last year to help finance the reactor’s restart.The environmental finding does not itself reauthorize power operations. Constellation has submitted a request for an exemption and three license amendment requests for NRC approval, all aimed at allowing the reactor to operate again.A reactor with an existing licenseThree Mile Island unit 1 shut down for decommissioning in 2019, although its renewed operating license was valid until April 19, 2034. Constellation is seeking approval to resume operations through that existing expiration date and has previously said it will look to extend operations to 2054.The closure was driven by economics. Then-owner Exelon said the plant had lost money for more than five years as low wholesale electricity prices reduced its revenue. It also failed to secure payments in three consecutive regional capacity auctions. Exelon argued that existing market rules did not adequately value nuclear power’s emissions-free generation, while proposed Pennsylvania policy changes failed to advance in time.The reactor is separate from Three Mile Island unit 2, the site of the 1979 accident. Constellation’s restart plan concerns unit 1, which operated for decades after the accident before its 2019 closure.Returning a closed reactor to service requires more than preparing its equipment. Constellation must also obtain the regulatory approvals needed to resume power operations, making the environmental finding one part of a wider restart process.Constellation targets a 2027 returnConstellation says work at the plant is progressing ahead of schedule. Employees, contractors, skilled craft workers and local partners are preparing the facility to generate electricity again.“Thanks to their dedication, the restart remains ahead of schedule, and we’re on track to return 835 megawatts of dependable, emissions-free power to the grid in 2027,” the company told World Nuclear News.The proposed restart would restore a source of nuclear generation in central Pennsylvania that has been offline for seven years. For now, the key remaining question is whether the NRC grants Constellation’s exemption and license amendment requests, allowing the plant to move from restart preparations back to power operations.

title: Advancing nuclear reactors: Argonne tests passive decay heat removal
content: Even when a nuclear reactor goes dark, it is not truly asleep. The chain reaction stops instantly, but a residual thermal ghost remains behind. Scientists call it decay heat. Unchecked, this persistent energy can warp steel, melt components, and turn a routine shutdown into a crisis.Now, researchers at the US Department of Energy’s Argonne National Laboratory are proving that we don’t need electricity or human intervention to keep it under control. But what’s required is just the simple, unyielding laws of physics.In a series of tests, engineers mapped out the behavior of a passive safety setup known as the Reactor Cavity Cooling System (RCCS) when heat levels fluctuate violently in real time.“Most advanced reactor vendors rely on passive systems like RCCS to prove their designs can stay safe even during unlikely accident scenarios,” said Argonne Nuclear Engineer Qiuping Lu. ​“Our experiments give them the high‑quality data they need to show regulators that their safety systems will perform as expected.”Pump-free cooling Even after a nuclear reactor shuts down, residual decay heat continues to radiate from the core and requires reliable, continuous cooling. ANL researchers evaluated the RCCS, a passive setup that circulates water through surrounding metal tubes using natural buoyancy and gravity rather than mechanical pumps. Warmer water rises toward an elevated storage tank while cooler liquid descends, carrying heat away without human or electrical intervention. This design was tested at the 59-foot Natural Convection Shutdown Heat Removal Test Facility, which revealed how liquid water and steam interact during realistic power shifts. It provided key data on system performance during boiling conditions. Argonne researchers simulated these real-world fluctuations at the NSTF facility through controlled tests across a range of scaled power levels. They also adjusted the height of the main water tank inlet, a key design variable that dictates total water availability and alters natural circulation patterns throughout the cooling loop.“We were asking two questions,” Lu said. ​“What happens when decay heat is higher or lower than designers expect? And does moving the tank connection up or down change how reliably the system runs?”Lower heat delays dangerous surgesDuring multi-hour power increases in the 59-foot NSTF testing loop, researchers monitored how water heated, boiled, and produced steam under simulated reactor conditions. And focused on “flashing”, a phenomenon where rising water vaporizes suddenly into steam due to dropping pressure rather than added heat. These sudden steam bursts induce flow surges and pressure swings that reduce cooling efficiency and stress reactor components, prompting to map out exactly where these instabilities originate, peak, and dissipate.The findings revealed two insights for designing the next generation of nuclear power. At a full-scale equivalent power of 2.4 megawatts, steam from flashing surged into the upper chimney just 20 minutes after boiling started. Drop that power to 1.75 megawatts, and the steam took 90 minutes. At 1.4 megawatts, the steam never reached the chimney.Tank inlet placement also strongly influenced overall stability. Mid-level inlets stabilized rapidly within 15 minutes, whereas lower inlets produced continuous flashing-induced instability throughout testing.It turns out that a few feet of pipe alignment can mean the difference between chaotic fluid surges and smooth, self-correcting cooling.These findings provide the concrete evidence necessary to satisfy strict nuclear regulations and streamline the global deployment of safer, meltdown-proof clean energy systems.

title: China unveils world's first robot designed to stay safe during faults
content: China has unveiled what it describes as the world’s first embodied AI robot equipped with a fully domestically developed electronic architecture. The robot was presented Monday in Yichang, Hubei Province, according to CCTV News.The architecture connects the robot’s AI decision-making with its physical actions. Its developers say the system offers a domestic alternative to foreign technologies used in this critical layer of robotics.The unveiling comes as China seeks greater control over the systems beneath its growing robotics industry. Developers also reported that the robot maintained safe operation during tests involving damaged joints, cyberattacks and implanted viruses.The system between thought and movementAn electronic architecture brings together a robot’s operating system, networking, software tools, computing chips and control functions. It determines how decisions made by AI are translated into instructions that the machine can carry out.The developers say their architecture allows control functions and AI computing to operate separately while remaining integrated. They describe it as a domestic foundation extending from AI decision-making to physical execution.“What AI ‘thinks’ is one thing, and what a robot ‘does’ is another. In between, there must be a reliable, secure and controllable underlying system. The electronic architecture is that system,” Li Qingdu, executive dean of the Institute of Machine Intelligence at the University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, told the Global Times.Li said the development reflects a broader shift in China’s robotics industry: from making individual components domestically to developing the underlying architecture that connects them. The announcement did not identify the robot’s manufacturer or provide detailed technical specifications.Safety under simulated failuresTesting personnel evaluated the robot under conditions that included joint damage, cyberattacks, and virus implantation, according to the report. It said robots using conventional electronic architectures suffered circuit failures, sudden shutdowns or loss of control under those conditions.The new robot reportedly continued operating safely. The reported results point to the architecture’s ability to respond quickly, isolate faults, and protect the system when something goes wrong, though the account did not provide test methods or independent verification.Those capabilities matter when robots work near people. Li pointed to concerns raised at robot competitions about possible collisions, arguing that the underlying system must keep a robot within physical and operational safety limits even when it encounters a fault or attack.A broader push for domestic controlThe robot’s electronic architecture is part of China’s effort to build more of its robotics technology at home. According to the developers, it provides an option that could replace foreign solutions for the systems connecting AI computing and machine control.“Localization here is not simply about replacing suppliers across the industrial chain. It is also about gaining autonomous control over the underlying systems of robots,” Li said.China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology called for a secure and reliable industrial and supply chain system by 2027 in a guideline released in 2023. A draft outline of the country’s 15th Five-Year Plan, covering 2026 to 2030, also identifies robotics as an emerging industry for accelerated development.

title: Floating battery brings 40-kW mobile charging to electric boats
content: U.S. electric marine propulsion developer Photon Marine will deploy a floating battery platform capable of bringing high-power charging to electric boats under a $1 million marine electrification project in New York.The company has received the inaugural MegaBoost award from the National Science Foundation Energy Storage Engine in Upstate New York. The project will combine an electric workboat, a 40-kilowatt fast charger, and a mobile floating energy storage system called ChargeBarge.At the center of the demonstration is a 24-foot workboat powered by Photon Marine’s Gen-7 P300 electric propulsion system. The vessel has already operated on the New York State Canal System through a pilot with the New York Power Authority and New York State Canal Corporation.Photon Marine now plans to demonstrate the technologies as one connected system rather than treating electric propulsion, energy storage, and charging infrastructure as separate pieces. The project is expected to culminate in late 2027 or early 2028.Charging takes to waterThe most unusual part of the project is ChargeBarge, a 32-foot floating platform carrying battery energy storage and high-power charging equipment.Instead of requiring permanent fast chargers at every waterfront location, the platform can move stored energy to vessels where it is needed. New York-based Derecktor Shipyards will fabricate the ChargeBarge.The platform is being designed for vessel-to-vessel charging, remote fleet operations and temporary events. Photon Marine also sees potential for supplying emergency power during grid disruptions.A separate 40-kW marine DC fast charger will provide fixed charging infrastructure for electric commercial, government, and recreational vessels operating on New York waterways.“Commercial marine electrification will only scale when operators can see that the technology works in the conditions they face every day,” said Marcelino J. Alvarez, co-founder and CEO of Photon Marine.“This project gives us the opportunity to demonstrate an entire electrification ecosystem, from the propulsion system to the charger to mobile energy storage, while building on the real-world operating experience we have developed with NYPA.”Boats become testbedsCommercial workboats are used for jobs including harbor operations, maintenance, environmental monitoring, and public safety. Electrifying them can be difficult because operators need durable, high-power propulsion as well as charging at waterfront locations that may lack suitable electrical infrastructure.Photon Marine’s approach combines fixed charging with mobile battery storage, potentially allowing fleets to begin electrifying without waiting for a widespread waterfront charging network.The demonstration will collect data on vessel performance, battery state of charge and health, charging use, and duty cycles. Researchers will also examine vessel-to-vessel energy transfers and potential interactions with the power grid.Photon Marine plans to turn those findings into a fleet-electrification playbook that other commercial operators could use when assessing similar systems.“MegaBoost is about closing the gap between a technology that works and a product or system that customers will actually deploy at scale,” said Fernando Gómez-Baquero, director of translation for the NSF Energy Storage Engine in Upstate New York.The $1 million award builds on the Engine’s smaller SuperBoost commercialization program. MegaBoost is intended for technologies that have moved beyond early development and are ready for demonstrations with customers at commercially relevant scales.

title: MIT builds tiny paper-thin robot that swims using living muscle cells
content: MIT engineers have developed a paper-thin swimming robot powered by a single layer of living muscle cells, demonstrating how biohybrid machines could move through water using far less biological material than previous designs.The small robot uses light-responsive muscle tissue grown on a thin gel skeleton to propel itself through water. Researchers demonstrated that it could swim and turn through a simple underwater maze by directing light onto its two fins.The robot can travel approximately four times its own body length in one minute at its fastest speed. While considerably slower than human swimmers, the researchers say the design demonstrates a new way to build small, efficient robots powered by living tissue.How the muscle-powered robot swimsAccording to MIT, The robot’s body consists of a gelatin-based film approximately half a millimeter thick, with two flexible sections that act as fins. Each fin is covered with a layer of living skeletal muscle cells that is thinner than a human hair.The cells are genetically engineered to contract in response to light. When researchers shine light onto one fin, the muscle cells twitch, causing the fin to flap and push the robot through the surrounding water.By directing light onto either fin and adjusting the timing of the illumination, the researchers can control the robot’s direction and speed. Activating both sides causes both fins to move.During testing, the team submerged the robot in a large petri dish and manually moved a light source above it. The robot followed the light as it navigated a maze placed inside the dish.The researchers describe it as the first demonstration of a very thin, two-dimensional, muscle-powered robot capable of locomotion.A different approach to biohybrid roboticsThe new design builds on earlier work by Ritu Raman, an associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, and her research group. In a previous experiment, the team developed an artificial muscle structure inspired by the human iris. Researchers grew muscle cells on a gel disk patterned with concentric and radial grooves. When light stimulated the cells, they contracted in different directions, causing the disk to stretch and squeeze. Although the earlier design demonstrated controllable movement, the displacement was limited to approximately 100 micrometers.For the swimming robot, the researchers needed to generate substantially more force. They found that the material supporting the muscle cells was just as important as the cells themselves.The earlier design used fibrin, an ultrasoft gel that could deform under the forces generated by contracting muscle. In the new study, the team experimented with different gel compositions, stiffness levels, and groove geometries to improve muscle alignment and force production.The researchers found that square-bottomed grooves encouraged the cells to align more effectively than curved grooves. Better alignment helped the cells fuse into muscle fibers that could contract in a more coordinated manner.The team also replaced fibrin with gelatin methacrylate, or GelMA, a material commonly used in tissue engineering. Stiffer formulations supported better cell alignment and stronger contractions.A film approximately half a millimeter thick provided enough structural support for the muscle cells while remaining flexible and light enough to move with them. The researchers also used a training routine involving repeated light stimulation to strengthen the muscle tissue before assembling the robot.Potential applications in aquatic environmentsConventional biohybrid robots often rely on bulky, three-dimensional structures made from millions of lab-grown muscle cells. The MIT team believes its thinner design could reduce the amount of biological material required and potentially improve movement efficiency.Living muscle tissue could eventually help robots perform delicate tasks in environments where conventional hardware may be difficult to deploy. Raman has suggested applications such as exploring fragile or unpredictable environments, including aquatic ecosystems.However, the current robot remains an early research demonstration. The researchers manually controlled its light source, and its swimming speed is still limited. The team says its next goal is to optimize the robot’s body design to swim faster.The findings demonstrate how carefully engineered materials and living muscle cells can work together to produce movement in extremely thin robotic structures, offering a potential foundation for smaller biohybrid machines.The study was published in the journal Advanced Functional Materials.

title: Natural hydrogen reservoirs could be used for underground storage, study suggests
content: Transitioning the world to zero-carbon energy requires storing vast amounts of hydrogen. A new study led by Shanghai Jiao Tong University has suggested that geological formations with naturally trapped hydrogen offer proven containment for large-scale underground energy storage. For instance, take the Albanian chromite mine. Inside this mine, a bubbling pool releases nearly pure hydrogen gas into the air. Energy experts previously dismissed these natural geological anomalies as hazardous and rare. Today, scientists believe these subterranean formations could offer a reliable solution to the clean energy transition’s biggest storage challenge.“The findings suggest that natural hydrogen reservoirs may be viable candidates for underground hydrogen storage,” the researchers stated. Nature’s underground vaultsScaling hydrogen into a major energy source depends largely on securing viable, high-capacity storage sites. Typical subterranean options cannot meet these demands. Salt caverns present severe geographical constraints, while aquifers and depleted hydrocarbon fields lack demonstrated, long-term containment integrity for hydrogen gas. Hence, these conventional options remain inviable for supporting a large-scale hydrogen economy.The Bulqizë reservoir in Albania formed along a massive fault zone. Located within an uplifted section of oceanic crust known as an ophiolite, the Bulqizë reservoir generates its own continuous supply of clean energy. Deep underground, groundwater comes into direct contact with iron-rich minerals such as olivine, triggering a chemical reaction called serpentinization. This natural process splits water molecules and steadily produces pure hydrogen gas within the surrounding rock formations. It has safely trapped hydrogen for thousands of years. That geological track record prompted researchers Lei Hou, Zhengxin Zhang, and Fengshou Zhang to test a bold idea: if nature already built a leak-proof hydrogen vault, why not reuse it as a commercial storage warehouse? Using advanced fluid-flow and underground chemistry models, the research team analyzed 72 different operational scenarios to test the site’s limits. The results were interesting. Natural chemical reactions and dissolution would consume less than two percent of the stored hydrogen, proving the subterranean vault retains gas with exceptional efficiency. Furthermore, the models revealed the reservoir could hold between 350 million and 480 million cubic meters of gas while supporting a daily throughput of 750,000 cubic meters.Fault risk Perhaps the most surprising discovery involves the fault line itself. Pumping gas in and out of a seismic fault line sounds like a recipe for earthquakes, but cyclic testing over a 10-year period showed the exact opposite effect. Standard gas pressure spreads out across the rock formations, homogenizing subterranean forces and actually decreasing the risk of the fault slipping over time.“Over 10 years, hydrogen storage in the reservoir would decrease the risk of the fault slipping by redistributing gas pressure,” the team noted. Utilizing naturally sealed fault zones could also cut the capital investments typically required for hydrogen containment. Energy companies might save substantial capital by tapping naturally occurring subterranean structures rather than excavating artificial caverns or modifying depleted reservoirs.Currently, the study is model-based only. If explored further, this study could open a promising new pathway to global, large-scale clean energy storage by showing that naturally occurring hydrogen traps can double as high-capacity power banks.

title: New geothermal well aims to tap hot rock without using water
content: U.S. geothermal energy developer XGS Energy will drill a deep vertical well in New Mexico to gather underground data needed to develop commercial-scale geothermal power that does not consume water.The U.S. Department of Energy selected the Houston-based company for federal funding as part of a $99 million program covering 21 geothermal projects across the country. XGS will work with Baker Hughes, New Mexico Tech and Sandia National Laboratories on the project.The appraisal well will collect downhole temperature measurements, logging information, core samples and continuous drilling data. XGS plans to use those findings to better understand underground heat resources and design future geothermal wells in the region.The project is particularly relevant to New Mexico because XGS’ geothermal system is designed to operate without consuming water. That could allow developers to tap underground heat in areas where geothermal resources are available but water is scarce.Drilling reveals hidden heatUnlike conventional geothermal projects that depend heavily on naturally occurring underground water, XGS is developing a closed-loop system that circulates a working fluid through sealed wells. Heat is transferred from surrounding rock into the system rather than extracting hot groundwater from underground formations.The upcoming well is primarily an appraisal project rather than a commercial power-producing well. Information collected during drilling will be used to improve thermal and geological models and reduce uncertainty before larger projects are developed.“New Mexico sits on a substantial and exciting geothermal resource, and we’re grateful to the Department of Energy for investing in the subsurface data needed to transform our nation’s abundant geothermal resources into affordable, reliable American energy,” said Lucy Darago, chief commercial officer of XGS Energy.Baker Hughes will bring drilling, formation evaluation and industrial expertise to the project, while New Mexico Tech and the New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources will contribute regional geological and geothermal expertise. Sandia will provide its experience in drilling technology and improving drilling efficiency.“We look forward to drilling this important appraisal well,” said Al Vickers, chief operating officer of XGS Energy. “The geological and operational data we collect in New Mexico will tighten our thermal and geologic models, inform how we design and construct wells across the region, and, in doing so, help us take another important step toward unlocking geothermal resources at scale in New Mexico.”Water limits lose gripNext-generation geothermal technologies are designed to expand geothermal power beyond locations that already have the combination of heat, water and permeable rock required by conventional plants.XGS says its approach separates geothermal energy production from dependence on natural water resources and specific geological conditions. The company ultimately aims to use the technology to provide continuous electricity to the grid in locations with accessible hot rock.The New Mexico project will also examine how drilling can be made more efficient and less expensive. Sandia said its contribution will draw on decades of work involving drill-bit performance, drilling costs and operational efficiency.New Mexico Tech, meanwhile, plans to use experience from the project to support geothermal workforce training, including its geothermal certificate program.The DOE selection does not yet guarantee that XGS will receive federal money. The company must first undergo award negotiations with the department, and DOE can cancel negotiations or withdraw the selection before funding is issued.

title: New stacked chip gives wearables local memory, tops 90% accuracy
content: Korean researchers have developed a vertically stacked semiconductor system that can process both recent and earlier signals, potentially allowing small wearable devices to analyze movements and physiological data without relying heavily on external computing.The technology was developed by researchers at KAIST, UNIST, and POSTECH. It uses carbon nanotube transistors controlled by a solid-state ionogel, a material containing mobile ions that influence how electrical current flows through the device.When voltage is applied, ions move through the material. They do not immediately return to their original positions after the voltage disappears, leaving a temporary electrical “memory” of earlier signals. Instead of treating that delayed response as a limitation, the researchers used it to process information that changes over time.By adjusting the concentration of ions and the thickness of the ionogel, the team created devices with different response speeds. The researchers then vertically stacked fast- and slow-responding devices, allowing different layers to process information over different timescales.Different layers remember differentlyThe faster layer responds more strongly to the latest input, while the slower layer retains information accumulated over a longer period. Combining their outputs therefore gives the system information about both what has just happened and what happened immediately before it.Previous ionic materials used for such devices have often been liquids or soft gels. Those materials can make precise semiconductor fabrication and multilayer stacking difficult. Turning the ionogel into a solid thin film allowed the researchers to better control its properties while building multiple device layers.The team tested whether the hardware could distinguish temporal patterns using four consecutive input signals that could each be switched on or off. The devices successfully differentiated all 16 possible combinations.Researchers also used measurements from the devices to create a simulation for classifying videos of moving handwritten digits. The system achieved validation accuracy above 90 percent when processing moving-image sequences played at different speeds.The approach could eventually help electronics process changing information locally rather than continually transferring raw data elsewhere for analysis. Potential applications include wearable devices monitoring movement and physiological signals.Wearables gain local memoryThe team demonstrated that the technology is compatible with different manufacturing formats. Researchers fabricated the devices on 4-inch wafers as well as flexible substrates, potentially making the architecture suitable for electronics that need to conform to non-flat surfaces.The devices also maintained stable electrical characteristics for 55 months after fabrication, according to the researchers.“These devices can be fabricated on large-area substrates using existing thin-film semiconductor processes, and they can also be stacked in multiple layers,” said Professor Jimin Kwon of KAIST.Kwon said the technology could be developed into chips that analyze movement and physiological signals in low-power devices such as smartwatches.However, the researchers have not yet demonstrated those power savings in an actual smartwatch. Further testing will be needed to determine how the architecture performs and how much energy it can save when integrated into real wearable electronics.The study was published in the journal Advanced Materials.
