title: AI and Battery Technology Take Center Stage at The Battery Show
content:
Market Analysis
Stationary Batteries
Design & Manufacturing
This year's Battery Show features expanded programming on artificial intelligence in battery design, manufacturing, and testing.
September 29, 2026
6 Min Read
Several panel sessions and keynotes at The Battery Show will discuss the challenges of battery storage and performance in AI data centers.
The Battery Show
The number of sessions at
The Battery Show
have been increasing the past few years as the role of AI in helping to design and manufacture more robust batteries has come into play. This year, the growth of data centers for AI infrastructure has not surprisingly prompted several sessions dealing with issues such as battery storage and transients.
Check out the all the related panel sessions and talks at this year’s Battery Show, taking place at Huntington Place in Detroit October 12through 15.
All times stated are Eastern.
AI in the Battery Space: Monetizing IP, Accelerating R&D, and Building Safer Batteries
Monday, October 12 | 9:00 AM - 12:00 PM | Room 140AB
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=254
Across three hours and four panels, practitioners who have actually deployed these tools will show what AI is doing today for battery businesses in terms of raising money, shortening development cycles, catching defects, and protecting intellectual property.
The first panel looks at AI tools that map what you have built to the money that wants it: tools that connect your patent portfolio to government grants and contracts, surface potential licensees, and find funding programs companies did not know they qualified for.
The second panel turns to the engineering bench, where large language models and agent-based tools are collapsing multi-day/week/month analyses into minutes, and where digital-thread platforms are changing how manufacturing data is used.
The third panel examines AI-assisted safety and quality testing — what is genuinely faster, what is marketing, and what it costs to deploy on a real line. The fourth panel, led by intellectual property attorneys, covers patent strategy when AI sits in your workflow, and the disclosure mistakes that quietly void protection.
Attendees leave with named tools, real numbers, and a short list of things to do when they get back to the office.
The Future of Battery Manufacturing: Risks and Opportunities in the Age of AI and Cold War Two
Tuesday, October 13, 11:00 AM - 11:30 AM Grand Ballroom B
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=260
In this keynote session, top-ranked economist, futurist, and bestselling author Jason Schenker examines how AI, reshoring, geopolitical tensions, critical minerals, tariffs, and supply chain risks are reshaping battery manufacturing and investment. Attendees will leave with practical insights on where the greatest opportunities and risks are likely to emerge over the next decade.
AI in Action: Real-World Impact Across the Battery Value Chain
Tuesday, October 13 | 11:00 AM - 11:30 AM | Grand Ballroom B
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=119
This panel brings together leaders across the battery lifecycle — materials R&D, product qualification, and high-volume manufacturing — to share how AI is integrating into their existing flows and delivering measurable impacts today. Moderated by Voltaiq CEO and Co-Founder, Tal Sholklapper, this session offers a rare cross-functional view into how AI is reshaping battery development and operations—and what it means for the future of the industry.
Each of the panelists will provide a grounded, real-world perspective on where AI is working—and where it’s not. The discussion will cut through the AI hype to discuss the tangible outcomes they are seeing in their respective domains: faster product development, improved throughput, reduced risk, and more efficient high-volume manufacturing.
AI, Data Centers, and the Next Energy Storage Supercycle
Tuesday, October 13 | 1:30 PM - 2:30 PM | Room 140CD
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=265
The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is driving unprecedented growth in data center construction, computing infrastructure, and electricity demand. As hyperscale facilities require increasing amounts of reliable, resilient, and continuous power, energy storage is emerging as a critical technology for supporting grid stability, backup power, renewable integration, and future energy security.
This panel will explore how AI is reshaping global energy demand and creating new opportunities for battery storage, grid modernization, and power infrastructure investment. Industry leaders from the energy, data center, utility, and battery sectors will discuss evolving power requirements, the role of energy storage in supporting AI-driven growth, emerging technologies, and the challenges of scaling energy infrastructure to meet future demand.
Attendees will gain insights into the intersection of AI, energy storage, and grid transformation, and why many industry experts view this convergence as the beginning of the next major growth cycle for the energy storage industry.
Batteries Behind AI: The Safety Challenges of Both Distributed and High-Density Energy Storage in Data Centers and how Large-Scale Fire Testing is Changing BESS Deployment
Wednesday, October 14 | 2:00 PM - 2:45 PM | Battery Tech Theater, Booth 6050
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=334
Chris Unangst will explore the critical role that battery energy storage systems play in supporting the rapid growth of artificial intelligence and data centers, while addressing the unique fire and life safety challenges these technologies present. The presentation will highlight how large-scale fire testing is transforming the understanding of battery hazards, providing valuable insights into thermal runaway, fire propagation, and emergency response. Attendees will gain a practical perspective on how testing data is shaping codes, standards, and risk informed design strategies, enabling safer and more efficient deployment of battery energy storage systems in data centers and other mission critical facilities.
Designing Battery Systems to Manage AI Data Center Power Transients: Architecture, Control, and Validation
Tuesday, October 13 | 3:30 PM - 3:50 PM | Room 141
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=61
AI-driven data centers produce some of the most demanding power profiles in modern electrical infrastructure. Training and inference workloads generate rapid, high-amplitude load transients that stress utility grids, trigger costly demand charges, and routinely delay facility interconnection by years. Conventional solutions — oversized grid infrastructure, static power correction, or large-format UPS systems — address the symptom at high capital cost without solving the underlying dynamic.
This presentation describes Beam Global's development of a battery energy storage system specifically architected to manage these transients. Fast-response, coordinated multi-timescale control flattens peak demand toward average load — reducing total power allocation required from the utility, shrinking interconnection requirements, and accelerating deployment timelines. The result is equivalent or superior grid-support performance with significantly reduced battery capacity. Beam's proprietary passive thermal management technology enables the aggressive cycling this application demands without compressing battery lifetime.
This work is being conducted in collaboration with the Intelligent Power Electronics at Grid Edge (IPEG) Laboratory at the University of Illinois Chicago, using real-time simulation and hardware-in-the-loop platforms to emulate realistic AI data-center load profiles. Preliminary findings on transient response, thermal behavior, and battery lifetime under high ramp-rate loading will be shared.
AI Meets Battery Science: Accelerating Materials Discovery with Large Quantitative Models
Thursday, October 15 | 2:30 PM - 3:00 PM | Room 140AB
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=12
Battery innovation is constrained by the enormous chemical design space and the slow design–make–test cycle used in traditional materials discovery. Artificial intelligence alone often fails to generalize beyond available training data, limiting its ability to predict properties for unexplored chemistries. One way to address this challenge is using Large Quantitative Models (LQMs) - an AI-physics framework that integrates machine learning with first-principles simulations to enable accurate predictions across broader chemical spaces.
LQMs combine large-scale datasets, high-fidelity density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and machine-learning potentials to model atomic interactions with near-quantum accuracy while achieving orders-of-magnitude faster computation. This presentation discusses AQVolt26, a largest dataset for halide solid-state electrolytes built from more than 300,000 r2SCAN calculations. The resulting LQM model achieves near-DFT accuracy while reducing compute cost by over three orders of magnitude and accurately reproducing experimental ionic conductivity trends.
The presentation illustrates how AI-physics platforms can dramatically accelerate battery materials discovery and enable scalable exploration of next-generation energy storage chemistries.
Looking Back, Moving Forward: The Evolution of the Battery Industry
Thursday, October 15 | 10:15 AM - 10:45 AM | Grand Ballroom B
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=297
Join industry veterans Bob Galyen and John Warner in this keynote presentation for a special closing fireside chat reflecting on the evolution of the battery industry and looking ahead to what comes next. The conversation will explore lessons learned, emerging opportunities, and the future of battery innovation and leadership, while marking a meaningful transition as Galyen passes the role of Advisory Board Chairman to Warner.

EnerVenue, an American battery startup, recently announced the opening of its first high-volume manufacturing line in Changzhou, China, rather than in Kentucky, sparking a critical conversation about the state of American manufacturing. This move, which dodged a $264 million factory project in Kentucky that would have created 450 jobs, highlights the challenges and missed opportunities in the US manufacturing landscape. Changzhou, where the factory is located, boasts one of the most complete battery supply chains in the world, with around 160 battery-industry companies operating in the city. This ecosystem includes engineers, suppliers, equipment manufacturers, and specialized talent, all located within a 50- to 100-kilometer radius. Such proximity fosters innovation, reduces costs, and accelerates production timelines.

In contrast, the US has improved its battery manufacturing ecosystem, often referred to as the "
Battery Belt
." This emerging industrial corridor spans states like Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky, Tennessee, and Georgia, where companies have made investments in battery production facilities. Companies such as Ford, General Motors, and LG Energy Solutions have established operations in this region, creating a foundation for a domestic battery supply chain.
Toyota Battery Manufacturing North Carolina. Courtesy of Toyota.
However, the Battery Belt is still in its infancy compared to the mature industrial clusters found in China. While individual factories are being built, the surrounding ecosystem of suppliers, workforce training, research institutions, and capital remains underdeveloped. Granholm’s post emphasizes that the goal should not be to win a single factory but to create an environment where entire industries can thrive.
She stated, “I’ve been obsessed with industrial clusters for years. At UC Berkeley, we launched the American Jobs Project to study how states could create good jobs by building clean-energy clusters — not just attracting a factory, but the suppliers, workforce, research and capital around it.”
EnerVenue’s Changzhou facility
EnerVenue
’s Changzhou facility shows a major step forward in battery production. The plant, which began production in September 2026, is the first in the world to manufacture the Aqueous Metal Cell (AMC) at scale. Phase 1 of the facility is rated at 250 MWh of annual capacity, with plans to expand to 1 GWh by 2027 and multi-gigawatt-hour scale by 2028. At full automation, the line is designed to produce approximately 300 fourth-generation AMC units per day.
Related:
$16 Million Prize to Boost US Critical Minerals Workforce
No other company on the market builds an Aqueous Metal Cell, so EnerVenue had to design and build the equipment specifically for the line. Courtesy of EnerVenue.
Henning Rath, CEO of EnerVenue, emphasized the groundbreaking nature of the facility: “The EnerVenue AMC is now being manufactured at scale, that’s what changes today. This is the only facility in the world making this high-performing water-based nickel-based battery; it’s the first battery of its kind that acts like infrastructure rather than a degrading asset.”
According to the announcement, the AMC is built for 30,000 charge cycles, operates in harsh environments, and carries zero risk of fire from thermal runaway. It uses abundant materials, avoids lithium and rare earths, and can recover and reuse its nickel at the end of its life. These features make the AMC a compelling alternative to lithium-ion batteries.
The role of IRA in building US industrial clusters
The EnerVenue story underscores the importance of industrial clusters in manufacturing success. Granholm connected EnerVenue’s decision to broader policy implications, particularly the dismantling of the
Inflation Reduction Act (IRA)
. However, the rollback of these policies has had severe consequences, with EV sales down 36% year over year. And battery manufacturing investment fell 47% in Q1 2026. Granholm argued that tariffs alone are insufficient to rebuild American manufacturing. Instead, a combination of supply-side and demand-side policies is needed to create industrial clusters that can compete with those in China.
Related:
Tapping Battery Compound Production Potential
Voices from the industry: Agreement and divergence
Granholm’s post sparked a wave of responses from industry experts, offering insights into the challenges and opportunities for American manufacturing. These responses can be classified into two categories: agreement with Granholm’s perspective and diverging views.
Agreement with Granholm’s perspective:
Seahum O., a regenerative AI expert, strongly
with Granholm’s emphasis on industrial clusters. She highlighted the Midwest, particularly Ohio, as a historical example of such clusters, citing First Solar as a success story. However, she lamented how America, despite being a pioneer in solar technology, has fallen behind in scaling and innovating clean energy.
“We invented solar in the 1800s, took it to market, and scaled it globally, only to watch the world take it farther while we stalled.”
Linus Beer, a managing consultant at E3,
supported
Granholm’s perspective, emphasizing the role of state-level initiatives in building industrial clusters. He pointed to the Massachusetts Clean Energy Center as a model, noting its grant programs to expand Climatetech test and demonstration sites in partnership with local businesses and research institutions.
Katie Mehnert, CEO in energy and industrials, and John Mossop, a fractional COO and M&A advisor, both
with Granholm’s focus on proximity and industrial clusters. Mehnert noted untapped potential in regions like Houston and the southern US, while Mossop stressed the need to develop the skills America needs to compete globally.
Diverging views
Antonio Reis, a manufacturing and product development professional,
expressed
skepticism about the IRA’s effectiveness as industrial policy. He argued that permitting delays and regulatory hurdles remain significant barriers to manufacturing at scale in the U.S.
“It still takes about two years, and a stack of agency and political work, to permit a metal-finishing line in the U.S. … If the goal is factories, start with permits that have a clock, rules that last the life of a line, and money next to people who have already shipped product.”
Reis also criticized the IRA for funding companies that announced projects without the capability to deliver, likening it to the “shovel-ready” stimulus programs of the past. He contrasted this with China’s approach, where regulatory processes are faster, and state support often offsets operating costs.
John Wind, an expert in decarbonizing chemical processes, took a more
critical tone
, blaming the Trump administration for sabotaging the clean energy industry in America. He argued that while the IRA was a great start, its impact has been undermined, leaving the future of US manufacturing bleak.
“Manufacturing in the U.S. has a very bleak future, except for coal plants, asbestos, and buggy whips, which will be booming.”
EnerVenue’s move to China highlights the challenges facing American manufacturing but also underscores the opportunities for revitalization. The company positions its AMC as a competitive alternative to technologies like pumped hydro, flow batteries, and compressed air, rather than competing directly with lithium-ion batteries on the price per kilowatt-hour. This strategic focus reflects the growing demand for energy storage solutions that prioritize longevity, safety, and environmental sustainability.
Investments in industrial clusters, such as the Battery Belt, will be critical to creating ecosystems that support advanced manufacturing. Additionally, leveraging public-private partnerships will play a pivotal role in ensuring the US remains a leader in clean energy and high-tech industries. By addressing these systemic challenges, American manufacturing can reclaim its position as a global powerhouse.

title: Redox-Flow Batteries: NMR-EPR for Energy Storage Solutions
content:
Components
Design & Manufacturing
Materials
Testing & Safety
Research
Understand how coupled NMR-EPR spectroscopy advances sustainable energy storage, enabling breakthroughs in AORFBs, CO₂ capture, and environmental remediation.
September 30, 2026
7 Min Read
EPR and NMR are complementary techniques in battery research.
AI illustration generated for Battery Technology.
The growing adoption of renewable energy sources such as wind and solar power has created an urgent demand for large-scale, flexible, and economically viable energy storage technologies, which balance intermittent generation with grid reliability to support net-zero goals.
Redox-flow batteries (RFBs) have emerged as one of the most promising storage technologies: rechargeable batteries that combine chemical tunability with engineering scalability. RFBs store energy in two liquid redox-active electrolytes, one catholyte and one anolyte, housed in external tanks and circulated through an electrochemical cell during operation to convert electrical energy into chemical energy and back. This unique architecture spatially separates energy storage from electrochemical conversion. Consequently, energy and power can be scaled independently, making RFBs particularly attractive for stationary and long-duration energy storage.
In aqueous organic redox-flow batteries (AORFBs), the problematic commonly used vanadium is substituted by an electroactive organic molecule as the energy storage medium. Their cost-effectiveness, flexible design, scalability, and capacity to safely discharge energy for extended periods hold strong potential in developing environmentally sustainable, large-scale electricity grids. However, they can have shorter lifetimes and lower energy density than current commercial vanadium RFBs.
Advancing AORFBs with NMR-EPR to enhance performance and sustainability
Understanding AORFB chemistry holds the key to prolonging lifetime and improving performance. An innovative coupled benchtop nuclear magnetic resonance-electron paramagnetic resonance (NMR-EPR) methodology developed at the Radboud University Nijmegen is being used to investigate the degradation pathways and energy density of advanced electrochemical systems. This article explores how the methodology has broadened understanding of AORFBs, including lifespan and charge/discharge cycles, and has supported the practical deployment of AORFBs in advanced research applications such as carbon capture and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) remediation.
NMR-EPR benchtop set-up for operando studies of redox-flow batteries. Credit: S. Testa et al., ChemRxi 2025 (CC-BY-4.0 [10.26434/chemrxiv-2025-m5k7k-v2])
Tracking redox processes by coupled operando NMR-EPR
EPR and NMR are complementary techniques in battery research. EPR detects unpaired electrons, whereas NMR investigates the structure, composition, and dynamics of diamagnetic species. The Evan Wenbo Zhao Group at Eindhoven University of Technology/Radboud University focuses on developing operando magnetic resonance methods for studying molecular electrochemistry in renewable energy storage.
Prof. Zhao explains the importance of the coupled NMR-EPR method: “Using EPR, we can look at organic radicals or paramagnetic compounds that are spectroscopically silent to NMR. If there is a diamagnetic species, however, NMR will detect it. Combining the two techniques gives a complete picture of the processes occurring within a sample. This is important in a flow battery system, where the chemistry can evolve from a diamagnetic system to a paramagnetic system and back again. We can detect both.”
There is a body of published work on NMR-EPR combinations, with some researchers using high-field NMR instruments together with a benchtop EPR. However, Prof Zhao believes that the method can have wider application and has pioneered a simpler approach using a benchtop NMR instrument.
He explains that both types of systems are appropriate for research into energy storage materials: “In battery research, low-field benchtop NMR systems are advantageous because they combine flexibility and ease of use with a compact footprint. Positioning the analytical instrument directly alongside the battery system significantly simplifies experimental setup. In contrast, high-field NMR provides excellent sensitivity and spectral resolution and is beneficial when working with low sample concentrations or when overlapping signals need to be separated. However, ferromagnetic materials and samples containing paramagnetic species may be challenging to study at higher fields.”
A flexible tool for RFB research
To make the
operando
experiments more accessible, dedicated control software such as CEEN has been developed to synchronize benchtop NMR, EPR, and electrochemical measurements in a single workflow. This enables time-aligned data acquisition and real-time visualization, helping researchers directly connect spectroscopic changes with electrochemical performance.
Prof. Zhao’s benchtop NMR-EPR technique has been used to monitor the reversible redox reaction of methyl viologen (MV) from the MV²⁺ to the MV⁺• radical in a viologen-based system by linking molecular changes directly to charge and discharge behavior. EPR also revealed radical electronic structure and provided evidence for π-dimer formation, a process relevant to radical stability and battery performance.
The methodology is also being applied to investigate the role of dissolved active species and solid boosters in mediated redox-flow systems.
IMDEA Energy Institute
, in collaboration with the Zhao Group, is studying how solid boosters can increase the energy density of mediated systems by combining the flow architecture of AORFBs with charge storage in solid electroactive materials.
Dr. Marcilla at IMDEA Energy explains: “In a conventional RFB, energy density is limited by the concentration of the active species dissolved in the electrolyte. In a mediated system, dissolved redox mediators shuttle charge between the reactor and a solid booster in the external tank, which enables additional energy storage. Coupled NMR-EPR allows us to track the mediator chemistry and radical intermediates in real time, revealing how charge is transferred to and from the solid booster.”
Understanding degradation and decomposition pathways
Degradation of the organic redox-active molecules is a limitation for almost all AORFBs. Prof. Zhao continues: “Combined NMR-EPR
operando
monitoring let us visualize what is happening within a battery, in terms of how operating conditions influence its degradation and performance. By manipulating the rate of charging or the flow rate, we can extend the battery’s lifetime.”
For example, research has revealed how the decomposition products from dihydroxyanthraquinone (DHAQ) in membrane RFBs can, under certain electrochemical conditions, be converted back to DHAQ. Operando NMR and EPR can therefore be used to hinder side reactions and to distinguish irreversible degradation from electrochemical regeneration pathways.
Alongside this, coupled NMR-EPR is also supporting the development of membrane-free AORFBs. IMDEA Energy has pioneered membrane-free RFBs based on biphasic systems in which two immiscible electrolyte phases create a natural liquid-liquid interface that separates the anolyte from the catholyte, replacing conventional membranes. Dr. Marcilla explains: “Performance of conventional RFBs strongly depends on expensive membranes able to prevent the cross-contamination of active species while providing effective ion transport. These ion-exchange membranes are usually perfluorinated and can contribute substantially to cost and environmental impact. Separating the catholyte and the analyte by thermodynamic partitioning offers an alternative strategy for controlling crossover without the need for ion-selective membranes.”
Dr. Singh explains the role of NMR-EPR in monitoring the success of the membrane-free approaches: “Organic molecules tend to form radical intermediates that may or may not be stable. Our goal is to find out exactly what happens at atomic level and how these processes ultimately affect capacity retention. This wouldn’t be possible without
NMR-EPR to monitor radical formation, chemical decomposition and crossover of the species through the liquid-liquid interphase during operation in real-time.”
Beyond RFBs: CO₂ and environmental chemistry
Understanding electrochemical processes is key not only for RFB research but also for supporting energy sustainability initiatives, such as CO
capture and conversion and NH
synthesis. CO
conversion into value-added chemicals is hampered by low selectivity and stability. The
Liu Group
at Johns Hopkins University uses
operando
characterization techniques to understand the reactions and degradation mechanisms of redox-active organic molecules under real-time conditions.
Prof. Liu explains: “We use inline coupled benchtop NMR-EPR to study organic molecules that are redox-active, changing their state so they can selectively capture and release CO
, ultimately helping manage greenhouse gas emissions. The intermediate molecular species are radicals, which are EPR responsive, meaning the NMR-EPR method gives us unique insight into their fundamental mechanisms. Similar mechanistic insights are also supporting research into environmental remediation, where understanding transient radical species is equally important.”
The Liu Group is also looking at the degradation of PFAS into benign molecules, using electrochemical reduction to break the strong carbon-fluoride bond. Prof. Liu continues: “One of our projects involves chemical transformation from a radical to an EPR-silent species. The NMR-EPR system helps corroborate our hypothesis, allowing us to track the concentration and the reaction timescale precisely.”
Coupled NMR-EPR – Driving research into a sustainable future
Developing improved electrochemical technologies for the future depends on the research going on today to gain a deeper understanding of how redox-active molecules behave under realistic operating conditions. Coupled NMR-EPR spectroscopy enables researchers to follow both diamagnetic species and radical intermediates in real time, providing valuable insight into degradation, crossover, charge-transfer processes, and molecular stability.
Important software developments, such as CEEN, and the use of benchtop instruments further support this approach, simplifying experiments so that synchronized electrochemical, NMR, and EPR data are easily acquired and visualized in real-time. Taken together, coupled NMR-EPR and integrated control software can provide a practical platform for advancing sustainable energy storage, including flow chemistry, electrocatalysis, CO₂ capture, and environmental remediation.

Assistant Professor, Institute for Molecules and Materials, Radboud University Nijmegen
Professor Evan Wenbo Zhao is a tenured Assistant Professor at the Institute for Molecules and Materials at Radboud University, and soon an Associate Professor at the Department of Chemical Engineering and Chemistry at Eindhoven University of Technology. His group focuses on magnetic resonance for electrochemistry and energy materials. He is a Dutch Vidi Awardee and ECS Toyota Young Investigator Fellow.

She earned her Ph.D. in materials science and engineering in 2019 from Stanford University under the guidance of Dr. Yi Cui and completed her postdoctoral training at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, working with Dr. T. Alan Hatton in the Department of Chemical Engineering. She has received multiple recognitions for her research, such as the NSF CAREER award, the Beckman Young Investigator award, the Packard Fellowship, the Electrochemical Society Toyota Young Investigator award, and the Sloan Research Fellowship.

She has published more than 145 scientific articles, co-authored nine patents and led numerous national and European research projects, including an ERC Consolidator Grant. He has published 40 scientific articles, authored three patents, and secured prestigious funding, including the César Nombela Talento Grant, the Ramanujan and DST-INSPIRE Fellowship. title: CoreWeave Targets Enterprises with Forge Platform
content:
CoreWeave has unveiled CoreWeave Forge, an integrated software platform for organizations to develop, run, and continuously improve AI models and agents. Announced today (Sept. 30) during the company’s Fully Connected event in San Francisco, Forge extends the AI cloud provider’s strategy beyond GPU infrastructure to the software layer enterprises need to develop, operate, and refine AI applications.
“We have moved from a focus on being the best provider for AI-centric infrastructure to delivering a plethora of AI services to enable customers to build AI applications on our platform,” said Corey Sanders, CoreWeave’s senior vice president of product management, at a media briefing during the Fully Connected event.
CoreWeave said Forge, available today,
unifies existing products
with new software into a stack for training, inference, evaluation, observability, and agent development. The platform is built around an “AI loop”: deploying models and agents, observing and evaluating them, and using results to drive continuous improvement.
Related:
The Next Generation of AI Infrastructure Design Starts with Efficiency
CoreWeave also introduced a partner network that provides validated integrations with ecosystem vendors. Early partners include VAST Data, CrowdStrike, and ClickHouse.
Hardware Updates: Nvidia Vera CPU and Vera Rubin NVL72
On hardware, CoreWeave is in the early phases of making Nvidia’s
Vera CPU
for AI agents available to customers, with some early access underway and broader testing to follow in the coming weeks, Sanders said. The company also said the
Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72
is now available on its cloud platform. AI startup Cognition is the first customer to run workloads on the AI hardware platform and was up and running in two days, he added.
Analyst View: Ecosystem and Hardware Investments Aim for Broad Appeal
IDC analyst Dave McCarthy said CoreWeave’s announcements show the company is trying to further separate itself from specialized AI cloud providers such as Nebius, Lambda, and Vultr, while competing with AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure for AI workloads.
“CoreWeave has recognized that it’s great to get these big AI labs, but if they’re going to build a long-term sustainable business, then they need to be able to appeal to a wider audience, including enterprises,” McCarthy said. “That requires a bigger ecosystem of software. It requires more capabilities – things that feel more turnkey and less like a DIY project.”
McCarthy added that CoreWeave is taking a multifaceted approach: “They’re not just trying to win on the software with Forge. They’re continuing to invest in Nvidia hardware, especially those Vera CPUs. They’re not letting off the gas on all the hardware stuff just because [they’re building] software.”
Related:
Centralized AI vs. Distributed AI vs. Edge AI: What’s the Difference?
CoreWeave Forge: Notebooks, Agent Lens, and RL Features at Launch
CoreWeave said Forge is available in three editions: Free, Pro, and Enterprise.
According to Sanders, new and updated tools include:
CoreWeave Notebooks:
managed Python notebooks that run in the same environment as production workloads.
CoreWeave Agent Lens
: an intelligent observability and continuous improvement tool for production agents that analyzes traces and generates insights.
RL Rollouts:
a new inference-related reinforcement learning capability.
CoreWeave Aria
, previously in preview, is now available. The AI research assistant helps customers move through the AI loop by analyzing data and recommending improvements, Sanders said.
Forge is open across the models, frameworks, and clouds that teams use, the company said.

title: Digital Realty’s LAX12 Bets on In-Data-Center Cable Landings
content:
Digital Realty is planning to build a cable landing station (CLS) inside its LAX12 data center in El Segundo, Calif., adding a new on-ramp for subsea capacity into the Los Angeles metro area. The company announced the project on Sept. 22 in partnership with Assured Communications, a specialist in subsea infrastructure design and delivery. The CLS is aimed at routes between Asia-Pacific and North America and is expected to begin supporting cables in 2028.
A cable landing station is where a subsea cable terminates on land and connects to terrestrial networks. Increasingly, hyperscale cloud and AI providers are bringing cables
directly to specific data centers
rather than terminating them at standalone landing stations. Assured is also a strategic partner to the landing operator for
AWS’s Sta’O’Nuk cable
“Digital Realty sees cable landing infrastructure as an increasingly important part of the broader connectivity ecosystem,” said Craig Waldrop, vice president of strategy and business development at Digital Realty, in an interview with
Data Center Knowledge
. “Subsea cables provide international capacity, but that capacity is most valuable when it can connect efficiently into the data centers, networks, cloud providers, and customers that need it.”
Related:
AWS Wires a New US AI Route Across the Pacific
Inside LAX12: Digital Realty’s First Turnkey Cable Landing Station
The planned CLS is designed to provide subsea cable operators with a turnkey solution for landing and powering their systems. Assured is supporting the design, engineering, and construction, drawing on its experience with subsea cable systems and landing infrastructure. The project is currently in development.
The station is a new type of project for Digital Realty. “LAX12 represents Digital Realty’s first turnkey cable landing solution and marks an important evolution in the company’s broader interconnection platform,” Waldrop said.
The approach is intended to pull landing infrastructure and surrounding networks into a single location. “That simplifies the path from subsea infrastructure into terrestrial networks, while creating increased flexibility for cable owners in how they distribute capacity once it reaches the US,” he said.
Why Put the Landing Station Inside the Data Center?
The goal is to bring subsea capacity closer to the networks and clouds that consume it.
“By bringing the landing point directly into an established interconnection environment, rather than treating the cable landing station as a standalone piece of infrastructure, the project creates a more direct bridge between subsea capacity arriving from Asia-Pacific and the broader digital ecosystem in Los Angeles,” Waldrop said.
He noted that in El Segundo specifically, the proximity of the beach landing to Digital Realty’s existing infrastructure provides a more direct path from subsea systems into terrestrial networks. The connection will run through Digital Realty’s
carrier-neutral model
“The value of a carrier-neutral model is that it gives cable operators a common landing environment that is not tied to a single network or cloud provider,” Waldrop said.
What’s Fueling Investment in Subsea Connectivity?
AI is a major driver of bandwidth demand, but not the only one.
“AI is contributing to demand for high-capacity and resilient connectivity, but this extends beyond any single workload,” Waldrop said. “As traffic patterns evolve and infrastructure requirements grow, Digital Realty sees subsea infrastructure as an important part of the underlying infrastructure customers need to connect globally.”
He added that demand for efficient, resilient connectivity continues to drive investment in greater capacity and route diversity. “While AI certainly contributes to that demand, it’s one of several factors shaping investment decisions,” he said. “Cloud adoption, content delivery, network expansion, and broader digital infrastructure growth are all driving continued investment in subsea connectivity.”

title: CATL to supply 313 MW/1.64 GWh BESS in Mexico - Energy Storage
content: CATL has signed an agreement with Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) to supply a 313 MW/1,639.45 MWh BESS to the La Alegría Solar project, which the Danish investment manager is developing in the Mexican state of Campeche. The configuration provides about 5.24 hours of storage at nominal power. According to CATL, La Alegría will be Mexico’s first BESS with more than 1 GWh of energy capacity and the country’s largest battery storage system to date. The announcement represents a substantial change from the project’s previously disclosed configuration. In March, Mexico’s Secretariat of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat) approved La Alegría Solar’s regional Environmental Impact Statement (MIA-R) with a 788.719 MWp solar plant and a 177.69 MW / 314.98 MWh BESS. The plant has a declared net installed capacity of 600 MW and 694.274 MWac of inverter capacity. The environmental design includes 1,151,416 solar modules rated at 685 Wp, 101 transformer stations and 202 inverters. The grid connection infrastructure includes a 34.5/400 kV step-up substation and a 2.85 km, 400 kV transmission line. The project covers 1,206.97 hectares and was submitted to Semarnat by Sunstone Power 2. The 1,639.45 MWh energy capacity now announced by CATL is approximately 5.2 times the 314.98 MWh included in the approved environmental documentation. The BESS power capacity also increases from 177.69 MW to 313 MW under the new configuration. Other configurations have also been disclosed during the project’s development. In April, CFE Calificados announced electricity hedging contracts with CIP, associated with Sunstone Power, for La Alegría Solar and La Esperanza Solar. At the time, La Alegría was presented as a 600 MW solar project with 300 MW of storage. The two projects together totaled 900 MW of solar capacity and 450 MW of storage and form part of the binding planning of Mexico’s Secretariat of Energy (Sener). CIP subsequently confirmed that La Alegría and La Esperanza are its first projects in Mexico and that both hybrid solar and battery developments were advancing toward final investment decisions. In August, the investment manager announced the close of its Growth Markets Fund II (GMF II), with commitments of approximately $3 billion, and said it had started construction of its first large-scale solar-plus-storage projects in Mexico. The Campeche government has put the combined planned investment for La Alegría and La Esperanza at $845 million, based on the 900 MW of solar and 450 MW of storage disclosed at the time. It also estimates about 1,800 construction jobs and electricity production equivalent to the consumption of more than 600,000 homes. For La Alegría, CATL will supply its TENER platform. The manufacturer introduced the technology in 2024 with a capacity of 6.25 MWh per 20-foot container and LFP cells with an energy density of 430 Wh/L. CATL says the system is designed to maintain its power and capacity without degradation during its first five years of operation. Compared with the previous generation of its products, CATL claims a 30% increase in energy density per unit of land area and a 20% reduction in the space required for the installation. CATL currently ranks first globally in both electric vehicle batteries and stationary energy storage cells. According to SNE Research, the company held a 39.2% share of the global electric vehicle battery market in 2025, with 464.7 GWh installed. In stationary storage, InfoLink data placed CATL among the world’s leading cell suppliers in 2025, while other industry estimates put its shipments at 121 GWh and its share of the global BESS cell market at about 20%. The company says it has five service centers in Mexico, located in Mexico City, Monterrey and Guadalajara, to provide support during system commissioning, operation and maintenance. Ray See, president of CATL’s Energy Storage Business Division for the Americas, said the value of utility-scale storage depends on combining advanced technology with reliable project execution and support throughout the system’s operating life. He said CATL expects its work with CIP on La Alegría to support the project’s long-term performance and the wider role of energy storage in Mexico’s power system. CATL also says it supplied more than 80% of the storage capacity awarded in Mexico during 2026 and puts the country’s new projects expected in the short and medium term at about 15 GWh. title: Cuba plans 100 MW of new storage - Energy Storage
content: Cuba has already installed 50 MW of battery storage and expects to add another 100 MW in October, according to President Miguel Díaz-Canel, who provided the figures during a recent program broadcast by Radio Rebelde. The planned storage deployment comes as Cuba accelerates its solar buildout. The country has installed 1,418 MW of PV across 144 parks and expects to exceed 1.5 GW by the end of 2026, said Díaz-Canel. More than 563 MW of PV systems have also been installed at consumer sites in the state and non-state sectors. Díaz-Canel said private-sector consumers have recorded the fastest growth in distributed solar and now generate 20% of their electricity consumption from PV, reducing their demand on Cuba’s national electricity system. Renewable energy sources account for 21.4% of Cuba’s electricity generation, according to figures presented by Díaz-Canel. Solar deployment is also being used to support water pumping. Cuba has installed 646 solar-powered pumps for supplying the population and more than 1,000 for livestock and irrigation, according to Díaz-Canel. The government also plans to receive another 200 MW of solar PV capacity dedicated exclusively to water-pumping systems. The aim is for water pumping to operate independently of the national electricity system during the first months of 2027, with the approach subsequently extended to other provinces. Cuba is also deploying renewable energy at public-service facilities. Díaz-Canel said renewable energy systems have been installed at 99% of polyclinics, 47% of hospitals, 89% of nursing and senior-care homes, 99% of maternity homes, 98% of funeral homes, 16% of homes for children without family protection, and 72% of banks. In the communications sector, 97% of radio stations have PV systems, along with 25% of Radio Cuba transmitters and 25% of Etecsa mobile base stations, according to Díaz-Canel. Cuban banks offer financing for renewable-energy installations for households and economic entities, while the government has also expanded tax incentives for renewable energy. Cuba has also established a feed-in tariff of 90 Cuban pesos per kWh for electricity supplied to the national grid by renewable-energy generators. title: FRV commissions 100 MW battery in Australia - Energy Storage
content: FRV has commissioned its first utility-scale battery project in Australia with the 100 MW/200 MWh Terang BESS now operating at full capacity. FRV Australia Chief Executive Michael Steiner said the commissioning marks a crucial milestone for company. It is FRV’s first standalone battery energy storage project in Austraia, increasing its portfolio of operational assets in the country to nine and adding dispatchable energy capacity to the developer’s predominantly solar generation portfolio. “The commissioning of Terang marks a defining moment for FRV Australia ,” he said. “The project demonstrates our ability to develop and operate utility-scale dispatchable energy infrastructure that supports Australia’s energy transition.” FRV said the 100 MW/200 MWh battery, sited near the town of Terang in Victoria’s southwest, will help strengthen the stability and resilience of the National Electricity Market (NEM) and support the state’s efforts to achieve its target of 65% renewable energy generation by 2030. The project received AUD 7 million ($4.87 million) through the Victorian government’s Energy Innovation Fund to support the deployment of grid-forming inverter technology designed to supply system strength services to the network. “It provides critical firming capacity during peak hours while helping to strengthen grid reliability,” Steiner said. The Terang facility incorporates 48 SolBank 3.0 battery containers supplied by Canadian Solar subsidiary e-Storage, and 38 inverters from German manufacturer SMA. Canadian Solar served as engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contractor for the project, with Sydney-headquartered TEC-C delivering the balance-of-plant works. Terang forms part of FRV Australia’s growing BESS portfolio that includes a 2.5 MW/5 MWh battery delivered as part of the Dalby Hybrid Power Plant in Queensland. The company is also building the 250 MW/500 MWh Gnarwarre battery in Victoria’s south, with completion targeted by the end of 2027. FRV Australia, owned by Saudi energy company Abdul Latif Jameel Energy and Canadian pension fund Omers, also has a pipeline of standalone BESS and solar-battery hybrid projects under development in New South Wales (NSW), Victoria and Queensland. In addition, the company has more than 1.3 GW of solar assets built or under construction across 10 projects in Australia, including the 300 MW Walla Walla solar farm in the New South Wales Riverina. title: Vattenfall to market 285 MW German battery portfolio - Energy Storage
content: Vattenfall will market four large-scale BESS with a combined power capacity of 285 MW in Germany. According to the energy company, the projects are being developed by an independent flexibility provider whose identity Vattenfall has not disclosed. They are located at four sites across different German balancing zones. Unlike virtually aggregated battery systems, Vattenfall says it will have direct control over the assets and their operation. The company describes the agreement as the first and largest marketing agreement to date for a physical battery portfolio in Germany spanning multiple balancing zones and grid operators. It also calls it the first physical battery portfolio of its kind in Europe. All four projects have reached financial close, according to Vattenfall, while three are already under construction. Commercial operation of the first system is scheduled from January 2027, and the agreements with Vattenfall run through 2036. The company did not disclose the storage capacity of the projects in megawatt-hours. Vattenfall will integrate the systems into its automated trading and optimization processes. Depending on market conditions, the batteries will participate in both wholesale electricity markets and balancing markets. The energy company aims to optimize a battery portfolio with a total power capacity of 1.5 GW over the coming years. It also says it has around 270 MW of its own battery storage capacity in operation or under construction, with a further 254 MW planned at Brunsbüttel. Vattenfall said long-term marketing agreements can also help facilitate the financing and construction of additional battery storage projects. title: ZE Energy acquires 1 GWh-plus BESS project in Italy - Energy Storage
content: French power producer ZE Energy has acquired a 200 MW / 1 GWh-plus battery energy storage system (BESS) in Troia, Apulia, southern Italy. The Elena project was acquired from UK-based solar and storage developer Aura Power and will have a storage duration of more than six hours. ZE Energy’s press notes indicated a “more than 1 GWh” capacity while Aura Power said 1 GWh. A six hour duration at 200 MW would imply a 1.2 GWh storage base, though this was not confirmed. The acquisition increases ZE Energy’s Italian standalone BESS portfolio to approximately 300 MW, including the 98.5 MW / 895 MWh Sessa Aurunca project , which is being co-developed with Octopus Energy Generation. ZE Energy said the Elena project is fully permitted, construction-ready and has secured a connection to Italy’s 380 kV transmission network in Troia. “With this 200 MW standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) project, Elena, we are reaching a new milestone in the development of our storage platform in Italy. Following on from Sessa Aurunca, this second asset confirms our ability to deliver innovative projects in a rapidly growing market,” said Nicolas Wolff, chairman of ZE Energy. ZE Energy is targeting 1.5 GW of installed capacity by 2030, with the strategy aimed around developing, acquiring, and building storage assets in France, Italy and Germany. The sale of the Elena project from Aura Power marks the company’s third BESS sale in Italy in the past year. Aura Power merged with Verdant Energy in August and has expanded its strategy beyond project development by transitioning into an independent power producer (IPP) in the UK, backed by shareholder CVC DIF. “We are very pleased to have completed this transaction with ZE Energy. The successful development and sale of Troia is a testament to the expertise and hard work of our development, transaction, finance, and technical departments and our external partners at Legance and JLL as well as the close collaborative relationship we developed with ZE Energy,” said Peter Sermon, global head of development. title: China's 2,250kW chargers are already in service, while US thinks about 750kW next year
content:
Just last week, Geely announced it would roll out 2.2 megawatt chargers, able to charge an EV in under 5 minutes. Those chargers are now already in service in 5 cities, with 15,000 charging sites planned by the end of next year.
Meanwhile, the fastest upcoming charger in the US, a respectable 750kW, is coming sometime next year, after being pushed back from 2026.
China’s EV industry has been advancing incredibly rapidly, and its EV charging ecosystem is no exception.
The country already has tens of thousands of megawatt-level chargers which can charge an EV in 5-10 minutes, but China’s EV companies are rolling out even faster charging as they compete over seconds, not minutes of faster charging times.
The latest development is Geely’s 2.2MW charger, announced just last week. The company even says that it uses an advanced thermal-control algorithm that helps increase longevity, which is a consideration when you’re pumping so much power so quickly into a battery.
2.2MW might be a bit of a misnomer here, since it’s shared by two charging heads. The charger runs at 1,500V/1,500A, but no cars exist (yet) that can accept a 1,500V charge, so instead two cars can get over 1MW of power simultaneously.
China’s scale and speed are phenomenal
But the real story is the scale and speed at which these developments happen. Geely released a 1.5MW charger in March of this year. Its 2.2MW charger comes just six months after that last development.
Even more impressively, Geely already has working chargers in the wild, just a week after the announcement. CarNewsChina cites National Business Daily and says that Geely’s chargers have already rolled out in five cities: Hangzhou, Shanghai, Ningbo, Jiaxing, and Xi’an.
The same happened when BYD announced its 1.5MW system in March. In just 5 months, the company installed 10,000 chargers. Geely plans a rollout of a similar scale, installing 15,000 chargers by the end of next year.
Geely also announced a partial purchase of NIO’s battery swapping unit, which is a bit puzzling for a company with leading fast-charge technology, but it doesn’t hurt to hedge your bets (well… until battery swapping fails as a concept and Geely’s $2 billion investment goes down the drain, but we’ll cross that bridge when we get there).
Compare to the US, which is both behind and moving slower
Meanwhile, it’s still rare to find even one or two 350-400kW chargers at a US charging station, let alone anything quicker.
We did get some news this week offering a reprieve: EVgo says it will release 750kW charging in America next year, which is about twice as fast as the current state of the art. Those chargers would take about ten minutes to charge an EV, assuming it can accept enough juice (so far, the upcoming Mercedes AMG GT is the only US EV that can handle numbers like that).
EVgo’s 750kW system will also share power between stalls, so we’re not sure what kind of juice it will deliver to each individual stall, but regardless the peak is still quite a lot lower than China’s.
What’s notable about the EVgo announcement is how long it took. It started with a partnership forged in 2024, which predicted availability in the second half of 2026. We’re now in that second half, and yesterday’s press release delayed availability until sometime in 2027.
So in the same amount of time as that delay – a half year – Geely added another 750kW to its already-mega-fast 1.5MW charging system.
As for other quick chargers in the US, the largest system is Tesla’s Superchargers. In 2022, Tesla announced its V4 Supercharger, with 500kW peak power.
It took about three years for the first of those to show up in the wild – the vast majority of Superchargers in the US are still capped at 350kW or lower (which CEO Elon Musk once referred to as a “children’s toy“).
Tesla also has a “Megacharger” system for its Tesla Semi, but that runs at 1.2MW, which is slower than the light-duty consumer offerings from either BYD or Geely.
The US chose to have worse charging
The US could have had a faster charging rollout, as President Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act and Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act built programs to help accelerate the buildout of these chargers.
But those programs have moved slower than they should, for several reasons both at the state and federal level.
The federal reasons have had to do with intentional roadblocks from the republican party, like illegally trying to pause disbursement of funds, dismantling the government office intended to increase efficiency, and making up rules to make it impossible to install faster chargers.
At the same time, republicans have shipped EV jobs to China by canceling Biden-era programs that had led to a renaissance in US manufacturing.
Top comment by OrangeFan
This is playing out like the phone charging cable fiasco except on a much more expensive grander scale. Cars and Charging stations are not disposable items that you throw away every couple of years. It took a long time to settle on USB C type and even then it took Europe basically forcing Apple to finally switch to USB C.
You can't play the same game with EV chargers, Europe is using CCS, United States is switching to NACS....slowly, China is using another connector all together that actually supports higher voltage. And remember, that unlike Gas Pumps, you NEED TO REPLACE charging cabinet with every change in charging speed. They cost a lot of money and companies that are concerned with return on their investment, are not going to rip out relatively fresh installations just to replace them with the next best thing. Likewise, people are not going to throw away EVs and replace them new faster charging ones, especially since EVs last a very long time.
You can blame one party or the other, but don't ignore the facts.
Then there has been the unfortunately bipartisan effort to put up tariffs against China. We may all finally be starting to realize at this point what a bad idea tariffs are for the whole economy, but tariffs on Chinese autos were also expanded greatly by President Biden, and there is currently an effort to ban any Chinese car from even thinking about crossing the border, even as a private vehicle on vacation from Canada or Mexico.
The intent seems to be to hide how advanced Chinese autos are from American consumers, so we don’t realize how much better automotive technology is in the rest of the world, outside of the city-in-a-hole we’ve created for ourselves.
But you don’t win a technology war, or a trade war, by refusing to participate. China is advancing automotive technology rapidly, and those advancements happen whether we’re covering our eyes and ears or not. The only way to compete is to get better, faster. And we’re already behind, so you better start moving faster than China if you want to catch up.

title: IONNA tops 180 charging sites, with discounts for these EV drivers
content:
Rapidly expanding DC fast charging company IONNA now has more than 180 sites open across the US, and EV drivers of four of its founding automakers’ brands can now get discounts when they plug in.
The automaker-backed network, which uses Alpitronic hardware and in-house-developed software, says it has more than doubled its footprint since the start of 2026 and is now the largest 400 kW charging network in the US.
IONNA’s eight founding automakers are BMW, GM, Honda, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and Toyota. They’re building a charging network open to all EV drivers with sites it calls “Rechargeries.”
More Circle K charging stops
More than 40 Rechargeries have opened at Circle Ks since IONNA announced its partnership with the convenience store chain in April.
As Electrek previously reported, the company aims to bring IONNA charging to more than 350 Circle K locations. That includes around 85 existing fast-charging sites that IONNA will upgrade and operate. The Circle K rollout features 400 kW chargers with both NACS and CCS connectors.
Discounts, without another charging app
Hyundai and Mercedes-Benz have joined BMW in offering IONNA 10% charging discounts through their automaker apps and Plug & Charge as of October 1. IONNA says its remaining founding automakers will follow.
Plug & Charge lets a compatible EV handle authentication and payment when it’s plugged in, so drivers don’t have to start each session through an app.
Volvo drivers now have Plug & Charge support on IONNA, with Toyota and Lexus support expected in October.
IONNA has also added integrations with Presto, ChargeHub, and EV Connect, bringing its supported partner apps to 19. Rather than asking drivers to download an IONNA app, the network is making its chargers accessible through other platforms.
“The industry has treated charging scale and charging quality as a tradeoff. Our growth and first-place customer satisfaction ranking show that drivers can and should expect both,” said Seth Cutler, CEO of IONNA. (IONNA ranked first for DC fast-charging satisfaction in J.D. Power’s 2026 US Electric Vehicle Experience (EVX) Public Charging Study.)
When I asked Cutler what he felt was the biggest challenge facing the company going forward, he replied that it was ensuring quality remained high amid the company’s rapid growth.
EV drivers get a say
IONNA has established a Driver Advisory Council made up of members of the EV community to provide feedback on network performance, customer priorities, and future products.
The Council’s first assignment is gathering feedback on IONNA’s new Driver’s Dashboard, which lets drivers check real-time details of their charging session by scanning a QR code on the charging screen.
The next step reaches beyond the charging sites. Starting in Q1 of 2027, IONNA plans to send ambassadors to its eight backing automakers’ dealerships to teach staff about EV charging – putting that information where shoppers are deciding whether to buy an EV.
I was delighted to hear this news when Cutler told me yesterday, because, based on my own experience with dealerships, there is a lot of room for growth in EV knowledge, which really impacts buyers’ experiences and decision-making.

For people with BEVs that charge on the slow side of today's charging curves, reaching your peak can make a road trip just a little bit nicer.

title: Range Rover Sport EV orders open at nearly $150,000 with up to 378 miles of range
content:
Range Rover

Peter Johnson
| Sep 30 2026 - 7:36 am PT
Range Rover Sport EV
is bringing new levels of performance with an all-electric powertrain, but it isn’t cheap.
Range Rover Sport EV prices and Range
After launching the flagship Range Rover Electric earlier this month, the luxury brand opened orders for its second fully electric SUV on Wednesday.
The Range Rover Sport Electric is now on sale in the UK, starting at about £110,000, or roughly $146,000.
Like the flagship model, Range Rover promises the Sport EV will match, if not outperform, the current internal combustion engine (ICE) version.
The electric SUV is “first and foremost a Range Rover Sport,” Martin Limbert, the brand’s managing director, said. By using an all-electric propulsion system, Range Rover was able to “unlock new levels of responsiveness and precision,” Limbert said.
Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the setup delivers up to 542 horsepower (550 PS) and 627 lb-ft (850 Nm) of torque, the most any Range Rover Sport has offered to date.
Range Rover Sport Electric (Source: JLR)
In Dynamic Launch Mode, the Range Rover Sport EV can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in as little as 4.3 seconds.
The electric SUV features “uncompromised all-terrain capability,” Range Rover said, with the ability to wade through 900 mm (35.4″) of water and climb a 45-degree slope.
It’s equipped with advanced tech, including virtual AWD, adaptive dynamics, twin valve dampers, and an electric active roll cage, making it the most dynamic Range Rover Sport in the lineup.
Range Rover Sport Electric (Source: JLR)
The Range Rover Sport EV gets up to 378 miles of WLTP range and up to 333 miles of real-world range using a 118.5 kWh battery.
Based on an 800V architecture with charging at up to 350 kW, the electric SUV can add up to 136 miles (220 km) of driving range in as little as 22 minutes. Charging from 10% to 80% takes about 22 minutes.
Inside, the interior remains very close to the current model, with a 13.1″ curved glass touchscreen running the latest Pivo Pro infotainment system. There’s also a 13.7″ instrument cluster behind the steering wheel.
Range Rover Sport Electric interior (Source: JLR)
Orders for the Range Rover Sport Electric opened in the UK, starting at about £110,000 ($146,000) for the base Dynamic SE trim.
That’s about £44,000 ($58,000) less than the flagship Range Rover Electric SUV, which starts at £154,070 ($200,000) in the UK. Deliveries are scheduled to begin next year.
The Range Rover Sport EV will launch in the US, but when has yet to be confirmed. It’s expected to go on sale sometime in 2027 as a 2028 model. The
Range Rover Electric
starts at $140,450 in the US, so you can expect it to be slightly less, at around $120,000 to $130,000.

title: Tesla Robotaxi fleets are the new crypto treasury for zombie companies
content:
Tesla Robotaxi
Tesla Cybercab
Fred Lambert
| Sep 30 2026 - 7:02 am PT
A pre-production Tesla Cybercab and the steering column bolted inside it, spotted in Berkeley. Photo: Adam Machacek
A Nasdaq-listed company worth about $2.4 million says it wants to buy 500 Tesla Robotaxis. KIDZ AI, formerly an online coding school for kids, announced today that it sent Tesla a “procurement inquiry” for the vehicles and plans an “Autonomous Fleet Operations Strategy.”
If the name doesn’t ring a bell, the playbook should. Tesla’s Robotaxi is turning into what bitcoin treasuries were for failing micro-caps in 2025: a buzzword you bolt onto a dying business to get the stock moving.
A kids’ coding school that keeps pivoting
KIDZ AI used to be called Classover Holdings. It sold online classes to K-12 students and went public through a SPAC merger in 2025.
The education business isn’t going anywhere good. According to the company’s
Q2 2026 results
, service revenue fell 34% year-over-year to $0.48 million, and it lost $2.5 million in the quarter. That’s more than five dollars lost for every dollar of revenue.
So it started pivoting. A lot.
In June 2025, Classover announced a deal for up to $500 million in convertible notes from Solana Growth Ventures, with up to 80% of the proceeds going to buy SOL tokens. It was a textbook crypto treasury play. Only an initial $11 million was funded.
A year later, in June 2026, the company rebranded as KIDZ AI and said it was dropping Solana for the Hyperliquid ecosystem and “yield-bearing stablecoin strategies.” The same month, it announced a push into GPU cloud and AI data centers. Since then, it has announced a $44.6 million, 60-month GPU compute deal, a stake in a data center in Cambodia, a “KIDZBot” robotics financing, and now, a fleet of Tesla Robotaxis.
That’s four hot sectors in about 15 months. Crypto, AI compute, robots, and self-driving cars.
The stock is down 99.97%
The market isn’t buying any of it, including today’s Robotaxi news. KIDZ jumped about 10% in pre-market trading after the announcement, then fell about 6% once the market opened. So much for the pump.
Zoom out and it’s worse. KIDZ stock is down about 99.97% over the last year, and the company’s market cap sat around $2 million.
To stay listed on Nasdaq, it did a 1-for-10 reverse split in June and then
a 1-for-15 reverse split in August
. That’s a combined 1-for-150 in about two months, and both filings cite Nasdaq’s $1 minimum bid price rule.
Now put the Robotaxi order next to that. Tesla hasn’t published a price for the Cybercab, but even at Elon Musk’s own “under $30,000” target, 500 of them would cost about $15 million. That’s roughly six times the company’s entire market value. KIDZ AI reported $8.88 million in cash and restricted cash at the end of June.
To be fair, the company says as much in its own release. The inquiry “does not constitute a binding order,” the plan is in a “preliminary planning, evaluation, and partner exploration phase,” and KIDZ AI “may determine not to proceed.” In other words, it’s a press release, not a purchase.
We’ve seen where betting on Musk’s Robotaxi ends
Earlier this month,
Tesla started circulating an interest form for Cybercab fleet buyers
at its underwhelming launch event, and anyone can now say they “submitted” something to Tesla.
But companies that bought into Musk’s self-driving pitch don’t have a great track record. MisterGreen, the Dutch Tesla-only leasing company, built a fleet of more than 4,000 Teslas partly on Musk’s claim that they were
“appreciating assets”
that would earn robotaxi money. Instead, Tesla’s price cuts crushed resale values, the robotaxi income never showed up, and
MisterGreen went bankrupt
, wiping out its bondholders.
And Tesla’s own Robotaxi service still barely exists at scale.
Its active fleet in Austin
is still extremely limited, not much bigger than where it was at launch in June 2025, while Waymo runs roughly 4,000 driverless vehicles.
Electrek’s Take
Last year, I wrote about
the “zombie pivot”
: companies with shrinking or broken core businesses announcing bitcoin treasuries to juice their stock. Semler Scientific’s chairman literally said his company was in the “zombie zone.” Metaplanet was a budget hotel chain. Classover/Kidz AI, with its Solana treasury, would have fit right in.
Now the crypto trade has cooled, and the new magic word is Robotaxi.
Musk has spent seven years telling people that Teslas will make money on their own, and he’s now
asking fleet buyers to take on the capital risk of Cybercabs
that Tesla doesn’t want to carry itself. When the buyer lining up first is a $2 million kids’ coding school that was a Solana treasury a year ago, that tells you a lot about who this pitch attracts.
If Tesla’s Robotaxi were truly profitable, Tesla would deploy them itself. It wouldn’t sell them to third-party to take the profits. Only zombie companies like Kidz AI can’t see that or ignore it for a stock pump.

title: 七部门：全固态电池2030年初步规模化应用
content:
9月28日，工业和信息化部、国家发展改革委、交通运输部、商务部、市场监管总局、国家能源局、国家铁路局七部门联合印发《新型电池产业发展“十五五”规划》（以下简称《规划》）。
《规划》明确提出，到2030年，我国新型电池产业规模实现稳步增长，全固态电池初步实现规模化应用。与此同时，《规划》还提出，先进电极材料、新型电解质、高端辅材等取得新突破，新体系电池研发取得重大进展，长寿命锂电池循环寿命达到15000次，头部企业产品缺陷率达到PPB级。
《规划》在“加快全链条创新发展”部分提出强化前沿和共性技术攻关，并明确要聚焦离子电导率和循环稳定性提升、成本优化等重点方向，加快突破全固态电池产业化技术。
在此基础上，《规划》还提出，前瞻布局新型碱金属离子电池、多价离子电池、金属－空气/硫电池、多功能复合材料结构电池、核电池等新一代电池体系，为后续技术演进留出空间。
具体到技术路径，《规划》在“共性和关键技术提升”专栏中将“全固态电池技术突破”单列一项，提出创新固态电池关键材料和工艺技术解决方案，畅通基础研究与工程应用的信息共享渠道。提升界面接触、高离子电导率、长循环寿命、工程化压力系统设计等关键技术，推动高电压、高比容量正极材料与新型锂金属基负极材料、无锂负极等融合应用。
在材料方面，《规划》提出提升高电导率、高性能固态电解质材料量产能力；在“先进材料和高端设备升级”专栏中，进一步提出，提升固态电解质稳定性和离子电导率。发展高空气稳定性硫化物、卤化物等固态电解质、高性能聚合物复合固态电解质。
在设备方面，专栏提出开发固态电池用等静压等设备。在产品方面，《规划》提出提高全固态电池、水系电池、超快充电池产业化能力。在系统集成方面，则要求聚焦固态电池、钠电池、液流电池等新型电池技术特性，开发定制化温控方案。
除技术和产业环节外，《规划》也对标准和知识产权作出安排。标准方面，提出推进全固态电池、钠电池等新型电池重点领域标准研制；知识产权方面，提出加强全固态电池、大容量长寿命储能电池、高比能钠电池等关键核心技术专利布局，储备一批高价值专利。
总体来看，《规划》从关键技术攻关、电解质与电极材料、制造设备，到产品产业化能力、热管理、标准和专利布局，对全固态电池的发展作了系统部署。

title: 协鑫集团、湖南裕能等8企锂电储能项目持续推进
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近期，协鑫集团、金宏科技、湖南裕能、中比新能源等企业在锂电、固态电池及钠离子电池领域的项目建设持续推进，涵盖正极材料、负极材料、电芯及储能PACK等环节。
徐州鑫锐锂电40万吨磷酸铁锂项目开工
9月28日，徐州鑫锐锂电40万吨磷酸铁锂项目在江苏徐州经开区正式开工建设。
据介绍，该项目是协鑫集团在动力电池、储能关键材料领域的布局，项目建成后将形成40万吨磷酸铁锂产能，进一步增强锂电正极材料配套供给能力。
金宏科技规划100GWh固态电池产能
9月24日，天津城建集团与威海金宏科技签署合作协议，计划分别在威海、大连、鄂尔多斯、西安、西宁建设固态电池生产线，总规划产能约100GWh。
根据协议，双方将围绕固态电池技术、产能建设及产业链等方面开展合作。金宏科技目前已建成0.5GWh固态电池生产线，产品包括35Ah、102Ah、105Ah和314Ah等规格，主要应用于储能、新能源汽车、无人机及船舶等领域。
湖南裕能西班牙正极材料项目扩产至7万吨
9月23日，湖南裕能公告称，公司拟将西班牙年产5万吨锂电池正极材料项目的建设规模调整至年产7万吨，同时项目投资总额由此前约9.82亿元增至折合人民币约16.50亿元。
该项目由湖南裕能全资子公司Yuneng International(SGP)Investment Pte.Ltd.持有的裕能国际（西班牙）新能源电池材料有限公司负责实施，目前已进入施工建设阶段。项目最初于2024年4月获批，规划年产5万吨锂电池正极材料。
对于此次调整，湖南裕能表示，主要考虑海外市场需求增长以及项目所在地建设、运营条件变化。
中比新能源12GWh钠离子电芯项目落户南京
9月23日，中比新能源与南京高淳经济开发区签署投资协议，计划建设12GWh钠离子电芯及系统集成制造项目。该项目规划总投资约30亿元，计划于2027年下半年推进建设。
据介绍，该项目产线采用锂钠共线设计，可根据市场需求在锂离子电池与钠离子电池生产之间灵活切换。项目建成后，将重点推进32140系列钠离子电芯规模化制造，并进一步拓展户用储能、便携储能、轻型交通工具及备用电源等应用场景。
2GWh动力储能电池项目签约落户金湖
据“金湖发布”消息，近日，2GWh动力储能电池项目签约落户江苏省淮安市金湖县。项目由广东某新能源科技有限公司等三方共同投资建设，计划于2026年12月开工改造，2027年9月建成投产。
据介绍，该项目主要生产动力柱型固态动力储能锂电池，产品将应用于工程装备、电动工具等新能源配套领域。项目建成后，将形成2GWh动力及储能电池产能。
横店东磁10GWh全极耳锂电池项目环评拟获批
近日，浙江省金华市生态环境局东阳分局发布公示，拟对横店东磁年产10GWh全极耳新型高效锂电池项目环评文件作出审批意见。
根据公示，该项目位于浙江省东阳市横店镇下莲塘村东磁高新产业园区，项目总投资19.02亿元。项目建成后，将形成年产10GWh全极耳新型高效锂电池的生产能力。
易储数智30GWh储能PACK基地投产
9月21日，易储数智旗下子公司江苏国峰元储新能源科技有限公司30GWh储能PACK集成智造基地在江苏宿迁正式投产。
据介绍，该基地按照工业4.0标准建设，主要开展储能PACK及系统集成产品的生产制造，已具备GWh级储能系统量产交付能力。基地投产后，将承担易储数智储能产品制造及交付业务。
蒙连新科技60万吨锂电池负极材料项目备案
近日，内蒙古二连浩特市发改委通过内蒙古蒙连新科技有限公司年产60万吨锂电池负极材料项目备案。
据悉，该项目总投资65亿元，建设地点位于二连浩特市边境经济合作区，计划于2027年4月开工建设，2029年12月完成建设。
项目规划建设12条箱式炉生产线、20条坩埚炉生产线，并配套建设辅助及附属生产设施、公用工程站及一体化环保治理设施。项目建成后，将形成60万吨/年的锂电池负极材料生产能力。

title: 超2.2GWh！国轩高科、亿纬锂能等6企披露最新储能订单动态
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近期，国轩高科、亿纬锂能、思源清能、禾迈、天能储能、阿诗特能源等企业相继披露储能订单及交付动态。
国轩高科交付埃及1.8GWh储能项目
9月28日，国轩高科埃及奈菲缇（Nefertiti）与荷鲁斯（Horus）1.8GWh独立储能项目启动首批发货。首批50辆重型卡车装载国轩高科自研的乾元智储5MWh储能系统，从金寨智造基地和南通基地同步发运，正式进入项目交付阶段。
该项目由阿联酋能源开发商AMEA Power开发，中国能建承建，总规模1.8GWh。项目建成后将成为非洲单体规模最大的独立储能项目，并提升光伏电站的消纳与削峰能力，同时强化扎法拉纳风电场的柔性调峰与电网支撑。
亿纬锂能400MWh独立储能电站并网
9月29日，惠州日盛200MW/400MWh独立共享储能电站正式并网。该项目位于广东惠州博罗县，搭载亿纬锂能自研储能电芯逾45万颗。
该项目作为亿纬锂能首个并网的电网侧独立共享储能电站，将为广东电网提供调峰调频支撑，平抑新能源出力波动。
思源清能交付芬兰30MWh储能订单
近日，思源清能一套10MW/30MWh簇控式交直流一体储能系统完成整装及出厂测试，正式发运至芬兰。这是思源清能在芬兰落地的首个储能项目。
该项目储能系统由思源清能自主研发并制造，投运后将主要用于当地电网调峰、调频，并提升区域电网对新能源的消纳能力。
禾迈储能落地马来西亚工商业项目
近日，禾迈与当地合作伙伴Plus Xnergy合作，为马来西亚石膏产品制造商Richwise Sdn.Bhd.部署HoyUltra 261A工商业储能一体机。该项目在企业原有光伏系统基础上配置储能，用于厂区用电调节。
HoyUltra 261A采用液冷设计，可适应马来西亚高温、高湿环境，并支持最高50℃环境下保持额定功率运行。
天能交付山西400MWh储能项目
近日，天能储能向山西200MW/400MWh新型独立共享储能电站项目交付首批20尺5MWh电池舱。
该项目为山西省新型储能领域重点工程，建成投运后将参与山西电网调峰、调频等服务，有助于提升区域新能源消纳能力。
阿诗特能源261kWh储能项目落地越南
近日，阿诗特能源（RCT Power）与建发新兴能源合作，在越南胡志明市落地一座储能充电一体化项目。这是阿诗特储能产品首次进入越南市场。
项目储能容量为261kWh，采用RCTerra Class 2.0工商业储能系统，并配套120kW和60kW双枪直流充电桩，主要服务当地VinFast新能源汽车充电需求。

title: 35,000 Cars: Now We Know How 'Limited' The Chevy Bolt's Run May Be
content:
Get one while you still can. General Motors is on track to make just 35,000 Bolts before production ends, Reuters reports.
Photo by:
Mack Hogan/InsideEVs
12:52pm ET
GM has said the new Chevrolet Bolt would be a "limited run" model. Now we know just how limited.
A union official told
that the Bolt's factory is on pace to produce 35,000 of them before production ends next year.
GM sold over 62,000 Bolts in its best year for sales, 2023.
When General Motors revealed the rebooted
Chevrolet Bolt
in October, it noted that the model would have
a "limited run."
For EV fans who were looking forward to a much-needed affordable option, it was a bit of a letdown. Now we have some sense of just how "limited" the cheap EV's run will be.
GM is on pace to build 35,000 Bolts by the time production wraps up at the company's Fairfax Assembly Plant in Kansas in the first quarter of next year, a United Auto Workers official told
. According to the official, Dontay Wilson, the plant had previously been on track to make around 150,000 units. (The figures,
notes, are based on daily production at the plant and not targets passed down by GM.) GM didn't comment on the Bolt's production targets when reached by the outlet.
The Bolt's short run reflects just how difficult and unpredictable the U.S. EV landscape has become since most
federal support was vaporized
. GM canceled the aging Bolt in 2023 as it retooled the Orion factory in Michigan to produce large electric pickup trucks like the Chevy
Silverado EV
. It reversed that decision just a few months later, saying it would develop a new version of the small EV. That led to a two-year hiatus for GM's cheapest EV in 2024 and 2025, despite it notching record sales during its last year on sale.
More On The Chevy Bolt
unveiled the revamped model
late last year, it looked about the same but was indeed a much more competitive offering. Charging power jumped from a painfully slow 55 kW to a healthier 150 kW. A new 65-kWh lithium iron phosphate battery pack boosted range to 262 miles. It landed as one of America's cheapest EVs, at $28,995 before destination fees.
But the timing also wasn't great for any new EV. Bolt sales kicked off early this year, after the end of the EV tax credit dampened demand. While GM didn't slash its EV lineup like some of its rivals, it did cut back production of EVs. In September,
Bloomberg
reported that GM had
planned to cut Bolt production
to one shift instead of two.
Bolt sales haven't exactly taken off. The company sold 4,224 units in the first half of the year. In 2023—between two bodystyle variants, rather than today's single option—Chevy sold some 62,000 of them.

title: BMW’s Cheaper i3 Has A Smaller Battery, But Its Range Is Still Impressive
content:
The new BMW i3 40 xDrive still comes with dual-motor all-wheel drive, but its battery has been downsized.
Photo by:
2:29am ET
BMW has introduced a more affordable i3 version in Europe, which is expected to land in the U.S. too.
The new i3 40 xDrive has less power and a smaller battery pack than the i3 50 xDrive.
It still comes with dual-motor all-wheel drive, and the range estimate is solid.
Hot on the heels of
the new BMW 3 Series reveal
, the German automaker has introduced a lower-priced version of the i3 electric sedan, according to
BMW Blog
. The new BMW i3 40 xDrive is now available in Europe, but it’s expected to make its way to the United States next year, after deliveries of the top-spec version start in the first quarter.
The entry-level EV packs an 82.8-kilowatt-hour battery pack that can be charged at up to 300 kilowatts. That’s nearly 26 kWh less and a 100-kW charging-power downgrade compared to the range-topping i3 50 xDrive, but the stats are still solid.
Photo by: BMW
According to
, the base electric sedan can gain 209 miles (337 kilometers) of range after a 10-minute top-up, while the total range on a full charge is a WLTP-estimated 441 miles (710 km). Charging from 10% to 80% takes 21 minutes.
The EPA numbers are not available yet, but when it makes its way stateside, the i3 40 xDrive should be capable of delivering around 321 miles (517 km) on a full charge. That’s 147 miles less than the top-spec i3, but it’s still plenty for daily driving and the occasional road trip.
Dual-motor all-wheel drive comes standard, as attested by the xDrive badge, with a maximum output of 369 horsepower and 384 pound-feet (520 Newton-meters) of torque. That’s 94 hp and 92 lb-ft (125 Nm) less than the i3 50 xDrive, but it’s still plenty for a sensible four-door sedan, with a quoted 0-to-62 miles per hour sprint in 5.4 seconds and an electronically limited top speed of 124 miles per hour (200 kilometers per hour).
Cutting a little bit of this and a little bit of that results in a lower weight, which should mean a better driving experience, despite the lower power. Compared to the 108.7-kWh i3 50 xDrive, the lower-powered, shorter-range i3 40 xDrive is 254 pounds (115 kilograms) lighter, tipping the scales at a relatively tame-for-a-modern-car 4,607 lbs (2,090 kg).
Gallery: The New BMW i3
The best part of it all is the price. In Germany, BMW wants €59,900 for the new entry-level i3, a healthy €6,000 less than its more powerful brother. Pricing for the U.S. isn’t available yet, but it’s sure to be less than the $62,850 starting price of the 2027 i3 50 xDrive.
An even more affordable i3 is expected to debut later next year. Dubbed the i3 40 eDrive, the upcoming entry-level EV will have a single rear-mounted electric motor and the same 82.8 kWh battery as the i3 40 xDrive.
