title: Ultium Cells retrofits Tennessee plant for LMR cell production - electrive.com
content:
Ultium Cells plans to convert its battery cell plant in Spring Hill, Tennessee, USA, to produce prismatic LMR cells. The new cell chemistry is set to be used in future General Motors electric vehicles starting in 2028, offering approximately 33 per cent higher energy density than LFP at similar costs.
Spring Hill to manufacture prismatic LMR cells for GM starting in 2028.
Image: General Motors
The joint venture between General Motors and LG Energy Solution is set to begin retrofitting work later this year, with he conversion expected to be completed by 2028. According to Ultium Cells, Spring Hill could thus become the world’s first plant to mass-produce prismatic LMR cells.
LMR stands for lithium-manganese-rich, a chemistry featuring a high manganese content in the cathode. GM and LG Energy Solution view this as a middle ground between cost-effective LFP cells and energy-dense high-nickel chemistries. Ultium Cells claims around 33 per cent higher energy density compared to LFP at similar costs. However, the company does not provide specific energy density figures.
The new cells are intended for use in future GM electric vehicles. As early as 2025, GM and LG Energy Solution had announced their plan to bring
prismatic LMR cells
to market maturity by 2028. At the time, the primary focus was on their use in electric pickups and large SUVs.
Ultium Cells aligns Spring Hill with new strategy
The retrofitting of Spring Hill aligns with a broader reorganisation of GM’s battery strategy. In June, the company’s battery chief, Kurt Kelty,
that LMR could play a central role in the portfolio in the future, and LFP might no longer have a place in electric vehicles.
The LFP cells produced in Spring Hill since June 2026 are intended for stationary energy storage systems by
LG Energy Solution Vertech
and not for electric vehicles. For vehicles, GM is now focusing more on LMR as well as continuing to use high-nickel cells for particularly long-range models.
However, LMR technology is not yet fully mature. Current challenges include durability, capacity loss, and limited fast-charging capability. GM and LG Energy Solution have been working on manganese-rich cell chemistries for years.
In the future, Spring Hill is set to unite multiple cell chemistries and formats under one roof. In addition to LMR and LFP, Ultium Cells will also produce high-nickel cells there; both pouch and prismatic cell formats are to be manufactured. Investments in the programmes and further site measures are expected to total around one billion US dollars by 2030. The retrofitting is also expected to create 500 new jobs. The site currently employs around 1,200 people.

title: Vianode and FAAM report successful graphite recycling from battery waste - electrive.com
content:
Norwegian battery material specialist Vianode and Italian battery manufacturer FAAM have demonstrated how waste graphite from battery production can be recycled into high-performance anode material. Both parties now aim to scale their approach for industrial use.
Image: Vianode
As part of a joint development programme,
processed graphite concentrate – recovered from anode production waste at
battery manufacturer FAAM
– into new battery material. According to Vianode, subsequent tests have shown that the recycled product “electrochemical performance comparable to virgin graphite materials”.
In the project, Vianode contributed its manufacturing technology for synthetic graphite, while FAAM provided its expertise in battery production. The partners describe their demonstration as another step towards solving one of the battery industry’s biggest circular economy challenges: recovering and reusing graphite while maintaining the performance, purity and consistency required for lithium-ion batteries.
Building on the results now presented, the companies aim to expand their collaboration to scale the recycling process for industrial use and further integrate recycled graphite into battery production. According to an accompanying statement, the goal is to enable a circular solution that improves resource efficiency, reduces waste and strengthens regional battery supply chains.
Background: While recycling infrastructure for battery metals such as nickel, cobalt and copper is advancing, graphite recycling remains a complex challenge. “Due to stringent requirements for material purity and battery performance, large-scale recovery and reuse of battery-grade graphite has remained limited,” states Vianode’s headquarters in Oslo. However, the current collaboration demonstrates a viable path to closing this gap.
“This collaboration demonstrates that graphite recycling can be both high-performing and scalable,” said Stefan Bergold, CCO at Vianode. “By leveraging our proprietary graphite technology, we can return production scrap directly back into the battery value chain without compromising quality. It also demonstrates the importance of European companies joining forces to strengthen regional supply chains and accelerate the transition to a more sustainable battery industry.” The Norwegian battery material specialist
also intends
to work closely with the German battery recycling company Cylib in this context.
Andrea Civitillo, CEO at FAAM, adds: “This achievement confirms that circularity for graphite is no longer a theoretical objective, but a concrete and scalable industrial reality. By combining our manufacturing expertise with Vianode’s advanced materials technology, we are demonstrating that production scrap can be reintegrated into the process without compromising performance.”

title: 1,500-mph F-16 gets drop-in combat tech to spot friend from foe faster
content: BAE Systems has received U.S. certification for a new Identification Friend or Foe (IFF) system designed to help F-16 pilots identify aircraft during combat operations.The Department of War awarded AIMS certification to the AN/APX-127(V)1 Combined Interrogator Transponder. The approval confirms compatibility with identification standards used by U.S. and NATO forces.IFF systems help military aircraft determine whether another aircraft belongs to friendly forces. That job becomes harder when pilots operate in crowded airspace or face rapidly changing threats.BAE Systems designed the new CIT to handle both sides of the process. The unit combines interrogation and transponder functions in a single box.Smaller path to modernizationThe AN/APX-127(V)1 keeps the same form factor as several CIT systems already used on U.S. and international aircraft. Operators can use it as a drop-in replacement for the AN/APX-113(V), AN/APX-125(V), and AN/APX-126(V).That compatibility can simplify upgrades for existing F-16 fleets. Maintainers would not need to redesign the surrounding installation for the newer identification equipment.The system also uses an open architecture. Engineers can introduce software updates without replacing the main hardware. That matters for aircraft expected to remain in service for decades. Digital systems can become outdated long before the airframe reaches the end of its service life.Seth Guanu, BAE Systems’ Combat Identification Products program area director, said the company designed the system with future missions in mind.“We are investing in the next generation of our IFF technology to support our customers’ missions for today and tomorrow,” Guanu said. He said the system gives pilots added security and real-time information across different threat environments.Mode 5 brings secure identificationThe certification covers AIMS Mark XIIB IFF with Mode S and Mode 5 capabilities. Mode 5 supports encrypted identification exchanges between compatible military systems.Secure identification helps pilots distinguish friendly aircraft from potential threats during complex operations. The information can support decisions when several aircraft operate within the same battlespace.The AN/APX-127(V)1 also adds receive channels for passive acquisition of Mode 5 Level 2 signals. It supports Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast In as well.The additional channels let the system receive more information about nearby aircraft. That data can supplement the CIT’s primary identification functions.Cybersecurity also features in the upgraded system. BAE Systems says the CIT supports current cryptographic requirements and cybersecurity resilience.More processing for future upgradesThe architecture also addresses the growing problem of electronic obsolescence across older aircraft fleets. F-16s can remain operational for decades, even as individual onboard systems require repeated upgrades.BAE Systems increased the CIT’s processing capacity and left room for future capabilities. Software updates can add functionality without forcing operators to replace the entire unit.The company has delivered more than 1,500 interrogators, 6,000 combined interrogator transponder systems, and 16,000 transponders over more than 80 years.Its IFF equipment supports U.S. and coalition operations across air defense, weapons systems, air traffic control, and range instrumentation.The certification gives F-16 operators a newer identification system without requiring a major change to the aircraft’s existing installation. The combination of drop-in compatibility, secure Mode 5 identification, and upgradeable software gives the system a longer runway for future modernization.

title: 3D-woven carbon-carbon tech lands $21.2M for hypersonic vehicles
content: Albany Engineered Composites will spend the next 30 months developing a new manufacturing base for carbon-carbon components used in hypersonic vehicles and solid rocket motors.The U.S. government has awarded Albany $21.2 million through its Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment program. The award supports work aimed at moving carbon-carbon thermal protection systems toward scalable domestic production.The project will be handled by Albany’s AEC Advanced Programs business. U.S. Army Contracting Command – Rock Island and Cornerstone Other Transaction Authority issued the award.Hypersonics need more capacityCarbon-carbon composites can survive environments that push conventional aerospace materials to their limits. That makes them particularly useful around hypersonic vehicles and rocket motors.Hypersonic vehicles generate intense heat as they move through the atmosphere at extreme speeds. Their thermal protection systems must shield critical structures without adding unnecessary weight.Solid rocket motors create another harsh operating environment. Their components face extreme temperatures during propulsion, placing similarly demanding requirements on thermal protection materials.The challenge extends beyond developing materials that can survive those conditions. Manufacturers also need reliable processes that can produce complex components repeatedly.Chris Stone, president of Albany Engineered Composites, said manufacturing presents a major challenge for these defense systems.“Hypersonic systems and solid rocket motors place extraordinary demands on the material systems,” Stone said. He added that Albany wants to establish the capacity needed to support production at scale.That production focus separates the project from a purely materials-development effort. Albany will work on the equipment, facility and processes needed to turn advanced composites into repeatable products.New production setupAlbany plans to establish a vertically integrated carbon-carbon manufacturing facility as part of the program.The company will begin with engineering studies and facility planning. Those efforts will guide equipment purchases and the selection of suppliers.Production engineering will also play a major role. Albany intends to install manufacturing equipment and develop the supporting infrastructure needed for carbon-carbon thermal protection systems.The company brings several existing composite manufacturing technologies to the effort. Its capabilities include 3D-woven near-net-shape preforms and Resin Transfer Molding.Those methods can help engineers create complex composite structures with less material waste and fewer manufacturing steps. Albany will combine them with its carbon-carbon densification capabilities.That combination matters because carbon-carbon production involves more than forming an initial composite structure. Manufacturers must also process the material to achieve the properties required for extreme environments.Strengthening U.S. productionThe project targets a broader problem across advanced defense manufacturing. Developing a capable component means little if industry cannot produce it at sufficient scale.Albany’s planned facility will add U.S.-based capacity for carbon-carbon thermal protection systems. The work could support future programs that require these materials in larger quantities.Brent Stevenson, Albany’s vice president of emerging markets and technology, said production readiness remains important for both mission areas.He pointed to Albany’s experience with 3D-woven composite preforms and Resin Transfer Molding. Those capabilities, he said, provide a foundation for developing scalable manufacturing methods.The award will cover facility development, equipment installation, and production engineering during the 30-month effort. Albany will also work through supplier selection and other steps needed to establish the manufacturing line.

title: Boeing to build US Navy's 6th-generation F/A-XX fighter jet fleet
content: The Pentagon has awarded Boeing a $20 billion contract to build the U.S. Navy’s next-generation F/A-XX fighter, officials announced on Tuesday. The sixth-generation aircraft will replace the Navy’s F/A-18 Super Hornet fleet beginning in the 2030s under the Next Generation Air Dominance program.The carrier-based fighter is being developed to extend the reach and survivability of U.S. naval aviation. It is also expected to operate alongside unmanned systems as the Navy develops a new generation of carrier aircraft.The contract gives Boeing its second major U.S. sixth-generation fighter program after the company was selected in 2025 to develop the Air Force’s F-47.Boeing wins Navy fighter competitionBoeing was competing with Northrop Grumman for the F/A-XX contract. The Navy said the new aircraft will incorporate open mission systems architecture, advanced mission systems and greater operational reach and capacity.The approach is intended to give the fighter greater flexibility as mission requirements and supporting technologies evolve.“It’s an honor to be selected to produce the Navy’s first sixth-generation platform. Backed by decades of work, bolstered by game-changing innovations and solidified by the investments we’ve made in new facilities uniquely suited to build multiple products with next-generation capabilities, our dedicated and talented team is ready to execute this critical program,” said Steve Parker, president and chief executive officer, Boeing Defense, Space & Security.Northrop Grumman acknowledged Boeing’s selection after competing for the program.“For F/A-XX, Northrop Grumman offered a highly survivable, digitally advanced sixth-generation fighter to the U.S. Navy,” Northrop said Tuesday. “We look forward to receiving additional information about their selection.”Super Hornet replacement takes shapeThe F/A-XX is intended to succeed the Navy’s F/A-18 Super Hornets during the 2030s. Its development is tied to the future of carrier aviation, where crewed fighters are expected to work with unmanned aircraft.At a May 2026 hearing, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle told a U.S. Senate panel that the next-generation system needed to “extend the reach, survivability and lethality” and be expected to work with unmanned systems.“Failure to field next-generation carrier aviation capability on schedule will introduce risk to air superiority, strike reach and the long-term viability of carrier-based operations in contested environments,” Caudle said.The Navy has provided limited information about the aircraft because its technical and program details remain classified.Boeing prepares production facilitiesBoeing said construction is continuing at its secure manufacturing facility in St. Louis, Missouri. The company describes the site as the largest of its kind in the United States and plans to use it as part of an all-digital aerospace design and manufacturing system.“Investment in facilities is just one part of the story; we’re also investing in technology and people so that we can deliver for our customers,” Parker added.The company says its investment is intended to support production of future combat aircraft, including the F/A-XX.Classified fighter enters next phaseThe Navy’s contract begins a major phase in the development of a fighter whose design remains largely undisclosed. Boeing said the technical and programmatic details of F/A-XX remain classified under U.S. national security and export laws.“Delivering two advanced fighters in parallel was always our plan, and we invested accordingly. We are ready and able to build multiple concurrent future combat aircraft franchise programs,” Parker noted.Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael Duffey described the program as a long-term investment in U.S. air combat capabilities.“The F/A-XX platform represents a crucial, non-negotiable investment in America’s national security and long-term air combat capabilities,” he said. “We are joining forces with Boeing to field these capabilities.”

title: China launches 4500-meter deep sea robot for South China Sea mission
content: China has reportedly launched a domestically developed deep-sea robot capable of operating at depths of up to 4,500 meters (14,764 feet) for a scientific expedition in the South China Sea. This added another piece to the country’s growing fleet of underwater exploration technologies.The 4,500-meter-class work-class robot departed Weihai Port in Shandong on September 28 and is heading to the South China Sea for a joint expedition with the Harbin Institute of Technology’s Weihai branch, according to Chinese state media. The mission is intended to test the complete system under real-world conditions and help move the technology from laboratory development toward industrial applications.The robot is equipped with a domestically developed seven-axis multifunction hydraulic manipulator. It incorporates technologies developed to address more than 30 technical challenges, including pressure-resistant sealing, high-power propulsion, long-distance underwater communications and multimodal autonomous navigation.It is designed for tasks including deep-sea oil and gas operations, underwater pipeline inspections, mineral-resource exploration, scientific sampling and emergency salvage.Built for the extreme deep seaAccording to CTGN, the vehicle’s 4,500-meter operating class puts it in an environment where pressure, communications, and navigation become major engineering challenges. China’s latest system is part of a broader push to develop domestically produced equipment that can operate farther below the surface and perform increasingly complex tasks.The country’s deep-sea capabilities have expanded across remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), and other robotic systems. In 2025, for example, China’s Haiqin 6,000-meter-class (19,685-foot-class) ROV reached 4,140 meters (13,583 feet) in the South China Sea while collecting biological and sediment samples. The system was also deployed alongside the full-ocean-depth Haidou-1 for coordinated underwater operations.China has continued to expand its ability to investigate the seabed this year. Its Mengxiang drilling vessel recently reached the 5,000-meter (16,404-foot) level while obtaining basalt samples from the South China Sea basin. Two ROVs also operated for more than 358 hours in total at depths of around 4,000 meters (13,123 feet) during the mission.Mapping the seabed for resourcesDeep-sea robots can provide access to environments that are difficult and expensive for conventional vessels and human crews to investigate. That makes them useful for geological surveys, environmental monitoring and the search for mineral resources.China has been building increasingly detailed maps of seabed resources. In April, the China Geological Survey reported a geochemical dataset covering more than 10,000 survey stations in China’s eastern waters. Researchers mapped the locations and concentrations of dozens of elements, including iron, manganese, copper and rare earth elements.Chinese geological researchers have also specifically identified deep-sea rare earths, polymetallic nodules and other seabed resources as targets for exploration. A separate deep-sea drilling and monitoring robot tested in the South China Sea earlier this year collected more than 2,000 sets of geological and environmental measurements. It was identified for potential use in exploring deep-sea resources.Underwater robots are also gaining military relevanceThe same technologies that let underwater robots map the seabed can also support maritime security and military operations. China has developed larger autonomous underwater vehicles capable of seabed mapping and long-duration operations. At the same time, military-related systems have been demonstrated for underwater reconnaissance, target detection and mine-related missions.That development is occurring alongside rapid progress in autonomous underwater swarms. On August 29, a team from Northwestern Polytechnical University and Xian Tianhe Maritime Technologies deployed 116 small autonomous underwater vehicles in a 50-by-20-meter (164-by-66-foot) swimming pool. The vehicles navigated in formation without human intervention for 34 minutes and covered 500 meters (1,640 feet), setting a Guinness World Record for the most autonomous underwater vehicles operating simultaneously.The swimming-pool demonstration and the new 4,500-meter work-class robot represent different ends of the underwater robotics spectrum. One tests coordinated autonomy among large numbers of small vehicles, while the other is designed to perform physical work at extreme depths.Together with China’s expanding seabed mapping, drilling, and underwater vehicle programs, they point to a growing effort to develop robotic systems that can survey, monitor, and work in parts of the ocean that remain difficult for humans to access.

title: China reaches 100 million hydrogen-boron fusion reactions per second
content: A clean energy firm in China has just achieved hydrogen-boron fusion reactions in the EXL-50U spherical tokamak, the nation’s first medium-scale spherical torus experimental device, at a rate exceeding 100 million per second.Hebei-based ENN Group revealed that the experiment resulted in more than 100 million fusion reactions per second. It is the first hydrogen-boron fusion reaction achieved by a commercial fusion company on its own device.Unlike deuterium-tritium (D-T) fuel, the primary fuel used in mainstream fusion research, hydrogen-boron fusion does not produce high-energy neutrons as its primary product. Instead a hydrogen proton fuses with a boron-11 nucleus. The reaction releases energy and produces alpha particles, or helium nuclei.The company announced the achievement on Monday, September 28. According to the researchers, it could provide novel insights into hydrogen-boron fusion. Fusion reaction milestoneMost fusion projects, including the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) in France, focus on D-T fusion because it can be achieved under less demanding conditions than alternative fuel cycles. It combines a deuterium nucleus with a tritium nucleus, producing helium-4, a high-energy neutron, and 17.6 megaelectronvolts (MeV) of energy.However, tritium is radioactive, scarce in nature, and expensive. D-T fusion also releases energetic neutrons that can damage the reactor materials and induce radioactivity in surrounding components. Hydrogen-boron fusion, by contrast, relies on comparatively abundant fuels and primarily produces charged alpha particles rather than high-energy neutrons.the EXL-50U (ENN Xuanlong-50) was built between 2018 and 2019.Credit: ENN GroupHowever, hydrogen-boron fusion is considerably harder to achieve as it requires vastly higher temperatures and strict confinement conditions. So, instead of trying to raise the temperature of the entire plasma, the team combined high-energy neutral beam injection with radio frequency waves. This stimulated particles in an energy range where hydrogen-boron reactions are more likely to occur, known as the first resonance peak. The process generated large numbers of energetic, or fast, protons in the plasma. These, then collided with boron nuclei and helped drive the fusion reaction rate beyond 100 million reactions per second. A fusion power raceThe company said more than 10 experts from international research institutes and universities reviewed the results. Meanwhile, repeatable measurements of alpha particles produced during the experiment provided evidence that the hydrogen-boron fusion reactions had, in fact, taken place.Yang Yuanming, an ENN engineer who led the fusion project, said that hydrogen-boron fusion has attracted interest from private fusion developers, including US-based TAE Technologies and Germany’s Marvel Fusion. He stressed that hydrogen and boron fuels are abundant and readily accessible.The approach could also offer another benefit. Hydrogen-boron fusion produces energetic charged particles. Future systems could potentially convert their energy directly into electricity, without using heat to make steam and power a turbine.However, there are still technical hurdles to overcome before the reaction could be used in a practical power plant. The team is now working to push the plasma to more extreme conditions. “[We will] strive to get the plasma to 100 million degrees Celsius (180 million degrees Fahrenheit) as soon as possible,” Yang said.SCMP reported that the company is also moving ahead with its next experimental platform. Earlier this month, it held a groundbreaking ceremony for Helong-2, its third-generation fusion device.

title: Fusion-built gyrotron to blast rock for deep geothermal energy
content: Quaise Energy is turning to hardware developed for fusion reactors to help drill into some of Earth’s hottest underground rock without conventional drill bits.Kyoto Fusioneering (KF) has received an order from Quaise for a gyrotron system that will power the company’s millimeter-wave drilling technology. The system generates high-power electromagnetic waves that can ablate, or vaporize, rock as a borehole advances.Quaise is developing the approach to reach superhot geothermal resources at depths and temperatures where conventional mechanical drilling can become difficult or uneconomical. Because energy is delivered from the surface as millimeter waves, the method does not require drilling hardware at the bottom of the hole.The agreement, signed August 17, marks the first commercial order for KF’s plasma-heating technology outside the fusion industry. The technology was originally developed because fusion experiments require powerful electromagnetic waves to heat plasma to extreme temperatures.Fusion hardware drills deeperAt the heart of the system is a gyrotron, a specialized vacuum electronic device capable of producing high-power millimeter waves. Quaise plans to direct that energy underground to heat rock intensely enough to remove it, replacing the mechanical cutting action of conventional drill bits.The company’s drilling concept emerged from more than a decade of research at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). Accessing superhot rock could allow geothermal projects to tap much higher-temperature resources and potentially generate large amounts of continuous power.KF already builds gyrotrons operating at frequencies from 28 GHz to 236 GHz. Its fusion projects include two dual-frequency units for the UK Atomic Energy Authority’s MAST Upgrade and a 1-megawatt system for Tokamak Energy’s ST40.The company has also supplied the first of two gyrotrons for the U.S. Department of Energy’s DIII-D National Fusion Facility. It has completed the design of a 1.5- to 2-megawatt-class system for Germany’s Wendelstein 7-X stellarator and ASDEX Upgrade. But drilling presents a different engineering challenge.Millimeter waves run continuouslyMany existing fusion experiments operate in pulses lasting only seconds. A geothermal drilling system, however, needs its millimeter-wave source to keep running as the borehole advances. KF said the gyrotron ordered by Quaise is specifically designed for continuous operation.That requirement could also benefit future fusion power plants. Unlike today’s experimental machines, commercial reactors are expected to require plasma-heating equipment capable of sustained operation. Building continuous-duty gyrotrons for geothermal drilling could therefore help develop technology needed by both industries.KF has been working on high-power, continuous-operation gyrotrons and power supplies for superhot geothermal applications under Japan’s NEDO Deep-Tech Startups Support Program since 2024. The Quaise contract is the first commercial order to emerge from that work.“The gyrotron supply chain has to grow well beyond its current size to meet what fusion will need, and it has to grow before that demand arrives, not after. KF is investing in that capability now and taking commercial work that builds it. This work with Quaise is an important part of that,” said Takashi Imai, Group CEO, Plasma Heating Group, Kyoto Fusioneering.KF plans to use experience from the project to support next-generation geothermal development, including efforts to access deep, high-temperature resources.

title: New EV concept tackles pollution electric cars don't get blamed for
content: A group of students has built an electric car that tackles a rising source of pollution: particles from tires and brakes. Their team, TU/ecomotive, created VENTRA, a sustainable concept car that captures these particles while driving and uses lightweight materials to help reduce tire wear. They revealed the car to encourage the auto industry to address emissions that come from more than just the exhaust.The student team from Eindhoven University of Technology pointed out that electric cars still create particulate matter, even without tailpipe emissions. Tire and brake wear, along with particles from the road, all add to pollution near roads.“No exhaust emissions does not necessarily mean no emissions,” said team manager Tim Spencer. Electric cars can also place greater loads on tires because they are generally heavier and can deliver strong acceleration.An electric system captures particlesVENTRA’s main feature is a system that collects tiny particles near the wheels. Rather than using a regular filter, it electrically charges the particles.The charged particles are then attracted toward a grounded collection surface positioned near the wheel. Once captured, they remain attached to the collection surface rather than continuing into the surrounding air.The collection system can be cleaned after driving with a vacuum cleaner or water. The students also plan to recycle the captured material. Their concept demonstrates this approach by reusing the collected particles as part of the vehicle’s interior.Computer simulations indicate that the system can collect about 24 percent of particles when the car is moving between 31 and 50 mph. At lower speeds, it could capture up to 42 percent.TU/ecomotive with VENTRA. (Image credit: Sarp Gürel)Cutting pollution through lower weightVENTRA also tackles particulate pollution by reducing the amount the vehicle generates in the first place. The team focused on the vehicle’s chassis, which can account for a significant portion of a car’s weight.Much of VENTRA’s chassis uses lightweight carbon-fiber-reinforced thermoplastic panels. This cuts almost 220 pounds from the vehicle.Lower weight means less force is placed on the tires during driving. The students noted that this can reduce tire wear and therefore decrease the amount of particulate matter released from the tires.The concept also includes the Clean Drive system, which monitors driving behavior. A dashboard display provides guidance aimed at smoother driving, including more gradual acceleration, gentler braking and less unnecessary steering.(Image credit: Sarp Gürel)Students target a wider emissions problemThe team said its work highlights a pollution source that can receive less attention than exhaust emissions. Tiny particulate matter can enter deep into the lungs, while some particles can potentially reach the bloodstream depending on their size and composition.Exposure has been associated with health risks including cardiovascular disease, strokes, impaired lung development, COPD, and lung cancer.The issue is also gaining regulatory attention in Europe. From November 2026, Euro 7 rules will introduce requirements covering emissions from brake and tire wear.“With VENTRA, we want to show what solutions are possible and encourage the automotive industry to look beyond the exhaust pipe when it comes to emissions,” Spencer added.

title: New catalyst could turn wood waste into cleaner jet fuel ingredients
content: A Rowan University research team is investigating how woody biomass could replace petroleum-derived components in aviation fuel, helping reduce the United States’ dependence on fossil fuels for flight.The project focuses on lignin, a natural polymer found in woody biomass, and a catalyst designed to convert selected molecules into aromatic compounds suitable for jet fuel.Jun Hee Jang, an assistant professor of chemical engineering at the Henry M. Rowan College of Engineering, received a $199,999 National Science Foundation grant to investigate the process and assess its economic potential.Replacing petroleum-derived fuel componentsAviation fuel contains a blend of compounds, including linear hydrocarbons, branched hydrocarbons, and aromatics. Producing sustainable alternatives requires addressing these different components rather than replacing the entire blend with a single substance.Researchers have already established processes for converting biomass, including vegetable oils, into hydrocarbons. Aromatic compounds, however, are typically sourced from petroleum, leaving an opportunity to develop renewable alternatives.Jang’s research examines whether lignin can supply those aromatics. The work forms part of broader efforts to expand sustainable aviation fuel production using renewable resources and reduce reliance on petroleum-based aviation fuel through 2050.If successful, the approach could support domestic fuel production while adding value to unused biomass feedstocks.The project targets aviation fuel components, with the catalyst’s performance and the process’s commercial viability still to be evaluated.A catalyst that selects by sizeBefore lignin can be converted into useful fuel components, researchers must break it into smaller molecules. That step produces a mixture containing molecules of different sizes.Some smaller molecules can be upgraded into aviation fuel components, while larger molecules cannot undergo the same conversion. Efficiently separating these groups presents a central challenge for the research team.Jang and his colleagues plan to develop a size-selective catalyst with a porous structure that admits smaller molecules while preventing larger ones from entering.Inside those pores, the smaller molecules can be converted into jet fuel-range aromatic compounds. The design therefore aims to control which parts of the mixture reach the catalyst’s conversion sites.Meanwhile, the larger molecules remain outside the porous structure, preserving properties that could make them useful in other applications.Turning potential waste into another productIn conventional catalytic processes, the larger molecules can become waste products. Jang’s approach instead seeks to retain them as potentially valuable co-products alongside the fuel aromatics.“By applying this catalyst, we can produce not only fuel aromatics, but also larger molecules that could have further functional applications,” Jang said. One doctoral student and one postdoctoral researcher will join Jang on the project. The postdoctoral researcher brings experience in designing chemical synthesis methods, while the doctoral student will conduct experiments and analyze the resulting products.Together, they will investigate how catalyst design affects reaction performance and evaluate the economics of scaling the proposed biomass-to-aviation fuel process.The grant comes through NSF’s Engineering Research Initiation program, which helps faculty at emerging research institutions establish independent engineering research programs.

title: New home wallpaper absorbs humidity from air to generate power for devices
content: Rooftop solar panels have officially hit the mainstream, topping over 6 million American homes. But your roof is no longer the only domestic real estate eyeing a green energy makeover.What if your living room walls could harvest electricity from thin air? Researchers at Binghamton University have unveiled a paper-based, energy-harvesting “wallpaper” that converts indoor humidity into real electric current. “We put a lot of energy into HVAC systems to remove moisture from the air, but if we use this concept, we could reduce or control moisture levels while also generating electricity,” said Professor Seokheun “Sean” Choi, a faculty member at the Thomas J. Watson College of Engineering and Applied Science’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering. Powered by moistureThe wallpaper technology depends on tiny moist-electric generators (MEGs). These microscopic powerhouses draw ambient water vapor from the air. Once trapped, the moisture forces ions inside the material to separate, creating a natural concentration gradient. That subtle shift creates a steady voltage between the front and back of the paper, and interestingly, no sunlight is required. Engineers have played with moisture-harvesting tech before, but previous designs focused almost exclusively on the unpredictable outdoors. Rainstorms can cause power to spike, while blistering sun can kill it completely.On the other hand, indoor air is a stable environment. Most homes stay between 30 percent and 60 percent humidity year-round. Better yet, everyday human life constantly recharges the system. Cooking dinner, taking a hot shower, or simply breathing out fills the room with untapped potential. To make the tech cheap, functional, and attractive, the team drew on “papertronics” — the art of printing electronic circuits directly onto paper. The layout works like a miniature circuit board. Glycerol applied along the outer edges acts as a sponge, snatching water molecules from the surrounding room. At the center sits a raised polymer layer patterned with wax. This central structure carefully controls how water evaporates, maintaining a directional flow of moisture across the sheet to keep electricity flowing continuously. Wallpaper to run IoT devicesThe researchers demonstrated the design’s practical power by building a full-scale wallpaper sheet with 1,596 interconnected units. A single unit produces roughly 0.34 V with a power density of 2.2 µW/cm² at 80 percent relative humidity. This large-scale array generated enough continuous electricity to power a wireless keyboard without any batteries.Beyond power, the array dropped indoor humidity in a test space from 38 percent down to 32 percent, proving its dual role as a passive dehumidifier. Nobody wants a living room wall crisscrossed with messy wires. To fix the aesthetic problem, the researchers routed every connection behind the wallpaper. You will not power a refrigerator with paper walls, at least not anytime soon. These sheets yield modest microwatt-level power, designed specifically for low-draw devices. Think smart thermostats, ambient temperature sensors, indoor climate monitors, and wireless keyboards. Instead of swapping out toxic batteries every few months, the growing constellation of Internet-of-Things (IoT) gizmos in modern homes could simply run off the walls.Homeowners could generate clean energy and ease the strain on their air conditioners by letting the walls do some of the work. Should Choi’s vision reach mass production, the next frontier of home energy efficiency could soon be hanging right on your walls.The findings were published in the journal Advanced Energy.

title: New laser sensor could track hydrogen leaks, underground sources
content:
Hydrogen is the smallest molecule in the universe. But its size makes finding and tracking it a massive challenge. Brint Tech co-founder and CEO Kathy Andersen believes that laser sensing could help solve that problem.
Andersen studied at Iowa’s Grinnell College. Before co-founding Brint Tech in June 2024, she served as the Director of Innovation and Entrepreneurship at the Lincoln Partnership for Economic Development. She also worked on energy and air-quality sensing devices and industrial product development.

title: Second ship of 100,000-ton Ford class carrier is set for 2027 delivery
content: The U.S. Navy has taken preliminary acceptance of the future USS John F. Kennedy (CVN 79), allowing the aircraft carrier and its crew to begin additional at-sea testing and training while Newport News Shipbuilding completes the vessel’s remaining systems work.The milestone was reached on September 29 following the carrier’s successful completion of Acceptance Trials in August. John F. Kennedy is being built by Newport News Shipbuilding, a division of HII, and remains on schedule for formal delivery to the Navy in spring 2027.Preliminary acceptance does not mean the carrier has formally entered Navy service. Instead, it allows the ship and its crew to conduct more testing and build proficiency underway while the shipbuilder continues final systems testing.“Achieving preliminary acceptance marks a new phase for the ship and her crew, allowing them to get more water under the keel as they test and train underway,” said Capt. Mark Johnson, the Navy’s program manager for Gerald R. Ford-class new construction.Carrier is nearly completeAccording to the Navy, John F. Kennedy is approximately 99 percent complete, with all major systems now finished. Newport News Shipbuilding is concentrating on final ship systems testing, including testing of the remaining four Advanced Weapons Elevators.The Advanced Weapons Elevators are a major part of the carrier’s weapons-handling system, moving weapons and other ordnance between the ship’s magazines and the flight deck. Completion and testing of the remaining elevators is therefore among the work still required before formal delivery.The Navy says preliminary acceptance lets a continue shipboard testing and crew training without waiting for every remaining shipbuilder activity to be completed. This parallel approach is intended to put CVN 79 on the fastest available path toward delivery and eventual combat readiness.Second Ford-class carrier moves closer to deliveryJohn F. Kennedy is the second carrier in the Navy’s Gerald R. Ford class, following the USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN 78). The class incorporates new systems and design changes intended to improve aircraft launch and recovery operations, weapons handling, and overall carrier operations.For Kennedy’s crew, the latest milestone means more time underway to become familiar with the ship while testing continues. The Navy and shipbuilder can also use this period to identify and address issues that emerge during operations at sea before formal delivery.The carrier previously completed its Acceptance Trials in August, an important testing phase in which the Navy evaluates whether the ship’s major systems and capabilities meet required performance standards. The subsequent preliminary acceptance marks a transition toward more extensive underway activity.The Navy’s current plan calls for formal delivery of John F. Kennedy in spring 2027. Until then, the ship will continue undergoing testing, training, and final construction work.Final testing continues before deliveryAlthough the carrier is almost complete, the remaining work illustrates why preliminary acceptance is not the same as operational readiness. The final Advanced Weapons Elevator tests and other ship systems testing must still be completed before the Navy formally accepts the vessel for service.The Navy says the arrangement allows its sailors to gain additional experience operating the ship while Newport News Shipbuilding finishes its remaining responsibilities.For CVN 79, the represents a step between construction and formal delivery. The carrier can now spend more time underway, but it remains in the testing and training phase as the Navy and HII work toward its planned 2027 delivery.

title: Seven-year hydrophone record maps Arctic sounds 500 meters below ice
content: A hydrophone sitting half a kilometer beneath the Beaufort Sea has spent seven years listening to the Arctic.Its recordings reveal how dramatically the underwater environment changes throughout the year. That matters for scientists trying to spot signals from earthquakes, explosions, and human activity.Researchers at Los Alamos National Laboratory analyzed the continuous recordings to establish a long-term acoustic reference for the region. Such records remain uncommon in the Arctic, where harsh conditions make sustained monitoring difficult.The team used data from one of NOAA’s Ocean Noise Reference Station sensors. The station sits 500 meters below the sea surface and records sounds traveling through the water.That long view gives researchers something they rarely have in the Arctic. It shows what normal underwater conditions sound like before an unusual event enters the picture.Ice turns into signalSea ice plays a major role in shaping that acoustic environment. Its influence becomes especially pronounced during the Arctic winter.Moving and deforming ice produces substantial underwater noise. Summer brings a different pattern, with waves becoming a dominant source of sound.Those seasonal shifts can complicate event detection. A signal that stands out during one season could become harder to distinguish during another. “Before you can reliably detect something unusual, you have to understand what’s normal,” said Siobhan Niklasson, the study’s lead author.Niklasson and her colleagues used the seven-year record to examine those changing conditions. Their analysis shows how the acoustic background varies across the year.The researchers also identified noise from seismic surveys that use air guns to investigate geology beneath the seafloor. Such surveys add another human-made source to the Arctic soundscape.Ocean carries distant signalsHydrophones can detect sounds that travel considerable distances through seawater. That capability makes them useful for monitoring remote parts of the Arctic.Earthquakes can generate underwater acoustic signals that reach sensors far from their origin. Explosions can create distinct signals as well, depending on their location and surrounding conditions. Ship traffic adds another layer to the acoustic picture. So do waves, wind, and marine activity.Separating those sounds requires more than simply detecting an increase in underwater noise. Scientists need enough background data to determine whether a signal represents something unusual.The Los Alamos study provides that context at one Arctic location. It also shows how environmental conditions can influence what monitoring systems can detect.Demand surgesThe timing matters as activity across the Arctic continues to change. Retreating sea ice is opening waters that were once difficult to reach for much of the year.More ships and resource exploration could introduce additional acoustic activity. Geopolitical interest in the region also creates greater demand for reliable monitoring.A longer acoustic record could help researchers track those changes against an established baseline. It could also improve their understanding of when natural noise masks signals of interest.The study does not attempt to create a single system for monitoring the entire Arctic. Instead, it provides a detailed reference for interpreting sounds recorded beneath the Beaufort Sea.Seven years of continuous listening now give researchers a clearer picture of that underwater environment. The findings could help determine what stands out when the Arctic gets unusually loud.The study was published in the Journal of the Acoustical Society of America.

title: Texas A&M students build 50-pound drone that carries 110 pounds
content: A team of Texas A&M University aerospace engineering students has built a 50-pound drone capable of carrying 110 pounds over four nautical miles, demonstrating a lightweight design at the first Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) Lift Challenge.Led by aerospace engineering professor Dr. Moble Benedict, the Advanced Vertical Flight Laboratory team was one of just six groups among 87 that completed the competition course on August 9 near the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force in Dayton, Ohio.The challenge required teams to transport as much weight as possible over the four-nautical-mile course. The Texas A&M drone completed the flight in 12 minutes while carrying barbell weights more than twice its own weight.Carbon fiber frame weighs just six poundsThe team’s main engineering achievement was reducing the drone’s structural weight while maintaining the strength needed to carry a heavy payload. The final design uses a carbon fiber frame with a central battery and eight arms supporting the motors and propellers. Rather than relying on conventional nuts and bolts, which can add significant weight, the students bonded the structure together.The resulting frame weighs just six pounds without the battery, despite supporting a drone capable of carrying 110 pounds. “We had to attach the weight in a clever way to allow the structure to be as light as it is,” Benedict said. “Allowing a six-pound drone to carry 110 pounds is the main innovation that we are proud of.”The team went through several design iterations before arriving at the final configuration, building five prototypes over just eight months. Benedict said the process would ideally take a couple of years, with much of the development time spent on design work and virtual simulations before the physical construction began.Battery power shaped the drone’s designThe team selected a battery-powered propulsion system, but its weight presented a major engineering challenge. The battery accounted for more than half of the drone’s total weight, forcing the students to account for its mass throughout the flight.Unlike fuel-powered aircraft, which become lighter as they consume fuel, the drone’s battery weighs the same at the beginning and end of a flight. “A battery weighs the same at the beginning of the flight as it does at the end,” team member Cayden Brown said. “We had to account for the same weight across the journey. A charged battery weighs the exact same as a dead battery.”A gas-powered system could have reduced weight, but Brown said it would have introduced greater complexity for a multirotor aircraft.Potential uses include disaster relief and surveillanceThe first DARPA Lift Challenge attracted around 480 concept submissions, with 110 teams invited to compete. Of the 87 groups that reached the competition, only six completed the course.Texas A&M’s team hopes to continue refining its prototype, which had a materials cost of approximately $10,000. Benedict said the design could eventually support applications such as disaster relief, package delivery, and surveillance.The drone remains a prototype, and the competition demonstrated its payload-carrying capability rather than establishing its readiness for operational deployment.“We’re very proud of this product,” Benedict said. “It’s still a prototype at this point, but it has the potential to be used for many realistic missions, especially for disaster relief efforts and surveillance.”

title: The 500-meter wiring harness shows how cars are being rebuilt
content:
For years, automotive engineers have had a deceptively simple way to measure how complicated a car has become: count the wiring.
A conventional car can contain several kilometers of wiring. Tesla’s Model 3 was once cited at about 1.5 kilometers. Elon Musk famously said in 2017 that the Model Y would
cut that to 100 meters
— a target that never became reality in the production vehicle.
Now a Chinese automaker is making the number a central engineering metric. Leapmotor’s new LEAP 5.0 architecture, unveiled in September, cuts the vehicle wiring harness to less than 500 meters, down from 1,500 meters when the company launched its Four-Leaf Clover architecture known as LEAP 3.0 in 2023 and 996 meters with LEAP 3.5.

title: Trump, top tech executives sign 'morally binding' safety accord
content: U.S. President Donald Trump and executives from some of the world’s biggest technology companies have signed a voluntary agreement aimed at putting safety controls around increasingly powerful artificial intelligence systems.The accord was reached Tuesday following a White House meeting attended by executives including SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. House Speaker Mike Johnson described the agreement as a “joint commitment” and a “statement of principles” covering internal controls.The agreement is expected to include internal and external reviews of AI technology. Trump said companies would largely be responsible for policing themselves rather than relying on new government restrictions.Asked whether the agreement was binding, Trump described it as “morally binding.” He also compared the document to a constitution, saying it offered “a form of protection.”Companies police themselves voluntarilyThe agreement comes as Washington debates how to respond to increasingly capable AI systems without slowing U.S. development of the technology. Trump has opposed new AI-specific regulations and favored voluntary oversight. An executive order signed in June established a program allowing companies to voluntarily provide the federal government access to powerful models before their public release.Whoever wins SI is going to win. President Trump will ensure that it's America. pic.twitter.com/dunRt4wPRY— The White House (@WhiteHouse) September 29, 2026The accord also follows Trump’s recent resistance to calls for additional safeguards. On September 14, he argued that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT,” while pointing to existing criminal and regulatory powers over technology companies.Eight days later, Trump moved to rebrand the technology. During his UN General Assembly address, he said U.S. government documents would use “super intelligence” instead of “artificial intelligence,” arguing that “artificial” makes the technology sound fake.Oversight committee under considerationDespite his resistance to additional regulation, Trump said his administration is considering an oversight committee of around 10 people that could “watch over the whole enterprise.” Details about its membership, authority or relationship with the voluntary accord have not been announced.Official. pic.twitter.com/BoTuIhxbTg— The White House (@WhiteHouse) September 29, 2026The safety debate has intensified as autonomous agents gain more capabilities. OpenAI-linked agents reportedly hit a UN Trade and Development website more than 16,000 times, while other agents breached an Australian government health website and compromised parts of Hugging Face’s systems. OpenAI has called the Hugging Face incident a “warning shot.”Some industry leaders have also sounded alarms over increasingly powerful systems. Amodei has maintained that poorly managed AI could pose a risk to humanity as a whole, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has warned that humans losing control of increasingly powerful systems is an outcome that “we must avoid.”Nvidia on Monday unveiled its Open Agent Safety Platform to keep autonomous agents within set boundaries. It combines OpenShell software with a hardware-based Sentry watchdog that Nvidia says can quarantine a suspicious agent within milliseconds if it moves beyond its permitted environment.The new accord appears to preserve Trump’s broader approach of encouraging rapid U.S. AI development while relying on voluntary commitments and company self-policing rather than new mandatory regulations. Its full text and the specific commitments made by participating companies have not yet been publicly released.

title: US firm to open solid rocket motor factory for tactical missiles
content: Avio USA has broken ground on a roughly 900,000-square-foot solid rocket motor factory in Hurt, Virginia, designed to produce thousands of motors annually for tactical missile programs.The facility at Southern Virginia Multimodal Park is expected to create approximately 1,500 technical jobs while adding a new supplier to the missile and munitions manufacturing base.Construction is scheduled to finish in late 2028, with production anticipated to begin in early 2029. The plant is being developed to serve multiple defense customers, including programs for Lockheed Martin and Raytheon.Expanding missile motor supplyThe project marks Avio USA’s first manufacturing facility in the United States. Its planned output is intended to expand the availability of solid rocket motors, a critical propulsion component for tactical missiles.Rather than supplying a single customer or missile program, the company plans to operate as an independent merchant supplier serving multiple manufacturers.“Our goal is to be an independent, open-source merchant supplier, able to support multiple customers and programs and provide major defense primes with an additional source for this critical capability,” said James Syring, CEO of Avio USA.“That means more capacity, more competition and greater resilience in the American rocket motor supply chain.”The approach gives defense manufacturers an additional sourcing option as they seek to increase production. The announcement identifies annual capacity in the thousands but does not specify an exact production target or list the missile systems whose motors will be manufactured there.Propulsion expertise meets local manufacturingAvio USA is a subsidiary of Rome-based Avio S.p.A., which develops rocket and space propulsion systems. The subsidiary operates under a Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency Special Security Agreement.The Virginia investment establishes a manufacturing presence that combines the parent company’s propulsion experience with a locally recruited workforce.“Avio USA is building more than a manufacturing facility in Virginia. We are building an American company and workforce that can bring Avio’s proven propulsion expertise to the U.S. defense market,” Syring said.Avio CEO Giulio Ranzo said the successful completion of the company’s capital raise provided resources for the investment.“Combining our proven expertise with local talent, we will support our customers and contribute to a more resilient defense supply chain,” he said. The company expects the project to generate roughly 1,500 technical positions in Southern Virginia, making workforce development a substantial part of the planned expansion.Defense manufacturers back additional capacityHITT Contracting is leading construction as the project’s general contractor. Its work covers delivery of the advanced manufacturing facility ahead of the planned production launch.Lockheed Martin and Raytheon both welcomed the additional rocket motor capacity and the opportunity to diversify their supplier networks.“This new facility is a significant step toward a more robust and diverse supply chain for solid rocket motors that are critical to our nation’s defense,” said Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed Martin Missiles & Fire Control.Raytheon’s Bob Butz, senior vice president of Operations, Supply Chain and Quality, said additional sourcing options support long-term growth across the defense industrial base.The factory’s planned early 2029 production launch would add another source of propulsion systems for tactical missile programs.

title: US scientists create soft porous material to improve lithium-ion flow
content: An interdepartmental research team at Rice University in the U.S. has developed a soft porous, and flexible material that selectively allows the movement of lithium ions and could help build better solid-state batteries in the future. Solid-state batteries are considered the future of energy storage as they rely on a solid electrolyte, which is safer and has higher energy densities. The liquid electrolyte in conventional batteries is prone to catching fire, and replacing it with one in solid state makes it less flammable. Moving lithium ions is only a part of the challenge in solid-state batteries; how the material behaves can be important too. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), a type of porous crystalline material, are usually used as solid-state electrolytes since they contain tiny, ordered channels that can either hold or move specific ions. This is a much preferred quality of an electrolyte material, but MOFs are rigid by nature, which can affect how they can remain in contact with electrodes. Porous, flexible MOFThe team of researchers from the departments of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, Chemistry and Materials Science and Nanoengineering, as well as the Advanced Materials Institute at Rice University, developed ZnBTCA that uses an aliphatic linker that makes the MOF softer and more adaptable. “MOF electrolytes are often designed primarily around how effectively they transport ions,” said Zina Deriche, a graduate student at Rice who was involved in the research. “Here, we’re showing that the mechanical properties of the framework can also be an important part of the design.”Both Zn and the aliphatic linker it is made from are abundant and hence low-cost components. In addition, the negatively charged structure makes it easier for positively charged lithium ions to move through its channels. “Bringing these properties together gives us a new way to design MOF electrolytes by considering how ions move and how the material behaves mechanically at the same time,” added Stavroula Alina Kampouri, assistant professor of chemical and biomolecular engineering at Rice in a press release. Overcoming short circuitsThe charging and discharging process inside a lithium-ion battery can create unwanted pathways through an electrolyte, raising concerns about short circuits. When they incorporated a flexible polymer into the electrolyte and placed it between lithium metal electrodes, the cells operated stably for over 300 hours, even as current increased during testing, without any short-circuiting. The researchers also replaced the sodium ions in the structure with lithium. They found that 95 percent of the mobile charge-balancing ions were lithium, and yet the structure did not break apart. This shows that mechanical flexibility, too, alongside chemical composition, pore structure, and charge, can be a design tool for researchers working on MOF electrolytes. “To our knowledge, ZnBTCA is the first MOF electrolyte built from an aliphatic linker with a flexible carbon-chain backbone,” said Sibani Lisa Biswal, chair of chemical and biomolecular engineering, at Rice. “What this work shows is that we can think beyond just the chemistry and pore structure of these materials. Mechanical flexibility can also become a design tool for developing MOF electrolytes for solid-state batteries.”The research findings were published in the journal Chemical Science.

title: US turns waste carbon into 2.5 barrels of synthetic jet fuel per day
content: A climate technology company has successfully produced synthetic aviation fuel from landfill-derived renewable natural gas (RNG) and captured industrial carbon dioxide (CO2) with its Aurora technology platform.The fuel was produced on a fully integrated demonstration line equipped with the 2.5-barrel-per-day Aurora Tri-Converter and Aurora Upgrader units. These were linked to an existing Fischer-Tropsch reactor run by Research Triangle Park (RTI).Aether Fuels, which is based in the US and Singapore, said that the demonstration covered the whole production process. It reportedly transformed waste-derived gaseous feedstocks into fully upgraded synthetic liquid jet fuel.Independent testing firm AmSpec confirmed that samples produced during the demo met the applicable ASTM specifications for Fischer-Tropsch Synthesized Paraffinic Kerosene (FT-SPK). “This is exciting progress for Aether as we march forward towards commercial deployment,” Conor Madigan, Aether Fuels CEO and co-founder, said. Jet fuel passes key testThe demo used mass-balanced renewable natural gas from landfill gas generated in Kentucky alongside captured industrial CO2. The company is believed to be the first in North America to produce ASTM-spec synthetic aviation fuel from mass-balanced RNG and captured industrial CO2 at this scale. As per Aether Fuels, the fuel complied with ASTM D7566 requirements applicable to FT-SPK. Under the ASTM D7566 standard, qualifying synthetic fuel can be blended with conventional kerosene at concentrations of up to 50 percent.Moreover, the blend requires no modifications to aircraft fuel tanks, pipelines, or airport fueling systems. Because the FT-SPK production route is already covered under ASTM D7566, the firm said its fuel does not require the establishment of a new ASTM pathway.“This demonstration proves Aether’s ability to scale up our integrated Aurora platform, take a feedstock through the complete end-to-end process, and produce on-spec synthetic aviation fuel,” Dhaval Shah, Aether Fuels CTO, said. “It is the culmination of over a year of hard work by Aether’s R&D team and is a tremendous milestone,” Shah continued, adding that the data collected during the demo is set to cut the technical risks associated with the firm’s next project.New fuel plant plannedThe achievement followed after an earlier Tri-Converter test with GTI Energy. The company now plans to develop Project Beacon, a commercial facility in Singapore with an annual production capacity of 2,000 metric tons. Set to produce around 50 barrels of fuel per day, the plant will have about 20 times the capacity of the latest demonstration equipment.“This is a significant achievement and puts us on the right track to successfully build and operate Project Beacon and the commercial projects that will follow,” Madigan said in a press release.Aether Fuels said larger projects are expected to produce ASTM D7566-compliant sustainable aviation fuel. This could reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by more than 70 percent compared with conventional jet fuel.“We started by systematically demonstrating each part of the Aurora platform at the pilot scale, then scaled our novel technology up more than 50X in standalone demo units, and in this most recent demonstration, brought these demo units together in an integrated line that produces ASTM spec jet fuel,” Madigan concluded.

title: US-backed 10,000-ton plant makes one-step steel, cuts 98% emissions
content: Hertha Metals plans to build a new U.S. facility capable of producing 10,000 tonnes of high-purity iron and steel using a single-step process that the company says can cut production costs by 25% and emissions by up to 98%.The Texas-based company raised $133.65 million in a Series A round to finance the Hertha Chalyx facility. The funding includes a $65 million equity investment from the U.S. government through the Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment program, alongside private investment led by Khosla Ventures and Doerr Capital.The plant is intended to address a major gap in the domestic supply chain for rare-earth permanent magnets. The U.S. currently imports almost all of the high-purity iron used for these magnets and has no domestic production capacity for the material, according to Hertha.Neodymium-iron-boron, or NdFeB, magnets contain roughly 70% high-purity iron by weight. They are widely used in electric vehicles, aerospace systems, radar equipment and other technologies, making domestic supplies increasingly important for U.S. manufacturing and defense.One reactor replaces severalAt the center of the project is Hertha’s Flex-HERS process, which replaces the conventional multi-step, coal-dependent blast furnace route with a single continuous reactor. The system can process different grades of iron ore and use either natural gas or hydrogen as the reducing agent.Hertha says the process can produce iron and steel at 25% lower cost than conventional blast furnaces. Using natural gas can reduce emissions by 50%, while switching to hydrogen could cut them by as much as 98%.“Every electric vehicle, aerospace platform, radar system, and data center depends on domestic iron and magnet feedstock suppliers,” said Dr. Laureen Meroueh, CEO and founder of Hertha Metals. “Hertha Chalyx closes that gap.”The facility is designed to produce both steel-grade and magnet-grade high-purity iron. Hertha says this could provide U.S. rare-earth magnet manufacturers with a domestic source of an essential feedstock as federal procurement rules drive demand for U.S.-made magnets.Production moves beyond pilotHertha already operates a 360-ton-per-year demonstration facility called Pi100 in Conroe, Texas. The company says it is currently undergoing supplier qualification with major U.S. rare-earth magnet producers.Chalyx is expected to break ground this year and will operate alongside the existing pilot plant. Together, the facilities will form an integrated site capable of producing both steel and high-purity iron.The company says its ability to use domestic iron ore while reducing reliance on conventional coal-heavy steelmaking could help establish a U.S.-based supply chain stretching from raw materials to finished magnets.The project also represents a substantial jump from Hertha’s current demonstration scale. At 10,000 tonnes of planned output, Chalyx would have nearly 28 times the annual production capacity of its existing 360-ton facility.Hertha says the combination of lower production costs, flexible ore inputs, and reduced emissions could make its process competitive with conventional steelmaking while supplying a material the U.S. currently depends on imports to obtain.

title: Watch: DYNA 2.1 humanoid handle laundry work without human assistance
content: California-based robotics firm DYNA Robotics launched DYNA 2.1, a physical agent designed to do tasks like laundry and folding clothes. The company announced the launch on September 29 and shared a video showing the humanoid in action. DYNA 2.1 completes these tasks without any human intervention, using its physical dexterity and complex reasoning skills. The firm is currently deploying the robot in hotels, laundromats, and restaurants.Its laundry demonstration moves beyond folding individual towels, showing how the machine handles a workflow that includes operating appliances, moving laundry, organizing finished stacks, and recovering from mistakes.From washing machines to folded towelsWe are releasing Dyna-2.1, the first Physical Agent that achieves reliable super long-horizon whole-body autonomy. It combines our brand-new semi-humanoid hardware with an agentic system built around Dyna-2 to handle ultra-long real-world workflows.Here is an uncut footage of… pic.twitter.com/kDt8UtS7EQ— Dyna Robotics (@DynaRobotics) September 29, 2026In a commercial laundry setting, DYNA 2.1 loads washers and dryers and actively turns the machines on. It can then bend down and reach into the back of a dryer to transfer bulk towels into a basket.Once the towels are removed, the robot snaps them flat, folds them, and sorts them into stacks according to size. It also places the finished stacks on shelves, crouching for lower storage spaces or reaching upward for higher ones.The system is designed to respond to physical errors without asking a person to intervene. If a towel falls onto the floor, it can pick it up; if a grasp fails, it can abandon that attempt and try again.“Our goal is to make general purpose robots commercially viable for real-world scenarios. Our customers need robots that complete an entire workflow for a full shift – without human babysitters – not just specific tasks,” said Lindon Gao, co-founder and CEO of Dyna Robotics.Two arms and four steerable wheelsThe robot’s hardware combines an upper torso and two arms with a base supported by four steerable wheels. Its arms accommodate either parallel-jaw grippers or dexterous hands for reaching and manipulating objects.The wheeled design provides mobility while avoiding the balancing demands associated with walking robots. Its upper body supplies the movement needed for tasks such as bending, lifting, and accessing shelves at different heights.A vision-language orchestrator reasons through complex workflows, while a whole-body controller coordinates driving and upper-body movements into integrated actions.Underlying these systems is DYNA 2, the company’s proprietary world action model. DYNA says it trained the model on one million hours of human and robot data to support physical skills and steerability.Measuring work between human interventionsDYNA evaluates the robot using Mean Time Between Interventions, or MTBI, which measures how long it operates before someone must step in.The approach focuses on sustained performance across connected tasks rather than success on an isolated demonstration. A laundry shift requires the robot to maintain progress through repeated actions, changing object positions, and occasional handling errors.During operation, the physical agent captures execution data, including the reasoning system’s decision traces and the controller’s joint loads. That information feeds back into the system through a continuous improvement loop intended to increase the amount of work completed between interventions.DYNA aims to extend the robot’s time between human interventions by feeding operational data back into the system.

title: Chloride passivation of SnO2 defects lifts carbon-based perovskite solar cell efficiency to 15.13%
content:
Chloride passivation of SnO2 defects lifts carbon-based perovskite solar cell efficiency to 15.13%
Researchers at Nanjing Tech University have developed a potassium chloride (KCl)-modified tin oxide (SnO
) electron transport layer (ETL) that suppresses interfacial defects and improves crystallization in carbon-based perovskite solar cells (PSCs). The modification, introduced during a low-temperature chemical bath deposition (CBD) process, raised the champion device's power conversion efficiency (PCE) to 15.13%, a 7.22% improvement over an unmodified reference device, while also improving long-term stability.
has become a popular alternative to TiO
as an ETL in both rigid and flexible PSCs, thanks to its high ionic conductivity and favorable energy alignment with perovskite films. Chemical bath deposition is a common way to fabricate SnO
layers because it operates at under 100°C, uses little energy, and scales well. However, aqueous CBD-grown SnO
films tend to suffer from non-uniform grain sizes and a high density of defect states, including oxygen vacancies and undercoordinated Sn4+ sites that trap charge carriers and reduce open-circuit voltage. To address this, the team introduced KCl directly into the aqueous CBD growth process.
The chloride ions passivate oxygen vacancies and undercoordinated Sn
defects in the SnO
film, promote lateral grain growth, and lower the ETL's resistivity, which improves fill factor. At the ETL/perovskite interface, the reduced defect density also supports more vertically oriented perovskite grain growth, cutting interfacial recombination and improving charge extraction. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy confirmed the successful incorporation of potassium and chlorine into the SnO
films, while X-ray diffraction showed improved crystallinity after the KCl treatment.
Beyond the efficiency gain, the modified devices showed reduced hysteresis and better moisture resistance. Unencapsulated devices retained 74.2% of their initial efficiency after 1,200 hours of storage under ambient conditions (20-25°C, 40-50% relative humidity), pointing to meaningfully improved environmental tolerance.
The researchers note that the CBD-based approach also offers simpler fabrication and lower production costs than conventional spin-coating methods, which they argue makes it a promising route toward scalable, low-cost carbon-based PSCs, a device architecture already valued for replacing noble-metal back contacts with cheaper, more stable carbon electrodes.

title: Guangdong's Jiuan Optics adds perovskite solar to $140 million smart-manufacturing project
content:
Guangdong's Jiuan Optics adds perovskite solar to $140 million smart-manufacturing project
Guangdong Jiuan Intelligent Technology, a Guangzhou-based maker of video surveillance and IoT hardware, has broken ground on the Jiuan Optics Third-Generation Photovoltaic and Intelligent Vision Industrialization Project, a roughly RMB 1.02 billion (about US$152 million) facility that includes an approximately RMB 120 million (about US$18 million) investment in perovskite solar photovoltaic technology.
The project marks a diversification beyond Jiuan's existing surveillance-camera and IoT hardware business, which the company has built since its founding in 2007. Alongside the perovskite solar segment, the facility will house optical component production supporting surveillance cameras and the industrialization of AI vision large-scale models.
According to the company, the site is intended to function as an integrated "five-in-one" smart IoT industrial base, combining hardware R&D and manufacturing, IoT software development, optical component production, AI vision model industrialization, and perovskite solar technology application under one roof.
The move reflects a broader pattern among Chinese electronics and hardware manufacturers of adding perovskite solar production alongside existing manufacturing lines, rather than perovskite solar being developed only by dedicated solar specialists.
