title: Wer wenig verdient und nicht privat laden kann, braucht beim Umstieg auf das E-Auto gezielte Unterstützung
content:
Wer wenig verdient und nicht privat laden kann, braucht beim Umstieg auf das E-Auto gezielte Unterstützung
Eine heute vorgestellte Studie des Öko-Instituts im Auftrag der Stiftung Klimaneutralität zeigt, wie sich Emissionen und Investitionen im Pkw-Verkehr auf unterschiedliche Haushaltsgruppen zukünftig verteilen. Heute verursachen Haushalte mit Dienstwagen die höchsten Emissionen. Sie elektrifizieren ihre Fahrzeuge aber am schnellsten. Ab Mitte der 2030er Jahre verteilen sich die verbleibenden Emissionen sehr viel stärker auf Haushalte mit geringem Einkommen und hoher Pkw-Fahrleistung. Gleichzeitig tragen Haushalte mit geringem Einkommen zu allen betrachteten Zeitpunkten die höchste relative Investitionslast.
Eine ergänzende Befragung der Stiftung Klimaneutralität zeigt, wo die Hürden liegen: Demnach ist der private Ladezugang die zentrale Voraussetzung für die Kaufbereitschaft. Hohe Anschaffungskosten und wenige erschwingliche Modelle bremsen den Umstieg von Haushalten mit geringem Einkommen. Die Stiftung Klimaneutralität empfiehlt deshalb, die Kaufförderung für Haushalte mit geringem Einkommen über 2028 hinaus fortzuführen und das Laden in Mietwohnquartieren gezielt zu verbessern.
Thomas Losse-Müller, Direktor der Stiftung Klimaneutralität: „Die Antriebswende kommt voran. Aber die Haushalte schaffen sie zu unterschiedlichen Zeitpunkten. Wer heute mit dem Dienstwagen die höchsten Emissionen verursacht, fährt schon 2030 in jedem zweiten Fall elektrisch. Ab Mitte der 2030er steigen die Kosten für die Haushalte, die wenig verdienen und trotzdem viel fahren müssen. Ihnen fehlt das Geld für den Umstieg auf ein E-Auto und oft der Stellplatz zum Laden. Wer nicht umsteigen kann, zahlt mit jedem Jahr mehr für Benzin und Diesel.“
Die Studie überträgt das Szenario „Klimaneutrales Deutschland“ der Agora Think Tanks auf die Haushaltsdaten der Erhebung „Mobilität in Deutschland“. Die Haushalte werden nach Nettoeinkommen, Pkw-Jahresfahrleistung und Anbindung an den öffentlichen Verkehr in acht Gruppen eingeteilt. Haushalte mit Dienstwagen bilden eine neunte Gruppe. Die Investitionen werden aus dem jährlichen Wertverlust neuer und gebrauchter Pkw ermittelt und auf die Gruppen verteilt. Die Stiftung Klimaneutralität ergänzt die Modellierung um eine Befragung von 3.000 potentiellen Käuferinnen und Käufern von E-Autos.
Das Emissionsprofil verschiebt sich bis Mitte der 2030er Jahre
Die Analyse zeigt, dass Haushalte mit Dienstwagen viel fahren und eher stark motorisierte Fahrzeuge nutzen. Diese Fahrzeuge werden besonders schnell erneuert. Im Szenario sind 2030 bereits 50 Prozent ihrer Pkw batterieelektrisch. Haushalte mit hohem Einkommen und hoher Fahrleistung folgen mit knapp über 30 Prozent. Am niedrigsten liegt der Anteil bei Haushalten mit geringem Einkommen und geringer Fahrleistung. Sie fahren ihre Fahrzeuge besonders lange und wohnen seltener im Eigentum. Bis 2035 verschiebt sich das Bild innerhalb der Gesellschaft bei den THG-Emissionen im Verkehr deutlich: Die höchsten Emissionen je Haushalt verursachen dann Haushalte mit geringem Einkommen und hoher Pkw-Fahrleistung. Sie stellen 9,3 Prozent der Haushalte. Ihr E-Auto-Anteil liegt 2035 bei 40 bis 45 Prozent, bei Dienstwagen sind es 76 Prozent. Steigende Kosten für fossile Kraftstoffe treffen vor allem diese Haushalte, da sie am spätesten umsteigen.
Investitionslast ist höher bei Haushalten mit niedrigen Einkommen
In absoluten Beträgen investieren einkommensstarke Haushalte mehr in Pkw. Sie besitzen mehr, neuere und größere Fahrzeuge. Gemessen am verfügbaren Nettoeinkommen tragen jedoch Haushalte mit weniger als 2.000 Euro im Monat in den Jahren 2030, 2035 und 2045 die höchste finanzielle Belastung. Am geringsten ist sie bei Haushalten mit mehr als 6.000 Euro. Bei wohlhabenderen Haushalten sinkt die finanzielle Belastung im Zeitverlauf deutlich, weil sie schneller elektrifizieren und dadurch Betriebskosten sinken.
Peter Kasten, Autor der Studie: „Neue E-Autos kommen zuerst dort an, wo Fahrzeuge frühersetzt werden: in Dienstwagenflotten und bei Haushalten mit hohem Einkommen und hoher Fahrleistung. Haushalte mit geringem Einkommen fahren ältere Autos, wohnen häufiger zur Miete und elektrifizieren deshalb später. Instrumente wie Social Leasing oder andere einkommensorientierte Kaufförderungen, die Haushalten mit geringem Einkommen und hoher Fahrleistung den Umstieg erleichtern, sind deshalb von hoher Bedeutung.“
Ladezugang und Anschaffungskosten entscheiden über die Kaufbereitschaft
Die Befragung der Stiftung Klimaneutralität bestätigt die Befunde aus Sicht der Käuferinnen und Käufer. Die materielle Lebenssituation bestimmt die Kaufneigung für ein E-Auto weit stärker als persönliche Präferenzen. Ohne private Lademöglichkeit wollen 14 Prozent der Befragten ein E-Auto kaufen, mit Lademöglichkeit sind es 51 Prozent. 70 Prozent der Befragten können derzeit weder zuhause noch am Arbeitsplatz laden. 29 Prozent sind dauerhaft auf öffentliche Ladesäulen angewiesen, weil sich im Wohnumfeld kein Ladepunkt nachrüsten lässt. Für sie ist eine günstige öffentliche Ladeinfrastruktur entscheidend. Die Befragten werden in verschiedene Segmente aufgeteilt. Die Preissensiblen und die Unentschlossenen nennen die Anschaffungskosten als zentrale Barriere. Ein wachsendes Angebot günstiger Gebrauchtwagen ist für sie deshalb entscheidend.
Politikempfehlungen der Stiftung Klimaneutralität
Die Stiftung Klimaneutralität leitet aus den Ergebnissen vier Empfehlungen ab.
Erstens war es richtig, die 2026 eingeführte Kaufförderung für E-Autos nach Einkommen zu staffeln. Sie soll aber spätestens Ende 2028 auslaufen. Haushalte mit geringem Einkommen brauchen auch danach eine Förderung. Sie sollte mit engeren Einkommensgrenzen fortgesetzt werden.
Zweitens muss das Laden für Menschen ohne eigenen Stellplatz bezahlbar und transparent werden. Dafür schlägt die Stiftung attraktive Ad-hoc-Preise an allen Ladesäulen, offengelegte Roaming-Entgelte und eine Markttransparenzstelle bei der Bundesnetzagentur vor. Parallel muss der Ausbau privater und öffentlicher Ladepunkte in Mietwohnquartieren schneller vorankommen.
Drittens sollte der Steuervorteil für Verbrenner-Dienstwagen sinken, am einfachsten durch eine Versteuerung mit 1,5 Prozent des Bruttolistenpreises. Die Kfz-Steuer sollte sich stärker an den CO₂-Emissionen ausrichten.
Viertens sollte die Entfernungspauschale in ein einkommensunabhängiges Mobilitätsgeld umgewandelt werden. Es entlastet Pendlerinnen und Pendler mit geringem Einkommen gezielter als der heutige Steuerabzug.
Thomas Losse-Müller: „Die Kaufförderung staffelt nach Einkommen, das war ein wichtiger Schritt. Aber sie endet, bevor die Haushalte umsteigen, um die es ab Mitte der 2030er Jahre geht. Für sie brauchen wir eine Anschlusslösung, die ohne Vorfinanzierung funktioniert. Genauso wichtig ist das Laden. Wer zuhause laden kann, spart Geld. Deshalb wollen diese Haushalte auch eher ein E-Auto kaufen. Wer keinen Stellplatz hat, braucht deshalb öffentliche Ladesäulen mit fairen und nachvollziehbaren Preisen. Ohne Ladezugang erreicht die Kaufprämie viele Haushalte nicht.“
Über das Öko-Institut
Das Öko-Institut ist seit seiner Gründung vor fast 50 Jahren eine der europaweit führenden, unabhängigen Forschungs- und Beratungseinrichtungen für eine nachhaltige Zukunft. Es erarbeitet Grundlagen und Strategien, wie die Vision einer nachhaltigen Entwicklung global, national und lokal umgesetzt werden kann. Das Institut ist an den Standorten Freiburg, Darmstadt und Berlin vertreten. www.oeko.de
Über die Stiftung Klimaneutralität
Die Stiftung Klimaneutralität hat im Juli 2020 in Berlin ihre Arbeit aufgenommen. Ihr Ziel ist es, Wege zur Klimaneutralität aufzuzeigen. Sie entwickelt in enger Kooperation mit anderen Denkfabriken sektorübergreifende Strategien für ein klimagerechtes Deutschland. Auf der Basis von guter Forschung will die Stiftung informieren und beraten – jenseits von Einzelinteressen. www.stiftung-klima.de

title: Youth in a Digital Society – Internationale Konferenz zu Chancen und Herausforderungen digitaler Medien
content:
Youth in a Digital Society – Internationale Konferenz zu Chancen und Herausforderungen digitaler Medien
Wie wirken sich digitale Medien auf das Aufwachsen junger Menschen aus? Welche Chancen bieten soziale Medien für Bildung, gesellschaftliche Teilhabe und politische Beteiligung? Und wie lassen sich Risiken wie Desinformation, problematische Mediennutzung oder psychische Belastungen wirksam begegnen? Diesen und weiteren Fragen widmet sich die internationale Konferenz „Youth in a Digital Society“, die am 8. und 9. Oktober 2026 erstmals an der Universität Potsdam stattfindet. Eine öffentliche Podiumsdiskussion am 9. Oktober um 15:30 Uhr bietet interessierten Gästen die Möglichkeit, sich aktiv am Austausch über die digitale Lebenswelt junger Menschen zu beteiligen. Der Eintritt ist frei.
Der Universitäre Forschungsschwerpunkt „Education for the Future“ organisiert die Tagung, die künftig einmal im Jahr Forschende unterschiedlicher Disziplinen zu dieser Thematik in Potsdam zusammenbringen soll. Ziel ist es, den internationalen Austausch über die Rolle digitaler Medien im Leben von Kindern, Jugendlichen und jungen Erwachsenen zu fördern und aktuelle Forschungsergebnisse mit Blick auf gesellschaftliche Herausforderungen zu diskutieren.
Im Mittelpunkt stehen sowohl psychologische als auch gesellschaftspolitische Auswirkungen digitaler Medien. Die Beiträge beschäftigen sich unter anderem mit Zusammenhängen zwischen Mediennutzung und psychischer Gesundheit, Fragen der Medienkompetenz und digitalen Resilienz sowie der politischen Meinungsbildung und Partizipation junger Menschen. Darüber hinaus werden Strategien und Interventionen vorgestellt, die einen verantwortungsvollen und gesundheitsförderlichen Umgang mit digitalen Medien unterstützen können.
Beide Konferenztage starten mit Keynotes international renommierter Wissenschaftlerinnen: Vicky Goodyear von der University of Birmingham spricht über „Digitale Medien, das Wohlbefinden von Jugendlichen und wirksame Interventionen“. Und Shelley Boulianne von der Mount Royal University, Calgary, nimmt „Instagram als Plattform für das politische Engagement Jugendlicher“ in den Blick.
Das Programm umfasst vier thematische Symposien, Posterpräsentationen sowie Roundtable- und Paneldiskussionen. Die Konferenz versteht sich als Plattform für einen interdisziplinären Dialog und internationale Vernetzung. Sie bietet Raum für Diskussionen, den Austausch neuer Ideen und die Entwicklung gemeinsamer Forschungsinitiativen. title: An AI “mind-reading” tool can reconstruct what you’re looking at from a brain scan
content:
An AI “mind-reading” tool can reconstruct what you’re looking at from a brain scan
Scientists hope it could be used to reconstruct a person’s inner thoughts, mental images, or even dreams.
A new AI tool can guess what you’re looking at just by analyzing your brain scans—and re-create that image with remarkable precision. It can go the other way, too, and predict a person’s brain activity based on what they’re looking at.
In the image above, for example, the left-hand image of each pair is what the user actually saw—and its right-hand counterpart is what the model reconstructed from the brain scan.
Michal Irani, who developed the tool with her colleagues at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel, hopes her “mind-reading” tool will ultimately reveal more about how the brain works, and could perhaps be used to help locked-in people communicate, or allow scientists to re-create the content of dreams.
Judy Illes, a neuroethicist and professor of neurology at the University of British Columbia in Canada, who was not involved in the research, describes the work as “magnificent.” “The idea [of using this approach] to help people with neurologic conditions … therapeutically is tremendously exciting,” she says.
But other scientists warn that a similar approach could be used to reveal people’s inner thoughts and mental imagery, potentially without their consent. “The results seem very impressive,” says Tommy Sprague, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Santa Barbara. “But if there’s a way to surreptitiously extract information about what you’re thinking about, then …150 years of sci-fi can come true anytime, and that’s worrisome in a lot of ways.”
Peeking into the brain
Neuroscientists have been working for years on ways to use functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to reconstruct what people see and what’s going on in their minds. The first attempts produced images that were blurry and hard to make sense of. Advances in technology—both in the fMRI scans themselves and in the tools used to make sense of the results—have led to improvements over the years.
Irani and her colleagues started by analyzing publicly available brain-scan data. Other researchers had already collected scans from volunteers who were shown hundreds of images while they lay in fMRI scanners.
fMRI uses a giant magnet to track the flow of oxygenated blood through the brain. Brain areas that “light up” on the scans are thought to be those that are particularly active at any given moment. The results are not especially specific—in typical fMRI scanners, each highlighted “voxel” of activity covers around three cubic millimeters, containing around 16,000 neurons.
But Irani and her colleagues used newer datasets collected using scanners with a higher resolution—each voxel covered around one cubic millimeter of neurons, she says. Those datasets showed what the brain activity of volunteers looked like when they viewed various images.
Other teams have done this too, and several other tools have been used to re-create images from brain-scan data. But they’re not good enough, says Irani. Say a person saw a banana. These models can generate an image of a banana, but it would look different, she says. “It wouldn’t have the same structure, the same position.”
A better decoder
The researchers wanted to more closely re-create the images that had been seen. The first step was to train an AI model on already available data from eight people who each had been shown around 9,000 images while in a high-resolution fMRI scanner.
Crucially, their “brain decoder” has two branches—one to predict the structure of an image (where the colors are, for instance) and a second to predict its content (for example, a bunch of bananas on a plate). The predictions allow a diffusion model, a type of AI best known for creating video and images by gradually cleaning up a noisy mess of pixels, to produce a much more accurate representation of what the person saw.
But to improve the models they needed more data—far more than was actually available.
To get around this problem, Irani and her colleagues trained another model—an encoder that can predict brain activity from an image. The team then used the encoder and decoder together to improve both tools.
It works like this: Start with a new image of, say, a leopard. Then use the encoder to predict what someone’s fMRI brain scan would look like when the person saw that picture. The decoder is then used to reconstruct the image. At first, the reconstruction probably won’t look much like a leopard, says Irani. But repeatedly training the models this way eventually leads to dramatic improvements.
This approach also allows the team to train their models on as many images as they want, even images that have never been shown to a person in an fMRI scanner. Irani says that around 70% of the training data is from images that were not originally paired with fMRI scans.
The resulting “universal brain encoder” can work on a scan from a new person with minimal calibration. In other attempts, a tool has typically required about 40 hours of fMRI data on anyone new before it can be used to predict what that person is seeing. Irani’s decoder only needs one hour of data, she says. The finding was presented at the Cognitive Computational Neuroscience conference in New York last month.
That could make it valuable for neuroscientists studying the brain, says Sprague. “None of us can afford 40 hours of imaging for a new subject,” he says. “It’s something like $600 to $1,000 an hour.” Tools like this one could speed up research, he says.
State of the art
The encoder and decoder aren’t perfect. “Of course we have failures,” says Irani. Over a Zoom call, she pointed out an image of a cake that her tool reconstructed as a pile of three sandwiches, and another of a dog in a bathtub that was reconstructed as a similarly colored goat in a bathtub.
But they represent the state of the art. In a comparison test, the tool was found to be much better than previously described ones. “All in all, really we outperformed the others by a significant margin,” Irani says. “Mind reading” is a “cute, jazzy name” for what they’re doing, she adds.
Irani is now planning to move beyond images to video and audio. She wants to be able to reconstruct what people are thinking about or imagining, and the contents of their dreams. “That’s something we don’t have yet,” she says. “But we’re striving to achieve it.”
Such a tool might enable people who are “locked in” and completely paralyzed to communicate using their brain activity alone, she says. It could also help scientists unpick some enduring mysteries surrounding the inner workings of our minds, such as what PTSD flashbacks look like.
Advances like this inevitably raise questions about mental privacy. What if some bad actor could reconstruct someone’s thoughts or memories?
“If you’d asked me that 10 years ago, I’d have laughed a lot,” says Sprague. Getting a willing person to lie still in a scanner and actively engage with a research question is hard enough; imagine making someone do it involuntarily. But Irani and other scientists are working on similar approaches to decode brain activity from EEG—electrical brain activity measures collected via a cap of electrodes or even through headphones.
And as models improve, it will become even easier to analyze the brain activity collected this way. “We have to be a little more serious about the ethical considerations,” says Sprague. He thinks Irani’s approach would probably “work quite well” in predicting images that a person is thinking about but not looking at.
The move to EEG would be a “game changer,” says Marcello Ienca, a neuroscientist and philosopher at the Technical University of Munich, Germany. Once an EEG device has been calibrated to a user’s own brain, it could be relatively easy for companies to extract additional information from that person’s brain—potentially without consent. Ienca can also imagine some courts allowing mental image reconstructions as legal evidence.
“I have no doubt that this is, you know, well-intentioned research, but I think it’s also pretty obvious that it could be co-opted for … ethically and societally problematic commercial uses,” he says.
Irani acknowledges the potential for misuse with the use of EEG. But she’s not concerned for now. “I’m trying to think only of good things,” she says.

title: How smaller, distributed batteries could help the grid
content:
If you want to install a big battery in New York City, you have to cut through a notoriously tough tangle of regulations. That’s made it difficult to get large energy storage projects on the grid.
Faced with those obstacles, some startups are getting creative, finding ways to use relatively small batteries in unexpected places, from induction stovetops to food carts. By deploying these more consumer-focused batteries, the companies are helping people directly, cutting pollution or power bills. And these units, while small on their own, could add up to a lot of capacity.
Large, utility-scale battery installations are coming online quickly around the world. But there’s been some pushback from communities—especially population-dense ones like NYC—because of concerns about relatively rare but high-profile
battery fires
“The number-one challenge that large-scale centralized energy storage providers have is the fact that their benefits are abstract and their costs are concrete,” said David Hammer, cofounder of PopWheels, at a New York Climate Week event on September 24.
PopWheels built a battery-swapping system for delivery drivers who zip around the city on e-bikes. Drivers swap out depleted batteries for fresh ones at a cabinet, avoiding the need to stop and charge. There are about 50 cabinets across New York City, and about 2,500 batteries in circulation, Hammer says.
The company recently started providing its batteries to food cart operators, allowing them to replace the gas generators they currently rely on. About four of its batteries can supply five kilowatt-hours of electricity, enough to roughly cover a day’s operation for many carts.
Others are looking inside homes. Copper, for example, is a company building induction stoves with integrated batteries. The appliances allow residents to cook if the power goes out, and they could also help homeowners avoid expensive electrical upgrades, because the battery provides some of the power when the stove is in use. “We’re not just selling a battery for resilience—we’re selling it for cost savings,” Sam Calisch, cofounder and CEO of Copper, said at the event.
Other companies, like Every Electric and David Energy are selling plug-in batteries for homes and businesses. Every’s battery is designed to be plugged in to an air-conditioning unit. The company provides the batteries and pays customers to reduce use during high-stress times. David Energy has a similar business model, but focuses on businesses like laundromats, parking garages, and gyms.
Because all these companies’ batteries are small or even integrated into another device, they don’t generally require grid upgrades or extensive permitting processes. Just plug them in and enjoy the benefits—similar to the
growing model of balcony solar
, with small modules that plug in and help offset a home’s or business’s energy demand.
The move toward more distributed batteries could be a huge change for the grid. “This is the biggest thing to happen in the power grid sector in the last 20 years,” says James McGinniss, cofounder and CEO of David Energy.
If every stove in America were shipped with a battery, it would add up to tens of gigawatts of power, Calisch said. That’s capacity that can be aggregated and tapped when the grid is stressed.
As batteries continue to get cheaper, they’ll likely find their way into more corners of our lives, bringing along many benefits. Cleaner air, cheaper power bills—there’s a lot to like. That being said, the need for large-scale energy storage isn’t going to go away—larger installations will do the crucial work of supporting intermittent renewables like wind and solar, so they can help meet more of our quickly growing electricity demand.
But I’m interested to see how far an aggregated horde of stoves, e-bikes, and window AC units could go in helping the grid. The grid is getting more congested, especially in dense cities like New York. Anything that could help avoid summer blackouts is welcome.

The Download: AI “mind-reading” and creative uses for small batteries
Plus: the Pentagon has tapped Elon Musk to co-lead a future warfare project.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
An AI “mind-reading” tool can reconstruct what you’re looking at based on a brain scan
A new AI tool can guess what you’re looking at just by analyzing your brain scans—and recreate that image with remarkable precision. It can go the other way too, and predict a person’s brain activity based on what they’re looking at.
The researchers hope the “mindreading” tool could reveal more about how the brain works. It could also help locked-in people communicate and, incredibly, maybe even allow scientists to recreate the content of dreams.
But other scientists warn that a similar approach could reveal people’s inner thoughts and mental imagery, potentially without their consent.
Here’s how AI is getting closer to reading images from the brain.
—Jessica Hamzelou
How smaller, distributed batteries could help the grid
Large, utility-scale battery installations are coming online quickly around the world. But there’s been pushback from communities, especially population-dense ones like NYC, because of concerns about relatively rare but high-profile battery fires.
Faced with those obstacles, some startups are getting creative, finding ways to use relatively small batteries in unexpected places, from induction stovetops to food carts. By deploying these more consumer-focused batteries, the companies are helping people directly, cutting pollution or power bills.
These units are small on their own, but could add up to a lot of capacity. And as batteries get cheaper, they could find their way into more corners of our lives.
—Casey Crownhart

title: Mondelēz Canada Invests in Sustainable Supply Chains
content:
Mondelēz Canada Invests in Sustainable Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Mondelēz Canada is supporting Canadian farmers and strengthening agricultural supply chain resilience. Credit: Getty Images
Mondelēz Canada invests in Area One Farms Fund V to develop a resilient Canadian food system, Naniss Gadel-Raab, President, Mondelēz Canada explains
Mondelēz Canada is investing in Area One Farms Fund V to strengthen Canadian agricultural supply chain resilience and support farmers in the transition to regenerative agriculture.
The investment, made through Mondelēz International's Sustainable Futures Impact Investment platform alongside impact investment firm Sagana, will provide growth capital to family farms across Canada.
The initiative aims to
reinforce supply chain infrastructure
Area One Farms partners with farmers to expand operations while maintaining farmer participation in land ownership.
Capital access for supply chains
Area One Farms works with growth-oriented Canadian family farms that have opportunities to expand but may face challenges accessing the capital required to do so. Through its partnership model, farmers and Area One Farms invest alongside one another, sharing the financial outcomes of the farm's performance.
Funding can support the acquisition of additional land, improvements to underproductive or retired farmland and investment in infrastructure, machinery and precision agriculture technology. The model is designed to strengthen the financial foundations of farming businesses while supporting increased agricultural production.
Investment in farm infrastructure and equipment could mean greater capacity to
supply food manufacturers
with consistent volumes. The model also supports the working capital and equipment needed to adopt locally appropriate regenerative agriculture practices, while sharing some of the financial cost and risk of that transition.
"Farmers are core to this transition (scaling regenerative agriculture), but they can't do it alone," says Christine Montenegro McGrath, SVP and Chief Impact & Sustainability Officer, Mondelēz International, on LinkedIn.
Christine Montenegro McGrath, SVP and Chief Impact & Sustainability Officer, Mondelēz International
"They're facing changing growing conditions, rising costs and the risk of adopting new practices. We need models that work across farming systems and geographies, delivering value for farmers while strengthening supply chains."
Key numbers
Mondelēz sources approximately 100% of its cocoa volume for chocolate brands through its Cocoa Life programme
It works with more than 257,000 registered farmers across the project
Mondelēz has made approximately 60% progress towards its 2030 GHG reduction target against its 2018 baseline
Around 96% of its total packaging is designed to be recyclable, with the company targeting 98% by 2030
The company has reduced its overall virgin plastic use by 11.5% compared with 2020 levels
Supply chain resilience through ownership
The partnership model seeks to help family farms grow while maintaining farmers' participation in land ownership across generations. Rather than following conventional farmland investment models based on investors acquiring land and charging farmers fixed rent, Area One Farms enables farmers to retain an ownership interest in the farm partnership.
Farmers can also have a pathway to increase their stake over time as the partnership develops. This structure is intended to give farming families greater opportunity to scale their operations while preserving their connection to the land.
"Most farmers who want to grow are not
short of skill or opportunity
. They are short of growth equity," says Joelle Faulkner, CEO at Area One Farms.
Joelle Faulkner, CEO at Area One Farms
"We invest as a co-owner, supporting them with capital and mentorship to scale and innovate. Mondelēz understands that a resilient supply chain starts on farms that are financially strong enough to invest in their soil and in the next generation and this investment lets us do that work with more farming families across Canada."
Supporting the next generation of farmers is relevant as agricultural businesses face pressure to invest in technology, infrastructure and more resilient production systems. These investments could show benefits for supply chain continuity as farms maintain operations across generational transitions.
We know that investing in Canadian agriculture helps strengthen the foundation of a resilient Canadian food system and the agricultural supply chains that are essential to food manufacturing in Canada.
Naniss Gadel-Raab, President, Mondelēz Canada
Financing sustainable supply chain practices
Alongside growth capital, Area One Farms can provide funding for the equipment and working capital needed to
adopt regenerative agriculture practices
. Farmers can receive agronomic support while implementing approaches such as reduced tillage and cover cropping, helping to address some of the financial barriers associated with changing farming practices.
The strategy can also support initiatives focused on improving soil health, increasing input efficiency, managing water resources and strengthening resilience to climate-related pressures. By sharing some of the costs and risks associated with the transition, the partnership model can give farmers greater capacity to invest in longer-term land management.
"As a company, we know that investing in Canadian agriculture helps strengthen the foundation of a resilient Canadian food system and the agricultural supply chains that are essential to food manufacturing in Canada," says Naniss Gadel-Raab, President, Mondelēz Canada.
Naniss Gadel-Rab, President of Mondelēz Canada
"Our commitment to Canada extends beyond the products we make; it includes supporting the farmers, families and communities that are helping build a
stronger, more sustainable food system
These locally appropriate practices are intended to support productive farmland while improving the environmental resilience of agricultural operations. Mondelēz Canada's investment connects access to capital with the longer-term resilience of the food system and the communities that depend on agriculture.
Expanding infrastructure across Canadian farmland
According to Area One Farms, the organisation has grown to more than C$800m in assets under management across more than 50 farm partnerships and 200,000 acres, building its model through four previous funds. Mondelēz Canada's investment in Fund V will support the expansion of this approach and enable Area One Farms to partner with additional farming families across Canada.
The investment is intended to support increased crop production while
advancing regenerative agriculture
practices suited to local farming conditions. For Mondelēz Canada, strengthening agricultural supply chains is connected to supporting the farmers and communities that supply ingredients and materials to the food manufacturing sector.
The initiative demonstrates how investment capital can be directed towards both the economic resilience of farming businesses and the longer-term sustainability of Canada's agricultural landscape.
"We have a playbook and enough demonstration that regenerative agriculture works, but financing the transition remains a big barrier," says François Ritchot, Investment Director and Food & Agriculture Lead at Sagana.
François Ritchot, Investment Director and Food & Agriculture Lead at Sagana
"Area One Farms offers a distinctive approach to address this. We were particularly attracted by the combination of disciplined real-asset investing, practical regenerative agriculture capabilities and tangible benefits for farming families, rural communities and the resilience of our food system."
Companies and partnerships
The Consumer Goods Forum
: Mondelēz International is a member and former co-chair of The Consumer Goods Forum, collaborating with industry leaders to drive positive change across food safety, human rights, data, forests, climate and plastic waste.
United Nations
Human Rights
: Mondelēz International partners with and is a member of industry affiliations dedicated to promoting and advancing human rights, including the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (UN Human Rights).
Tropical Forest Alliance
: Mondelēz International supports the Tropical Forest Alliance and its multi-stakeholder approach to creating a forest-positive future through collaboration between industry, NGOs and producing governments.
World Cocoa Foundation
: Mondelēz International supports the World Cocoa Foundation’s multi-stakeholder approach to accelerating cocoa sustainability through collaboration, shared learning and knowledge across the cocoa supply chain.
: Sagana is a private investment firm focused on long-term equity investments in public and private companies. Founded by Adam Metz, the firm takes a patient, concentrated approach to investing, often holding positions for extended periods. Sagana emphasizes fundamental analysis and works closely with management teams. The firm is known for its low-profile operation and disciplined investment philosophy, targeting businesses with strong competitive advantages and sustainable growth potential.

Supply chain volatility
IntegrityNext is hosting IntegrityNext Innovation Days New York on October 8, 2026. From 9:00am to 1:00pm, leaders will gather at The Mezzanine. Senior executives across supply chain, procurement and sustainability will use this space as an opportunity to discuss visibility, risk management, decision-making and supply chain resilience.
The event will focus on how the supply chain is changing, with supplier networks becoming increasingly complex. Trade disruption, supplier dependencies and shifting market conditions can all influence operational and financial performance.
Some organisations are strengthening resilience through sourcing changes, while others are expanding and diversifying their supplier networks to reduce dependency and improve continuity across critical areas.
Organisations are taking different approaches, but the need for better intelligence is consistent. Supplier,
operational and market risks
can quickly affect sourcing decisions, production and customer commitments, while gaps in visibility can slow the response when conditions change.
This event will give leaders an opportunity to share perspectives, compare approaches and explore how stronger supply chain intelligence can support better decisions.

Supply chain risk is increasingly a business performance issue.

Developing resilience amid risk
At the event, IntegrityNext will also share findings from its latest
Global Supply Chain Resilience Study
2026. The report explores how risk is being managed by organisations around the world, taking insights from procurement, supply chain, sustainability, compliance and risk management professionals.
The study explores what leaders are doing to strengthen resilience, alongside where there are still gaps. Leaders from organisations with 1,000 or more employees took part in the survey. Out of this, it was found that 43% of US organisations have integrated or fully embedded sustainability into their risk management processes.
Alongside this, only 17% report having visibility across multiple supply chain tiers. This demonstrates a significant visibility gap, leading to greater exposure to risk. Organisations, therefore, need to move past fragmented data, instead welcoming collaboration across the tiers. Leaders also need greater intelligence so they can take more informed action at an earlier stage in the disruption.
Supply chain risk is increasingly

title: T&E analysis: sufficient European battery cells by 2030 - electrive.com
content:
In an analysis of the EU's planned local content requirements for batteries, T&E has concluded that a sufficient number of 'Made in EU' battery cells will be available by 2030. This contradicts the current claims of the automotive industry.
View inside CATL's battery factory in Arnstadt
Image: CATL
For months, the EU and its member states have been discussing
draft proposals
for the ‘Industrial Accelerator Act’ (IAA) introduced in March, which aims to boost production and competitiveness within the European Union. These measures also affect the automotive and battery industries: for example, the European Commission plans to introduce so-called Local Content provisions that would prioritise ‘Made in EU’ EVs – i.e., those manufactured within the EU – in public procurement and funding programmes.
Special conditions for local value creation in the EU are also envisaged for traction batteries in electric vehicles. This has recently caused significant concern, as the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) has
examining whether the European battery supply chain can meet the requirements of the legislative package. The result: a significant gap. ACEA argues that there is a time lag: a new battery factory can take nearly a decade from announcement to full-scale industrial production. Even projects launched today may not reach full capacity until around 2035. ACEA is therefore calling for more time and a phased introduction of Local Content requirements, particularly for cells and cathode active materials.
European battery cell production to meet demand by 2030
However, the think tank Transport & Environment (T&E) has now presented its own study, concluding that sufficient ‘Made in EU’ battery cells will be available by 2030. T&E itself emphasises that the analysis contradicts the recent claims of the automotive industry – namely, those of ACEA.
According to the study, European cell production will already be sufficient by 2027 to fully cover the demand for funded company cars and a significant portion of funded private cars. By 2030, both segments could be supplied with enough European battery cells – provided that projects with a medium probability of implementation are also realised. However, a quarter of the cell capacities announced since 2022 have been cancelled or put on hold. Germany is particularly affected, with its project pipeline for 2035 halved, according to T&E. The organisation cites examples such as
ACC in Kaiserslautern
closure of Cellforce by Porsche
. On the other hand, VW subsidiary PowerCo was able to open its
first cell factory in Salzgitter
in December 2025, which, once ramped up, will significantly increase local value creation in the battery supply chain.
Notably, the ownership structure of European cell production is also striking: according to T&E, more than 85 per cent of active capacity is owned by non-European companies, with South Korean manufacturers accounting for 72 per cent of production. The South Korean manufacturers in question are likely LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On, which operate cell factories in Poland and Hungary, respectively. Another major cell manufacturer is the Chinese battery giant CATL, with its
factory in Arnstadt near Erfurt
and its second European factory in Debrecen, Hungary, which has just
started test production
For the ‘Made in EU’ requirements, it is the production location rather than the manufacturer’s country of origin that matters. In other words, the establishment of Asian battery cell manufacturers in the EU also helps meet the Local Content criteria, as local production within the EU is the decisive factor.
“Since the collapse of Northvolt, there has been considerable scepticism in Germany about whether it is possible to build a domestic battery industry. Yet our data shows that Germany is already a relevant location in the European battery ecosystem and has great potential. When Berlin debates the future of German industry, much of the focus is on products of the past, such as the internal combustion engine. It is time to shift the focus to industries of the future, like the battery industry. Supporting an effective Industry Accelerator Act would be an important step here,” said Susanne Goetz, Senior Advisor for E-Mobility at T&E Germany.
Xavier Sol, Director Sustainable Investments and Batteries at T&E, added: “Recent years have shown that, unfortunately, a strong European battery value chain won’t build itself – the competition from Asia is simply too large. Without smart demand-side rules for locally produced battery components, Europe risks its qualification in the race for clean tech. Building a secure, local value chain can ensure security of supply, create jobs and economic resilience”
T&E identifies larger gaps in precursor materials. For cathode active material (CAM), although 529,000 tonnes of annual European capacity have been announced for 2030, only around 177,000 tonnes remain after weighting projects by their probability of implementation. The uncertainty is even greater for pCAM (cathode precursor material): of the announced projects with a total of 552.6 GWh cell equivalent, T&E considers only 217.9 GWh likely to be achieved by 2030. The organisation therefore advocates maintaining the planned cell and CAM requirements of the Industry Accelerator Act and, in addition, introducing minimum quotas for pCAM and anode active material from 2032 onwards.

title: Vianode seeks partner for cooperation or acquisition - electrive.com
content:
Norwegian battery materials specialist Vianode is seeking a partner for its next expansion phase. According to CEO Burkhard Straube, the company is open to various options, ranging from cooperation to a full acquisition.
Image: Vianode
Vianode is a Norwegian specialist in synthetic graphite and has been operating its first large-scale production facility, named ‘Via One’, in Herøya, Norway, since 2024. According to the company, this is “the world’s most sustainable synthetic anode graphite plant”. Vianode has been producing the material since 2021, initially using a pilot plant in Kristiansand.
Since the end of 2025
, Vianode has also been constructing a second plant in St. Thomas, in the Canadian province of Ontario. The facility is set to be located near Volkswagen’s PowerCo plant and is referred to by the Norwegians as ‘Via Two’.
However, GM is considered the anchor customer there
rather than Volkswagen.
As CEO Burkhard Straube recently told
, Vianode is now reaching its limits and will need support in the future. The company is therefore looking for a partner who can contribute capital, industrial expertise, or broader strategic collaboration for the next phase of expansion. Straube told the news agency that Vianode is open to various options, ranging from a partnership to a full acquisition, and specified that the company has engaged JP Morgan to assist with the process.
According to
, the Swedish private equity firm Altor has been Vianode’s sole funder since 2024. The previous investor, Norsk Hydro, withdrew as a shareholder at that time. The agency report now states that Vianode hopes to find a partner by the end of this year. The company is one of the few non-Asian players in the production of synthetic graphite.
adds that China controls approximately 95 per cent of the global supply of battery-grade graphite.
Straube is convinced that customers also have an interest in a strong supplier. Altor spokesperson Andreas Hamrin added: “It is an attractive case for the right partner, with Vianode having proven both its technological and commercial viability.”
Once fully ramped up, Vianode’s Norwegian plant is expected to produce around 2,000 tonnes of graphite battery material annually – enough for approximately 35,000 electric vehicles. However, in 2023, the company shifted its expansion focus to North America, where, at that time under US President Joe Biden, there were greater incentives and regulatory support. Production there is currently scheduled to begin in 2029 – significantly later than originally planned.

title: 100,000-ton US nuclear aircraft carrier enters shipyard for overhaul
content: The US Navy’s nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Harry S. Truman (CVN 75) arrived at Newport News Shipbuilding on September 30, 2026, to begin a major midlife overhaul involving reactor refueling and extensive modernization.The work follows years of advance planning and prepares the carrier for the second half of a service life expected to span more than 50 years.Truman becomes the eighth Nimitz-class aircraft carrier to undergo a refueling and complex overhaul, or RCOH, at the HII shipyard in Virginia.Preparing for the overhaulNewport News Shipbuilding has already conducted thousands of inspections and preliminary tasks to prepare for the carrier’s arrival. The shipbuilder also ordered materials with long procurement lead times to support the project.“We’ve taken a proactive approach, from ordering long lead-time materials to conducting thousands of inspections and preliminary work, to ensure the RCOH of USS Harry S. Truman is successful,” said Bryan Caccavale, NNS vice president of program management.“This extensive engineering and construction project to ready the ship to rejoin the fleet is a team effort, across shipbuilders, suppliers and our Navy partners, and we are honored to do our part,” he added.The preparations support an overhaul that brings together nuclear refueling, structural maintenance, and upgrades across much of the ship. HII describes the RCOH as representing nearly a third of all maintenance and modernization performed during an aircraft carrier’s service life.Reactors and ship systemsA central part of Truman’s overhaul involves defueling and refueling its nuclear power plant. The project also includes major upgrades to the propulsion plant and combat systems.Beyond the reactors, shipbuilders will carry out extensive modernization in thousands of compartments and tanks, along with work on most ship systems. The scope reaches from the carrier’s internal spaces to the equipment that supports its movement through the water.Newport News Shipbuilding will blast and paint the hull and freeboard and repair the carrier’s propellers, sea chests, shafts, and rudders.These tasks make the availability a broad recapitalization effort, combining maintenance of existing equipment with modernization intended to support the carrier’s continued role in the fleet.HII said the resulting ship would be capable of supporting current and future national strategy objectives while serving as a centerpiece of naval operations for decades.Contract supports carrier’s next chapterHII announced a $5.1 billion contract for Truman’s RCOH on September 29, 2026. Options, if exercised, would raise the cumulative contract value. “Our team has been diligently working to get ahead on this critical engineering and construction project that will prepare USS Harry S. Truman for the second half of her service life,” Caccavale said in the contract announcement.“When the ship arrives at NNS, we’ll apply that same diligence to working with our suppliers and Navy partners to ensure a successful recapitalization of CVN 75,” he said. The carrier returns to the shipyard that built it. Truman was christened in 1996 and delivered to the Navy in 1998.According to HII, the overhaul will prepare Truman to return to the fleet and continue operating for decades.

title: 119 gas turbines to bring 1.7 GW of mobile power to US data centers
content: Siemens Energy will supply 119 gas turbine cores for mobile power systems in the United States, adding more than 1.7 gigawatts of planned generation capacity as electricity demand from data centers and industry continues to climb.The multi-year agreement with Dynamis Power Solutions covers SGT-400 gas turbine cores, each capable of producing about 15 megawatts. The first batch is scheduled for delivery in 2027.Dynamis will integrate the turbines into its DT18 hypermobile power packages, which are designed to bring generating capacity online faster than conventional power infrastructure. The systems can provide either temporary or permanent power.The companies are targeting data centers, oil and gas operations, utilities and other industrial facilities that need additional generation without waiting for large, fixed power plants to be built.Mobile turbines target demandThe deal comes as rapidly expanding data centers and other energy-intensive industries put additional pressure on U.S. power supplies. Mobile generation systems offer another way to add capacity where grid connections or new permanent generation may take longer to develop.The SGT-400 is a compact industrial gas turbine platform. With roughly 15 MW available from each of the 119 cores, the agreement represents approximately 1.785 GW of turbine capacity based on the stated individual output.“The demand for reliable and flexible power generation continues to grow as industries expand and energy needs evolve,” said Karim Amin, member of the executive board of Siemens Energy.“Together with Dynamis, we are helping customers access generation capacity quickly by combining proven gas turbine technology with innovative deployment concepts.”Dynamis’ DT18 is based on engineering used in the company’s larger DT35 mobile power system. The company says the new package is designed to combine utility-scale generation with a smaller footprint and faster installation.Power plants go mobileUnlike a conventional stationary power plant, the DT18 packages are intended to be transported and deployed where additional electricity is needed. That could allow operators to expand generation as demand changes or move equipment between sites.“This agreement marks another major milestone not only in our mission to deliver power where and when our partners need it most, but also to answer the market’s growing need for flexible power solutions,” said Matt Crawford, chief executive officer of Dynamis.“With ~2GW of packaged power, Dynamis has established the lead position in the hypermobile power market, and these SGT-400 packages will significantly expand that capacity.”The turbines will be manufactured at Siemens Energy’s facility in Lincoln, United Kingdom, which serves as the company’s global manufacturing center for small gas turbines.For Dynamis, the order substantially expands the amount of generation equipment available for its mobile systems. For Siemens Energy, it represents a sizable deployment of its SGT-400 platform into a U.S. market where data centers, industrial expansion, and other large electricity users are increasing demand for quickly deployable power.

title: 456 nuclear reactor-powered data center in Utah proposed by US firm
content: Silicon Valley needs energy, and it is looking to turn central eastern Utah into a nuclear-powered computing capital.Energy startup Valar Atomics has submitted a proposal to construct “Project Beehive,” an ambitious industrial development spanning roughly 9,000 acres of public and state land near Price, Utah. The core proposal includes 456 small, gas-cooled nuclear reactors that would generate an estimated 9.6 gigawatts of power. That is more than double the entire state’s average energy output. Utah currently generates an average of 4 gigawatts of electricity, with summer peak demand reaching nearly 10 gigawatts.On September 17, the Utah Trust Lands Administration unanimously approved a lease for 640 acres of state trust land earmarked for the effort. The Bureau of Land Management is reviewing the project. It aims to combine small, gas-cooled nuclear reactors with manufacturing facilities to power a massive AI data center.However, environmental advocates caution against moving too fast on public land. Helium-cooled nuclear reactorsArtificial intelligence requires vast computational capacity. Computing power demands electricity. Project Beehive plans to use helium-cooled nuclear reactors instead of traditional water-cooled designs. This gas-cooling approach lowers water consumption, making it ideal for data infrastructure located in the dry American West. Moreover, the proposed complex is expected to manage both nuclear fuel production and on-site waste storage. The proposed gas-cooled reactors utilize TRISO (Tristructural Isotropic) fuel. Wrapped in ceramic and carbon layers, TRISO fuel is designed to withstand extreme heat without melting down, providing passive safety mechanisms. Valar Atomics demonstrated its central innovation, the Ward 250 microreactor, in the Utah desert roughly 30 miles from the proposed Project Beehive site. The microreactor first achieved criticality in June inside a tent structure in the Utah desert. Weeks later, during a July 1 demonstration, the firm used electricity generated by the reactor to power a single Nvidia microchip.NPR reports that non-nuclear construction could start as early as late this year, with initial reactors slated to go live in 2028.Local activists are expressing strong concern over the proposal, which joins a growing wave of data center developments across Utah. Neal Clark of the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance voiced alarm that federal and state officials are advancing the massive project on public lands. Critics have also questioned the economic distribution. They argue that local residents bear long-term nuclear safety risks while out-of-state tech corporations capture the majority of the financial reward.Trump’s push for SMRsProject Beehive highlights the grand ambitions of a new era of companies driving a nuclear power resurgence. These ventures are supported by the Trump administration, which has introduced extensive regulatory reforms to streamline the testing and deployment of small modular reactors. Earlier, the U.S. Department of Energy selected the firm under Executive Order 14301 to achieve reactor criticality on American soil by July 4, 2026.“Under the framework of Executive Order 14301, we are part of a coordinated national effort to restore American dominance in nuclear technology,” the company stated earlier. The project now rests on federal environmental review processes.If the BLM deems Valar Atomics’ application complete, it will issue a formal Notice of Realty Action. That step triggers an environmental impact analysis under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), opening mandatory windows for public comment before any federal land leases are finalized.

title: Airborne robot makes soft water landing, converts to autonomous sailboat
content: Mother Nature spent millions of years perfecting the maple seed’s gentle spiral to the forest floor and the fish’s swift flick through open water. She never thought to combine them.Robotic experts at Singapore University of Technology and Design and MIT just did. Introducing ALBATROSS, a hybrid robot that leaps out of the sky like a spinning seed, splashes into the water, and instantly morphs into an autonomous, wind-driven sailboat. Short for Airborne Lander with Buoyant AuToROtating Sailing Sensor, the device offers a low-cost solution to a difficult engineering problem: building a machine that operates in both air and sea without collapsing under its own weight.“In repeated field trials at two reservoirs in Singapore, the robot sailed autonomously using a Rule-Based (RB) controller after being deployed from 150 meters in the air,” the team noted. Drop, splash, sailTypically, dual-environment drones are heavy, complex, and ruinously expensive. And require bulky motors to fight gravity in the air and separate propulsion systems to navigate currents below. ALBATROSS could change that. Instead of fighting physics, it borrows from nature’s cleverest hacks. During a 150-meter drop from the sky, its two rigid wingsails spin passively like a falling maple seed. It achieves a soft, controlled, spinning descent without relying on heavy engines or draining battery power.The moment it hits the surface, the transformation begins.Those same aerial wings lock into place as wind-driven sails, turning the fallen lander into an agile aquatic scout. Beneath the waterline, a tail rudder modeled after a fish fin takes over. When the breeze dies, the fin flicks to push the craft forward; when the wind picks up, it guides the vessel upwind toward its target.The ~1-kg ALBATROSS robot autorotates during air descent to cut its fall speed to ~7 m/s, reducing impact energy 18-fold so it survives impact with the water. Upon landing, the craft passively self-rights and transitions its dual wingsails to wind propulsion without active morphing, achieving a high 91 percent effective mass usage across air and water. In low-wind conditions, the platform drives itself forward up to 0.4 m/s through an oscillating fish-tail rudder. The design proves how recombining distinct bio-inspired components can expand operating envelopes without adding extra weight.Borrowing from nature By reusing its body parts for dual roles, the design team stripped the robot down to just three actuators and three primary sensors. It is lightweight, lean, and deceptively simple. In field tests across two Singaporean reservoirs, ALBATROSS proved it could survive high-altitude drops and immediately start sailing autonomously using a rule-based navigation controller. Computer simulations show that with Reinforcement Learning algorithms, the craft can even master complex waypoint missions entirely on its own.The development highlights a fresh approach to bio-inspired robotics. In an accompanying commentary, researchers suggest that nature serves best as a versatile library of individual biological mechanisms rather than an exact blueprint. Multimodal robotics combines diverse locomotion modes into a single platform to navigate across different environments. While animals excel at repurposing biological structures for multiple habitats, nature should serve as a flexible parts library rather than a strict blueprint. Robotics engineers can select, adapt, and recombine individual biological mechanisms to address specific technical challenges that evolutionary pressures never encountered.With climate monitoring and disaster response demanding faster, cheaper eyes on the water, ALBATROSS shows that sometimes the best way to conquer two worlds is to simply drop in and let the wind do the work.

title: Bill Gates-backed nuclear fusion firm inks 6200-mile reactor tape deal
content: Commercial nuclear fusion has moved one step closer to reality. Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) has signed the largest supply deal of its kind with Japanese manufacturer Fujikura Ltd. Under the agreement, CFS will purchase more than 10,000 kilometers (around 6215 miles) of high-temperature superconducting (HTS) tape to build its first fleet of commercial power stations.Fujikura is expanding its production lines in Japan. The agreement signals a critical shift for the fusion industry. Teams are moving past small-scale lab tests and assembling the industrial supply chain needed to build actual power stations.The first tape deliveries will head to Chesterfield County, Virginia. There, CFS is preparing its flagship Fall Line Fusion Power Station, designed to be the world’s first grid-scale fusion facility.Keeping the energy containedCFS’s design centers around a tokamak, which is a hollow, ring-shaped chamber designed to recreate the conditions of a star. Inside the tokamak, extreme heat and pressure force atomic nuclei together.The challenge is keeping that reaction contained. The resulting plasma reaches temperatures of over 100 million degrees, far hotter than the center of the sun, and would vaporize any physical wall it touches. Only invisible, highly concentrated magnetic fields can suspend it safely in place.This engineering hurdle explains why the Fujikura contract is so pivotal. Early fusion reactors relied on bulky, low-temperature magnets that generated modest magnetic fields and demanded sprawling cooling systems. To generate sufficient power, those experimental facilities had to be built on an enormous scale.Building stronger electromagnetsHTS tape allows engineers to build stronger electromagnets within a compact footprint. These intense magnetic fields trap high-energy plasma inside a far smaller vessel, dramatically reducing construction costs and engineering complexity.CFS is currently constructing SPARC, a prototype machine designed to prove net energy gain—meaning the reaction produces more power than it consumes. Once SPARC hits that milestone, the company plans to replicate the design at commercial scale under the plant name ARC.“This partnership with Fujikura demonstrates how we’re actively placing orders and getting ready to execute our ARC power plant,” said Bob Mumgaard, chief executive of CFS. He noted that scaling the technology requires global partners willing to invest ahead of commercial deployment.Global funding supportThe move also tightens trade ties between Tokyo and Washington in advanced manufacturing. Fujikura chief executive Naoki Okada said the deal will establish a long-term business base extending into the 2030s, when commercial fusion plants are expected to feed electricity into regional grids.The announcement caps a busy funding period for CFS. Backed by Bill Gates, the American developer recently raised $1bn in fresh capital. That round included direct investment from South Korea’s Hyundai Motor Group to explore manufacturing partnerships. With money in hand and key components secured, the company is betting that private industry can deliver clean fusion energy ahead of state-run initiatives.

title: Boeing 777 boosts hypersonic testing capacity by 35% for US defense
content: Stratolaunch is adding a Boeing 777-200ER to its hypersonic testing fleet, giving the company another aircraft capable of carrying its Talon-A vehicles into the air.The Mojave, California-based company announced the acquisition on Sept. 30. It said the additional carrier will raise its overall flight capacity by 35 percent and expand where it can conduct missions.The 777 will join Stratolaunch’s existing carrier aircraft, Roc and Spirit of Mojave. Engineers will modify the widebody to release Talon-A vehicles through its fuselage.That work should finish in 2027. Once operational, the aircraft will give Stratolaunch another option for putting reusable hypersonic test vehicles into flight.Bigger fleet for flight testingStratolaunch has been expanding its flight operations as demand for hypersonic testing increases. Adding another carrier could give customers more opportunities to schedule missions without relying on a single aircraft.The company also expects the larger fleet to support operations from different locations. That matters for test programs that require specific ranges, weather conditions, or mission profiles.Three carrier aircraft could also support parallel missions. Stratolaunch said the additional capacity will help reduce scheduling constraints and support a higher flight cadence.The 777 brings another advantage through its size and range. Engineers can use the aircraft as a reusable first stage, carrying Talon-A to altitude before releasing it for a hypersonic flight.That approach allows the test vehicle to begin its mission from the air. It can also help researchers collect data during flight profiles that ground-based launch systems cannot easily reproduce.Talon-A is driving demandTalon-A has become the centerpiece of Stratolaunch’s hypersonic testing business. The autonomous vehicle launches from a carrier aircraft and conducts high-speed atmospheric tests before returning for recovery.Stratolaunch said it passed 10 successful hypersonic flights with Talon-A in July. The milestone came several months after the company secured a $90.8 million contract under the Department of War Test Resource Management Center’s MACH-TB program.That award covers air-launched capability test vehicles. The program gives Stratolaunch another major avenue for supporting U.S. hypersonic development.Zachary Krevor, Stratolaunch’s president and CEO, said the 777 will strengthen the company’s ability to meet customer demand. “As demand for hypersonic technologies continues to grow, we’re building the operational scale to make routine hypersonic testing a reality,” Krevor said.He added that the aircraft will provide greater flexibility as Stratolaunch works to increase its testing capacity.Another carrier enters the mixThe 777 acquisition gives Stratolaunch three carrier aircraft with which to plan future missions. That additional aircraft could become particularly useful as government and commercial programs seek more frequent flight opportunities.Hypersonic development depends heavily on flight testing and the data collected during those missions. More available carrier aircraft can give engineers additional chances to evaluate vehicles and onboard systems under real flight conditions.The new Boeing 777 will not enter service immediately. Stratolaunch must first complete the modifications needed to accommodate Talon-A and its air-launch requirements.Its planned 2027 completion will mark another step in the company’s effort to expand its testing infrastructure. Once the aircraft joins the operational fleet, Stratolaunch will have more room to schedule missions and respond to customers seeking additional hypersonic flight data.

title: Chinese lidar laser sensor detects 1,200-mph F-35 from 38 miles away
content: A Chinese missile research team has simulated a laser-based seeker detecting an F-35 stealth fighter from 38 miles away at night.The concept uses single-photon lidar to detect faint laser reflections from an aircraft. If developed into a missile seeker, the technology could offer another way to track stealth fighters beyond visual range.The research explores a sensing method that could complement the radar and infrared systems already used in air combat.Lidar targets stealth aircraftResearchers at the China Airborne Missile Academy modeled a single-photon lidar designed for missile deployment. The system operates at a wavelength of 1,064 nanometers.Lidar sends laser pulses toward a target and measures the light that returns. Single-photon systems can detect exceptionally weak signals, which makes them attractive for compact sensing applications.Missile designers face strict limits on available space, weight, and electrical power. The researchers therefore modeled a relatively small optical system rather than a large airborne sensor.The simulation used 1-millijoule laser pulses and a 100-millimeter lens. Atmospheric transmission, sky background, and detector noise also factored into the calculations.Detector recovery time received particular attention in the model. After registering a photon, the detector needs a brief period before it can record another signal.The researchers calculated that the lidar needed a signal-to-noise ratio of 8.8 decibels. A minimum of 9.4 detected photons would provide enough return signal to establish a track.Night pushes range to 38 milesLighting conditions produced a substantial difference in the modeled performance. The simulated seeker detected the F-35C from 17.2 miles during daylight.At night, the maximum range increased to 38.2 miles. Reduced background light gave the lidar a cleaner optical environment for detecting weak returns.The model also examined the quality of the target information available at shorter distances. At 17.2 miles, depth accuracy reached roughly 8 inches.Transverse resolution came in at approximately 20 inches at the same range. Such measurements could provide a missile seeker with more information than simple target detection. The figures remain predictions from a computer model.Narrow beam creates problemA longer detection range does not automatically solve the problem of finding an aircraft. Lidar relies on a narrow laser beam rather than the broad search coverage of radar.The issue matters because the F-35 already carries weapons capable of engaging targets beyond the simulated lidar range. The AIM-120D-3 AMRAAM provides a long-range air-to-air option.For closer engagements, the F-35 can carry the AIM-9X Sidewinder. Its imaging infrared seeker provides another method for identifying and tracking aircraft.The Chinese researchers chose the 1,064-nanometer wavelength partly because stealth aircraft have fewer dedicated countermeasures against active laser sensing.China has also displayed other airborne laser concepts. The 303 Research Institute recently exhibited a suspended laser weapon pod at an event in Beijing.Shenyang Aircraft Corp. has separately referenced laser weapons in design material associated with future Chinese stealth fighters.The lidar study adds another potential application for airborne laser technology. Turning the modeled performance into a practical missile system would require further development and testing.The study is published in the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Aero Weaponry.

title: High-tech computing to be tested in lunar orbit for future data centers
content: A new commercial payload agreement will demonstrate advanced AI computing capabilities in lunar orbit. Starcloud revealed that its computing payload, designated SC-1L, will fly onboard Firefly’s Elytra orbital vehicle to validate the core capabilities of a future data center around the moon that can support lunar surface and orbital infrastructure.Pairing Starcloud’s AI computing payload with our Elytra vehicle“We’re proud to collaborate with innovative customers like Starcloud and collectively take another step toward establishing the infrastructure that will power a permanent human and robotic presence at the moon,” said Ray Allensworth, Vice President of Spacecraft at Firefly Aerospace. “By pairing Starcloud’s AI computing payload with our Elytra vehicle and Solux vision system, we’re demonstrating how data can be captured, processed, and delivered from lunar orbit, laying the groundwork for the computing infrastructure future lunar operations will depend on.”Integrated on Elytra, Starcloud’s SC-1L processor will ingest data from Firefly’s onboard Solux vision system, perform high-power AI computing on orbit, and rapidly transmit the processed data back to Earth. The demonstration builds directly on Starcloud’s recent AI computing demonstration in low Earth orbit, extending those proven capabilities into lunar orbit, according to details available.Starcloud is being onboarded to Firefly’s third lunar mission that’s targeted to launch no earlier than 2028. For this mission, Firefly’s Elytra orbiter will first serve as the transfer vehicle and communications relay for Firefly’s Blue Ghost lander that will land on the Moon’s Gruithuisen Domes and operate several science and technology instruments as part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative. Following completion of the mission, Elytra will remain in lunar orbit for five years to enable customer payload and imaging operations, including Starcloud’s demonstration, according to a press release.High-power AI computing“Space is the future of data centers, and the Moon is the next frontier for that vision,” said Ezra Feilden, Cofounder and CTO at Starcloud. “We successfully validated our ability to run and train AI models on enterprise grade GPUs in low Earth orbit, and now we’re taking this proven technology to lunar orbit. Onboard Firefly’s Elytra vehicle, we’ll demonstrate high-power AI computing and further prove we can process massive volumes of data right where it’s generated to support the growing infrastructure beyond Earth.”Formerly known as Sol3, Firefly’s Solux vision system onboard Elytra enables spacecraft to autonomously navigate, land, and track their orientation in space environments where Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) and GPS are unavailable. Elytra will also have high-resolution telescopes onboard to enable Firefly’s Ocula lunar imaging service that provides advanced lunar surface mapping, mineral detection, and reconnaissance.This will be the second Elytra vehicle Firefly is deploying to lunar orbit following the launch of Blue Ghost Mission 2, targeted for no earlier than 2027. Each Elytra vehicle is designed to remain in lunar orbit for up to five years, enabling more rapid revisit times of the lunar surface for government and commercial customers, as per the release.

title: How the world's first nuclear submarine started a new era of warfare
content: For submarines, slipping beneath the surface was only part of the challenge. The harder task was staying underwater while traveling quickly over long distances.USS Nautilus helped overcome that limitation. Commissioned on September 30, 1954, in Groton, Connecticut, it was the world’s first nuclear-powered submarine. Its arrival gave the U.S. Navy a vessel that could sustain underwater operations far beyond the capabilities of earlier diesel-electric boats.That breakthrough reshaped submarine operations, challenged established methods of hunting them, and opened a route beneath the North Pole.What made Nautilus different?Conventional diesel-electric submarines relied on batteries to power their propulsion motors underwater. Those batteries eventually needed recharging, requiring the submarine to surface or use a snorkel so its diesel engines could draw air. This dependence restricted how freely the boats could operate beneath the waves.Commanders had to manage battery reserves carefully. Traveling faster consumed stored energy more quickly, while recharging required access to the atmosphere.Nautilus used nuclear propulsion to overcome this constraint. Its reactor supplied heat to produce steam, which drove propulsion turbines and electrical generators. Unlike diesel engines, the system did not require atmospheric oxygen to generate propulsion power.The practical advantage was sustained underwater mobility. Nautilus could travel long distances submerged without repeatedly interrupting its voyage to recharge propulsion batteries.However, its commissioning and first sailing were separate milestones. After entering service in September 1954, Nautilus remained dockside for additional construction and testing. It first got underway on nuclear power on January 17, 1955.Its early voyages demonstrated the difference. During a May 1955 shakedown trip toward Puerto Rico, Nautilus covered 1,381 miles submerged in 89.8 hours. The Navy records this as the longest submerged cruise achieved to that date, at the highest sustained submerged speed recorded for a period exceeding one hour.How did it change submarine warfare?A submarine’s effectiveness depends partly on its ability to move without being located and intercepted. Nautilus gave commanders greater freedom to maintain speed underwater and quickly leave a search area.That presented a challenge for forces trained to hunt earlier submarines. During evaluations in 1956, the Navy tested how Nautilus’ increased speed and endurance affected contemporary anti-submarine warfare practices.The findings were significant: methods inherited from World War II were ineffective against a submarine with these capabilities. Nautilus’s performance required a reassessment of existing submarine-hunting tactics.Its military importance therefore extended beyond its own missions. Operating it in exercises helped the Navy understand the challenges posed by nuclear-powered submarines.The term “nuclear-powered” described its propulsion system. Nautilus carried six torpedo tubes and was not a ballistic-missile submarine.Why was its North Pole voyage important?Nautilus’ most famous achievement came in 1958 during Operation Sunshine, a mission to travel submerged beneath the North Pole.The first attempt encountered drift ice in relatively shallow Chukchi Sea waters, blocking the submarine’s passage. Nautilus returned to Pearl Harbor before making another attempt.On August 3, 1958, it successfully passed beneath the geographic North Pole, becoming the first submarine to complete that passage.The voyage demonstrated the reach of sustained underwater propulsion. Beneath Arctic ice, where access to the surface was restricted, freedom from routine battery recharging offered a decisive operational advantage.Nuclear propulsion did not make voyages unlimited. Supplies, crew endurance, maintenance, and eventual refueling remained constraints. Nautilus underwent its first reactor-core replacement in 1957 after logging 60,000 nautical miles.Its lasting contribution was giving submarines the ability to travel farther and sustain speed underwater, expanding where and how they could operate.
