title: Humanoid robots decommissioned in Terminator-style molten steel leap
content: Figure has gone full Terminator with its retired humanoid robots, sending them into a vat of molten steel.The robotics company sent F.02 units to a foundry in Imatra, Finland, where the machines autonomously leaped into a 75-ton electric arc furnace. The furnace then reduced the robots to molten metal.The unusual disposal effort followed the arrival of Figure’s newer F.03 fleet. Keeping the older robots operational no longer made sense, according to Figure. Disassembling each machine also threatened to consume engineering time needed for the company’s next-generation F.04 robot.The solution created a difficult engineering problem of its own. Figure needed to destroy proprietary hardware without exposing custom components or intellectual property. That ruled out conventional dismantling for much of the fleet.Furnace became the answerFigure eventually found a Finnish foundry willing to accept the robots. Facilities in the United States and Mexico had rejected the idea because of the lithium-ion batteries inside the machines.The company even sought help from former MythBusters members during the search. The breakthrough came after Arnold Schwarzenegger encouraged Figure to melt the robots. Schwarzenegger later joined the project.Engineers first had to teach the F.02 machines how to make the jump. Figure installed large airbags at its San Jose headquarters and trained robots to leap from a second-floor building.Stunt performers provided movement references for the training. Engineers then developed a control model in simulation. It had to guide each robot into a precise landing zone at an unfamiliar foundry.That requirement left little room for error. The team had never tested the robots inside the Finnish facility before shipping them there.Six melts, 24 hoursThe foundry’s electric arc furnace uses three large graphite electrodes to melt steel scrap. Figure had only six melting cycles across a 24-hour window.Each cycle offered roughly 20 minutes before the molten steel cooled enough to develop a solid crust. Extreme temperatures created another problem for the electronics.Electromagnetic fields also disrupted equipment around the furnace. Cameras and other electronics failed during the operation. Figure said the robots continued executing their trained movement policies despite those failures.The F.02 units ultimately disappeared into the furnace, but their material did not stay in Finland. Figure shipped the resulting metal bars back to the United States.The company now plans to machine that recovered material into a limited run of F.02 commemorative artifacts. The pieces will preserve material from the retired robots in a much smaller form.Most of Figure’s F.02 fleet has now been destroyed. A handful remain stored at the company’s headquarters.The project also served as a real-world demonstration of autonomous robot control under extreme conditions. Figure emphasized that the footage was not generated digitally. Its robots physically traveled to Finland and performed the furnace jumps themselves.Here are some of the behind the scenes for the F.02 DecommissionTo be clear: we actually trained our robots to jump autonomously, shipped them to Finland, and had them leap into a vat of molten steel pic.twitter.com/snm3Mz2v8z— Brett Adcock (@adcock_brett) September 30, 2026Figure introduced the F.03 in October 2025 as its next-generation humanoid platform. The robot features a redesigned sensory suite and hand system built specifically for Helix, Figure’s proprietary vision-language-action system.F.03 also brings changes aimed at home use, including softer exterior materials, wireless charging, and an improved audio system. Figure also made battery safety improvements for operation around people.

title: Light-based processor targets power and bandwidth limits of GPUs
content: Q/C Technologies, a San Francisco-based developer of optical computing systems, is teaming up with a U.S. Department of Energy nanotechnology center to develop an optical processor that could eventually run artificial intelligence workloads using light instead of relying solely on electronic computation.The company announced a collaboration with the Center for Integrated Nanotechnologies (CINT) at Sandia National Laboratories to advance its optical processing unit (OPU). The proposed hardware is intended primarily for inference, when trained models process new data to generate results.Instead of performing computations entirely through conventional electronic circuits, Q/C’s approach uses the interference of light to carry out certain mathematical operations. Optical computing could potentially address power, bandwidth and scaling constraints associated with increasingly demanding computing workloads.The project remains at the research stage. Q/C and CINT will study nanophotonic components and determine which optical operations and device technologies could form the building blocks of a scalable OPU architecture.Light tackles heavy computingOne major goal is to establish a technical roadmap for moving beyond incremental improvements to graphics processing units. Researchers will examine some of the difficult problems that have prevented optical computing from becoming a mainstream alternative to electronic processors.Those challenges include performing nonlinear operations, incorporating memory, maintaining computational precision, minimizing optical losses and integrating photonic components with conventional electronics. Solving them will be important if individual optical components are eventually to operate together as a practical computing system.“Access to CINT’s scientific expertise and advanced research capabilities in photonics and nanoscale technologies represents an important step as we develop our proprietary optical computing platform,” said Joshua Silverman, executive chairman of Q/C Technologies.“As AI infrastructure faces increasing constraints in power consumption, bandwidth and scalability, we believe optical computing has the potential to fundamentally change how computationally intensive AI workloads are processed.”CINT gives the project access to expertise in nanoscience and nanophotonics at Sandia, one of the Department of Energy’s national laboratories. Sandia has approximately 17,000 employees and an annual budget of about $5 billion, with research spanning areas including microelectronics, photonics, advanced materials and high-performance computing.Building an optical processorThe collaboration will focus not only on individual photonic devices but also on determining how they could eventually be combined into Q/C’s proposed OPU. The company says the work should help identify and prioritize technologies needed for its architecture.“This collaboration provides an opportunity to accelerate our work toward a practical, scalable optical computing architecture,” said Yossef Ehrlichman, chief technology officer at Q/C Technologies.“We believe this work with CINT will help us define the pathway from fundamental optical capabilities to an integrated OPU architecture.”Q/C says its longer-term goal is to develop optical processors with substantially higher clock speeds and bandwidth while consuming less energy than traditional computing architectures. Those remain development targets rather than demonstrated performance figures for a finished processor.The company is also building infrastructure for the project. It recently established a 4,800-square-foot integrated photonics laboratory in San Francisco to support its work in photonics, computing, and the development of the OPU architecture.

title: Midair nightmare on Flydubai Israel flight: 14,000-ft plunge, stabbing
content: Flydubai Flight FZ1073 was supposed to make a routine trip from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday morning. Instead, the Boeing 737 Max 8 plunged thousands of feet after a violent confrontation erupted inside its cockpit.The aircraft carried more than 170 passengers as it crossed Saudi Arabian airspace. Flight-tracking data later showed the jet lost nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds. What followed turned a normal commercial flight into a hijack scare. Israeli officials said one pilot stabbed the other and apparently tried to crash the aircraft.Passengers and crew members eventually forced their way into the cockpit. They subdued the suspected attacker and helped restore control of the aircraft.The jet then diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely. Both pilots went to a hospital with injuries, while Saudi authorities arrested the suspected attacker.Flight turns dangerousFZ1073 departed Dubai International Airport bound for Ben Gurion International Airport near Tel Aviv. The route normally crosses Saudi Arabia and Jordan, making the aircraft’s position unsurprising when the emergency began.The situation changed rapidly as the aircraft flew over Saudi Arabia. Flight data showed a dramatic loss of altitude before the first emergency signal appeared.The descent lasted less than a minute. The aircraft dropped nearly 14,000 feet during the initial plunge, according to Flightradar24 data cited by Reuters.That sudden change would have been immediately noticeable inside the cabin. Passengers later described screams and confusion as people realized something was seriously wrong.The aircraft also transmitted emergency signals during the incident. One signal indicated a general emergency, while another corresponded to unlawful interference or a hijacking situation.That second signal escalated the security response. Israeli authorities scrambled fighter aircraft as officials tried to determine what had happened aboard the commercial jet.Cockpit fight eruptsThe reason for the emergency soon became clearer. Israeli officials said the co-pilot attacked the pilot with a knife. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the co-pilot appeared to be trying to crash the aircraft after stabbing the other pilot.The injured pilot has since been identified as Indian national Smit Machchhar. He suffered stab wounds during the cockpit confrontation, which Israeli officials are investigating as a possible attempt to seize control of the aircraft.Passenger accounts described a chaotic scene near the cockpit. One passenger’s family member said she heard screaming before seeing a man holding a knife and a pilot on the floor.The violence left both pilots injured. Saudi officials later confirmed that the captain and co-pilot received hospital treatment after the aircraft reached Tabuk.At that point, passengers faced a problem beyond the physical attack. Someone inside the flight deck had allegedly attacked a member of the crew while the aircraft remained airborne.Netanyahu said passengers and a crew member eventually entered the cockpit. They reportedly found the injured pilot and subdued the suspected attacker.A second group of pilots also played a crucial role. Netanyahu’s spokesman said two off-duty pilots were traveling aboard the flight and later took over the aircraft.Passengers regain controlThe cockpit intervention appears to have been the turning point. Once passengers and crew restrained the attacker, the aircraft could be stabilized and redirected toward a suitable airport. The replacement pilots then prepared for an emergency landing.Tabuk became the destination. The airport’s air traffic control center received a distress call from FZ1073 requesting an emergency landing at 8:44 a.m. local time.Emergency crews prepared for the aircraft before it touched down at 9:45 a.m. The Boeing landed safely, bringing the immediate danger to an end.The passengers could not continue to Israel immediately. They remained in Saudi Arabia for about eight hours as Flydubai arranged replacement aircraft.A replacement Flydubai flight eventually carried the stranded passengers toward Israel. The aircraft later landed at Ben Gurion Airport in Israel, ending the ordeal for those aboard the original flight.❤️🙏🇮🇱 ISRAELIS HOME AFTER FLYDUBAI HIJACKING ATTEMPTAll Israeli passengers stranded in Saudi Arabia after today’s attempted Flydubai hijacking have returned home.PM Netanyahu met passengers who helped subdue the attacker.One woman recalled: “I didn’t pray for the plane to… https://t.co/E0OhbCXmRn pic.twitter.com/SrNBlvztt9— Mossad Commentary (@MOSSADil) September 30, 2026Both original pilots remained under medical care after suffering injuries during the cockpit confrontation. Saudi authorities also arrested the suspected attacker.Israeli authorities are also examining whether terrorism could have played a role. Officials have not ruled out that possibility, but they have not established a terrorist motive or explained what triggered the cockpit confrontation.The incident has left investigators with several unanswered questions. Flydubai has not established why the cockpit confrontation began, and officials have cautioned against premature speculation.Investigators must now reconstruct the cockpit struggle and the aircraft’s rapid descent. They will also examine the emergency signals and the actions that allowed the Boeing 737 Max 8 to recover.

title: NASA prepares humanoid robots to handle dangerous jobs on moon, Mars
content: When humans finally set up camp on the moon, they will not be alone. But will share the dusty extraterrestrial home with metallic coworkers who do not need oxygen, sleep, or coffee breaks.At NASA’s Johnson Space Center, the 16-member Dexterous Robotics Team is laying the groundwork for a future where humans and advanced robots work side by side in deep space.Science fiction has mostly imagined metallic overlords replacing human explorers. But NASA has a vastly different objective. The strategy is simple: let machines take the hits so humans can do what they do best. Robots can endure conditions that are fatal to humans, operate for long durations without life support, and reduce the massive costs and risks associated with crewed missions.“Our team is not trying to replace human explorers with robots but instead make human exploration safer and more sustainable by developing highly capable, reliable, and trustworthy robots to work in extreme environments,” said Shaun Azimi, Dexterous Robotics Team lead. “If we can send more capable robots, we can reduce the risk and make people more effective in doing the things that people do best.”NASA’s steel astronautsSpace features severe hazards like intense radiation, extreme temperatures, vacuum conditions, and destructive dust that jeopardize human survival. Robots operate without oxygen, water, food, or bulky suits, functioning reliably in these harsh environments. Therefore, assigning automated systems to high-risk tasks such as repairing station exteriors, inspecting damaged hardware, and scouting uncharted surfaces would keep human crews out of harm’s way.The team’s expertise was forged through iconic space platforms like Robonaut 2, which spent seven years aboard the International Space Station, and Valkyrie, NASA’s first bipedal humanoid. Today, those years of field experience are driving brand-new initiatives.At the center of this push is iMETRO — the Integrated Mobile Evaluation Testbed for Robotics Operations — a facility designed to bridge the gap between concept and reality. Equipped with space habitat mockups, simulation tools, and a rugged outdoor rock yard, iMETRO gives engineers and private partners a practical space to test robotic hardware and software.A major engineering hurdle for lunar and Mars missions is radio delay (ranging from a few seconds for the Moon to over 20 minutes for Mars). The software tested at iMETRO enables semi-autonomous execution, where astronauts or ground control give high-level commands, and the robot handles the granular hand-eye coordination independently.For the moon and MarsThe facility takes away the guessing game. In one test, software developed by PickNik Inc. let a robotic arm locate a spacecraft hatch, turn the latch, pull open the heavy door, and transfer cargo inside. In another project, a NASA intern built code enabling a commercial arm to inspect and maintain a station-style cold stowage freezer routinely.These trials do more than improve software. They reshape design thinking. Habitat designers are learning that small adjustments, such as adding larger handles or installing brighter lights, can benefit robotic workers just as much as human astronauts.The immediate target is humanity’s first lunar outpost, the Moon Base. But the vision stretches further out into the solar system. The team is already mapping out applications for future human missions to Mars. It will ensure that wherever people go next, their automated partners will be right beside them to share the heavy load.

title: New US facility deal targets breakthroughs in quantum RF sensing
content: A new agreement signed between an American institue and an Australian university is set to explore quantum radio frequency (RF) sensing, sensemaking, which is quantum signal interpretation and analytics, and related technologies.The new three-year memorandum of understanding (MOU) is signed by Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) and Australia-based Adelaide University.The joint research team launched first-phase, hands-on evaluations of superconducting quantum RF sensors for signals intelligence applications at the Jesper Munch Quantum Laboratories at Adelaide University in South Australia. Signals intelligence is the field of collecting, intercepting and analyzing electronic signals to support defense, communications and emergency response. “Unlike conventional antennas that get bulkier in size as frequencies get lower, quantum RF device size is independent of frequency,” said Staff Engineer Michael Quinn, who leads quantum RF research and development in SwRI’s Defense and Intelligence Solutions Division offices in Warner Robins, Georgia.“These systems achieve broad coverage, kilohertz to terahertz, with the same compact hardware. They provide more critical information and take up less space, which is a major advantage, especially for defense and intelligence missions where size, weight and power are critical considerations.”RF devices provide broad coverageThe team revealed that in superconducting materials, RF signals vastly affect the dynamics of electrons, the negatively charged building blocks of atoms. Ultrasensitive, longer-range quantum RF sensing devices use changes in electron trajectory to extract more information out of the RF environment than conventional antennas. Precision circuits made of superconducting materials produce raw data that yields accurate signal measurements. Superconducting quantum RF systems leverage the unique properties of superconducting materials, enabling highly sensitive detection and characterization of signals across a broad electromagnetic spectrum. Compact quantum systems offer the potential to replace bulky antennas, especially aboard military ships and aircraft with limited space.Adelaide University’s quantum laboratories include a state-of-the-art molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) system that “grows” advanced superconductor and quantum materials one atomic layer at a time, like a 3D printer. The MBE transforms raw materials into a Superconducting QUantum Interference Device (SQUID) supercooled to -452.47 degrees Fahrenheit to activate superconducting properties and an RF wave response, according to a press release.New material architecturesResearchers are exploring new material architectures designed to raise SQUID operating temperatures, reduce cooling requirements and improve portability and operational practicality. The collaboration unites Adelaide University’s expertise in superconducting quantum materials and sensor development with SwRI’s strengths in advanced RF engineering, signals processing and operational applications, as per the release.“The SwRI team tested and assessed selected performance metrics of the superconducting quantum RF technology developed by Adelaide University,” said Professor Giuseppe C. Tettamanzi, director of the Jesper Munch Quantum Laboratories and leader of Adelaide University’s superconducting quantum technologies research program. “By combining our complementary expertise, Adelaide University and SwRI are accelerating the development and maturation of quantum RF technologies with the potential to address the challenges of increasingly congested electromagnetic environments and complex operational scenarios. This collaboration demonstrates the value of deep scientific alliances between Australia and the United States in advancing technologies critical to future security and economic prosperity.”

title: OpenAI model to take on complex chip design, refine it on its own
content: OpenAI and Synopsys are developing a specialized model that can directly operate professional chip-design tools, with the goal of helping engineers move from design objectives to verified silicon faster.The companies have signed a multi-year agreement to jointly develop GPT-Synopsys, which will combine OpenAI’s frontier models with Synopsys’ electronic design automation (EDA) software and semiconductor expertise. OpenAI will also license Synopsys’ EDA tools to develop the model. Unlike a general-purpose model connected to engineering software, GPT-Synopsys is being designed to become an expert user of the tools themselves. It will learn to run EDA workflows, interpret results, and repeatedly modify designs based on those results.Engineers will be able to give the system objectives involving power, performance and area (PPA), timing or verification. Agents will then operate the tools, analyze their outputs, implement changes, and iterate toward verified results that engineers can review.Model learns engineering tools“The future of semiconductor engineering requires dramatic acceleration of the chip design process without compromising PPA or first-time-right silicon,” said Sassine Ghazi, president and CEO of Synopsys.“Together with OpenAI, we’re bringing frontier intelligence to chip design to help more companies develop and accelerate advanced silicon, while maintaining the rigor and trust required for manufacturing success.”GPT-Synopsys will run on OpenAI-hosted infrastructure and integrate with Synopsys.ai and Synopsys Autopilot, the company’s agentic engineering platform. It is also being designed to work with customers’ existing agent systems. Early technology engagements with semiconductor customers are already underway, although the companies did not name them. The deal builds on Synopsys’ broader push toward autonomous chip engineering. Just two days earlier, the company unveiled its Autopilot platform and long-horizon AgentEngineer systems, which can plan and execute multi-step engineering workflows. Synopsys said deployments of the technology have demonstrated up to 50x faster verification closure, 20 percent higher coverage and a 30 percent productivity boost.The partnership effectively aims to shift some chip-design work from engineers manually operating individual software tools to agents capable of carrying out longer sequences of engineering tasks.Agents iterate chip designs“We’re using our most advanced technology to improve the systems that power AI,” said Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI.“With Synopsys, we’re bringing that work to chip design, helping engineers explore more designs and get to a working chip faster. By helping them build better chips, we can build better AI and bring it to more people.”OpenAI is also expanding deeper into chip development itself. Earlier this year, it unveiled Jalapeño, its first custom inference accelerator developed with Broadcom. The chip went from initial design to manufacturing tape-out in nine months, with OpenAI’s models used to speed up parts of the design and optimization process.The companies will jointly offer the compute, model and software licenses needed to use GPT-Synopsys. Their agreement also includes joint research and development, a shared revenue framework and plans to bring the technology to customers worldwide. Synopsys says customer-specific chip-design data will not be used to train the model. Data will be encrypted both at rest and in transit, while customers will have configurable controls covering retention, permissions, and auditing.

title: Second-ever reactor trial at DOME to test MW-level nuclear battery
content: A Houston startup will test an experimental “nuclear battery” in the Idaho desert next year, marking a key milestone for next-generation clean energy.The US Department of Energy selected Deployable Energy to run trials at the Idaho National Laboratory in 2027. The firm will test its microreactor inside the Demonstration of Microreactor Experiments facility, known as DOME.Deployable Energy is only the second company chosen to use the testbed. Nuclear developer Radiant carried out the inaugural test there earlier this year.Unlike traditional atomic plants, which require massive containment structures and produce gigawatts of electricity, microreactors are compact and portable. Deployable Energy’s prototype, called the Nuclear Unity Battery, is designed to generate one megawatt of electric power (1 MWe).Specific technical configurationThe machine uses a specific technical configuration: light water moderates the nuclear reaction, while circulating helium gas cools the system.“The test builds on the company’s earlier work achieving zero-power criticality through Nuclear Energy Launch Pad and will provide an opportunity to evaluate system performance, integration, controls, safety and operational procedures at increased scale,” noted INL.Officials view these demonstrations as essential for modernizing the power grid.“Testing at facilities like DOME is how we move these technologies closer to deployment,” said Chimi Zacot, acting deputy assistant secretary for Nuclear Reactors at the energy department. He added that the initiative supports the goal of providing affordable, reliable electricity across the country.Meeting technical benchmarksDeployable Energy won its slot following a competitive application window in July 2026. The testing campaign is entirely self-funded by the company.However, access to the site is not guaranteed. To keep its schedule on track, the firm must hit strict benchmarks for technical readiness, fuel procurement, and regulatory clearances.“The company must meet specific milestones throughout the process to maintain its allotted time in DOME and ensure efficient use of the test bed,” highlighted the lab.National Reactor Innovation Center (NRIC) director Brad Tomer noted that interest from commercial developers remains high.“We have a strong pipeline of companies interested in the DOME,” Tomer said, calling the momentum vital as developers push toward commercial markets.Practical engineering solutionThe test site itself represents a practical engineering solution. Located at the laboratory’s Materials and Fuels Complex, DOME officially opened in April 2026 as the world’s first facility designed specifically to run fueled microreactor tests producing up to 20 megawatts of thermal energy.Instead of building a new shell, engineers repurposed an empty structure: the containment dome of Experimental Breeder Reactor-II. The building measures 80 feet (24 meters) wide and 100 feet tall.By reusing an existing, reinforced building, researchers avoided years of construction. The facility provides private innovators with pre-built safety barriers and monitoring instruments, dramatically reducing the capital needed to collect real performance data. That data is critical, as developers must eventually satisfy strict federal regulators before any commercial reactor can connect to the public grid.

title: Trump unveils $200 billion US energy plan spanning nuclear, gas
content: President Donald Trump has unveiled plans for up to $200 billion in South Korean investment in U.S. energy infrastructure, including eight large nuclear reactors, a nearly 6.5-gigawatt Texas power complex and the long-planned Alaska LNG project.The package could channel billions of dollars into U.S. power generation as electricity demand rises from data centers and manufacturing. It forms part of South Korea’s broader $350 billion U.S. investment commitment tied to a trade agreement with Washington.“We’re thrilled to announce one of the largest energy infrastructure investments in American history,” Trump said.The first formal investment is a $22.3 billion combined-cycle gas power complex in Encinal, Texas. Known as Project Star, the 6,472-megawatt development is designed to deliver electricity directly to nearby data centers, with initial commercial operations expected in 2029 and the full complex targeted for 2032.Texas power feeds dataU.S. property developer Related Companies and power producer NextEra Energy will lead the project, while Texas-based Lewis Energy Group will provide the site, natural gas, water and other infrastructure.South Korean companies are expected to seek contracts covering equipment, engineering, construction and long-term maintenance.The package could also support one of the largest proposed expansions of U.S. nuclear capacity in years. Project Power establishes a framework for up to $120 billion for eight large reactors: six Westinghouse AP1000 units and two South Korean-designed APR1400 reactors.Six gigawatt power generation facility. Eight new large scale nuclear power plants. The crucial Alaska LNG plant.The Dealmaker-in-Chief, President Trump, has revolutionized American energy. The Trump Administration is ushering in a new era of American energy dominance. 🇺🇸📈 pic.twitter.com/jm2jK70ytM— The White House (@WhiteHouse) September 30, 2026Construction is proposed in three stages, while about $100 billion would cover construction and another $20 billion would be held as contingency reserves. The countries have also discussed an advance payment of up to $10 billion to secure long-lead components such as reactor vessels, steam generators and reactor coolant pumps.The framework, however, does not mean all eight reactors have been approved for construction. Individual sites, ownership structures and schedules remain undecided, and each project will require separate commercial assessments and approvals.The nuclear push comes as the U.S. looks for significantly more electricity to serve expanding data centers and manufacturing facilities. The Trump administration has also been pushing to increase domestic nuclear generation.Alaska pipeline gets boostTrump also highlighted the Alaska LNG project, a decades-old proposal to move natural gas from Alaska’s North Slope through an approximately 800-mile pipeline to a liquefaction and export facility in Nikiski.The project is designed to transport roughly 3.9 billion cubic feet of natural gas per day and produce up to 20 million metric tons of LNG annually, according to the White House. The fuel could then be shipped to Asian markets.Alaska LNG has struggled for years with financing, high projected costs and questions over commercial viability. South Korea has not given the project an unconditional green light and says its participation will depend on the economics.“It is true that the project has a weaker commercial case,” South Korean Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said. “But from a strategic perspective, we need to examine it because South Korea’s gas supply routes are highly vulnerable.”“We have agreed with the United States that we will not proceed unless the project is commercially viable,” Kim added.Together, the Texas, nuclear and Alaska proposals are expected to account for most of the $200 billion investment commitment, potentially adding major new gas, nuclear and LNG infrastructure across the U.S.

title: US Air Force orders 22 more F-15EX jets to replace aging jet fleet
content: The U.S. Air Force has awarded Boeing a $2.38 billion contract to manufacture 22 more F-15EX Eagle II fighters, expanding its procurement of aircraft intended to replace aging F-15C and F-15D jets.The Lot 7 agreement was announced on September 29, ahead of the fiscal year deadline. It keeps all 22 aircraft within available funding despite the effects of production disruptions and rising defense industry costs.Boeing said the award brings the total number of F-15EX aircraft under contract across Lots 1 through 7 to 120.Keeping procurement on trackThe agreement uses congressionally provided reconciliation funding to sustain F-15EX production. According to the Air Force, negotiations accounted for the effects of a 2025 production disruption and broader inflation across the defense industrial base.The F-15 Program Office and Boeing reached an agreement that preserved the planned quantity while staying within the available resources.“Lot 7 reflects a disciplined approach to executing available resources while balancing the realities affecting defense production,” Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich, portfolio acquisition executive for the Fighters and Advanced Aircraft Directorate, said in the release.“The team remained focused on affordability, production continuity and delivering the aircraft needed to modernize the U.S. Air Force’s fighter fleet for the threats we face today and into the future,” he continued.The award supports near-term manufacturing while the service continues to evaluate its future fighter requirements and acquisition plans.Replacing older Eagle fightersThe F-15EX builds on the established F-15 design, introducing updated systems to support the Air Force’s fleet modernization.Described by the service as a multirole heavy fighter, the Eagle II incorporates advanced avionics, large-area cockpit displays, a digital backbone architecture, and enhanced survivability capabilities.Its intended role includes replacing aging F-15C and F-15D aircraft while providing room for further modernization as operational requirements change.Boeing describes the aircraft as the most advanced version of the Eagle family, with an all-glass touchscreen cockpit and advanced mission systems.The company’s September announcement also followed the recent delivery of F-15EX-22, the first aircraft supplied under the Lot 3 contract. Boeing said it planned further Lot 3 deliveries through the remainder of 2026 and was working with the Air Force to increase production to two aircraft per month. Coordinating the contract awardThe Air Force presented the Lot 7 negotiations as an example of its acquisition transformation approach, bringing specialists together to resolve procurement challenges.The effort involved personnel working across program management, contracting, pricing, engineering, financial management, and logistics. Their task included assessing changing production conditions and aligning the purchase with available funding.An integrated negotiation team coordinated work across these areas and elevated issues that required senior-level decisions. The service said this approach maintained accountability for cost, schedule, and aircraft quantity.Senior department leaders supported coordination and decision-making as the team worked through affordability and execution challenges before the fiscal year deadline. The latest contract sustains Eagle II production as the Air Force moves forward with replacing its older fighters.

title: US conducts rare nuclear blast detection test at Nevada site
content: The U.S. energy department’s National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) has conducted an underground chemical explosive test in Nevada to study how difficult-to-detect nuclear blasts could be identified. The experiment took place at the Nevada National Security Site and was designed to improve detection of low-yield explosions linked to potential testing by China and Russia.The non-nuclear test took place inside a tunnel at the site, which is about 65 miles northwest of Las Vegas. The location was also used during the development of the first U.S. nuclear weapons. NNSA said Wednesday that measurements collected during the experiment will help scientists improve models and algorithms used to identify and characterize foreign nuclear detonations.Testing a harder-to-detect explosionThe experiment used a conventional chemical explosive, with no nuclear weapon or nuclear detonation involved. It focused on a method known as “decoupling,” which can reduce the signals produced by an underground explosion. NNSA said the test was intended to strengthen U.S. capabilities for identifying what it described as a “decoupled” explosion.The agency linked the test method to what the United States determined China conducted at its Lop Nur nuclear test site in June 2020.“Just as a stealth aircraft looks smaller on radar, decoupling can greatly muffle the signals detected by nuclear detection sensors, making a large explosion appear smaller,” the statement said.In a conventional underground test, a device is placed deep underground near surrounding rock. The resulting shock waves travel through the ground and monitoring equipment can detect them. A decoupled test uses a large underground chamber that can reduce the seismic signals reaching sensors.Sensors capture data from the blastResearchers used several types of advanced sensors during the experiment to study the explosion and its effects. The equipment included accelerometers and seismometers for measuring ground motion.The test also used infrasound sensors, electromagnetic sensors, chemical and radiotracer samplers, and meteorological instruments. NNSA said the collected measurements will support scientific models and help refine detection algorithms.The broader objective is to improve how scientists estimate the characteristics of underground explosions. Better measurements could help U.S. monitoring systems identify nuclear detonations and determine their properties when they occur.NNSA did not provide a date for the experiment.Test follows calls to resume nuclear testingThe announcement comes after President Donald Trump called for the United States to resume underground nuclear weapons testing. In October 2025, Trump said he had instructed the Pentagon to immediately restart nuclear testing on an equal basis with China and Russia.“We’ve halted [testing] many years ago, but with others doing testing, I think it’s appropriate to do so,” he said at the time.No U.S. underground nuclear weapons test has taken place since that announcement.The latest Nevada experiment does not represent a return to nuclear explosive testing. The United States has maintained a moratorium on nuclear explosive tests since 1992.

title: US' nuclear reactor to get 190-MW more energy generating capacity
content: A Maryland-based company, Constellation Energy, has announced a long-term agreement with Amazon to support the continued investment in and expansion of the Calvert Cliffs Clean Energy Center, Maryland’s only nuclear plant and largest source of clean energy. Constellation’s new deal with Amazon is expected to enable more than $3 billion in Maryland infrastructure investment, including state-of-the-art improvements across the entire 1,790-megawatt plant and approximately 190 megawatts in total of new, emissions-free generating capacity coming online between 2030 and 2032.“This agreement demonstrates how private investment can strengthen critical energy infrastructure,” said Joe Dominguez, chairman, president and chief executive officer, Constellation.“Amazon’s commitment supports the long-term operation of Calvert Cliffs for generations to come and creates a strong foundation for future investment in both the facility and in advanced nuclear technologies.”Expansion of Calvert Cliffs’ generating capacityThe expansion of Calvert Cliffs’ generating capacity will be supported by a 20-year agreement, which includes 690 megawatts of power, including the 190-megawatt uprate. The parties have also entered into a related retail supply agreement to support Amazon operations in the 13-state PJM market. In addition to making the uprate possible, Amazon’s long-term commitment will help provide Constellation with the revenue certainty to relicense the plant for another 20 years and make progress toward the development of new clean energy power plants at the site, adding to Maryland’s supply of clean and reliable energy, according to a press release.Located in Lusby on the western shore of the Chesapeake Bay, Calvert Cliffs produces approximately 80 percent of Maryland’s clean energy and enough electricity to power the equivalent of more than 1.3 million homes. The facility employs more than 800 people and contributes about $21 million annually in taxes that support schools, roads, and other public services, according to the release.Amazon committed to investing in carbon-free energy“Amazon is committed to investing in carbon-free energy to strengthen the grid and benefit the communities where we operate,” said Kerry Person, vice president of AWS Global Operations and Data Center Delivery. “This long-term agreement with Constellation sustains the continued operation and expansion of Maryland’s largest source of carbon-free energy, supports hundreds of jobs, and brings significant new generation to the regional grid.”The companies highlighted that the latest agreement will also help Amazon manage its energy costs for facilities throughout the region. All the electricity generated by Calvert Cliffs will continue flowing to the PJM regional grid just as it does now, demonstrating how large energy users can support investments in new, reliable generation while strengthening the broader electric system.The agreement comes at a time when electricity demand is increasing rapidly, particularly because of data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure.Large technology companies require substantial amounts of electricity around the clock. Unlike intermittent sources such as wind and solar, nuclear plants can provide continuous electricity while producing no direct carbon emissions during generation.Beyond the immediate capacity increase, the agreement could play an important role in extending the operating life of Calvert Cliffs.

title: CEA-INES sets new flexible perovskite record at 21.2% efficiency
content:
CEA-INES sets new flexible perovskite record at 21.2% efficiency
Researchers at the CEA's National Solar Energy Institute (INES) in France have raised their internal efficiency record for flexible perovskite solar cells to 21.2%, up from a previous 19.2%, on cells built on a PET substrate.
The improvement came from incorporating an anti-reflective coating and redesigning the cells' electrical connections to reduce energy losses. The result was achieved on an active area of 0.28 cm² - nearly three times larger than the 0.092 cm² device that currently holds the world record for flexible perovskite cells, at 24.52%. The team says the result shows that flexible perovskite cells can be scaled up in area while retaining a large share of their efficiency.
Flexible perovskite cells are of interest for applications such as smart textiles, space systems, and building integration, alongside compatibility with large-scale manufacturing. Achieving high efficiency on flexible substrates is more difficult than on rigid glass, since the polymer substrates require lower processing temperatures that can introduce defects into the perovskite structure.
The work was carried out as part of JUMP INTO SPACE, a four-year Horizon Europe EIC Pathfinder Challenge project (October 2024–September 2028) coordinated by the University of Rome Tor Vergata, with a consortium of seven partners across five countries, including CEA, ONERA, Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin, the Universities of Turin and Siena, UNINOVA, and Polish perovskite manufacturer Saule Technologies. The project's overall goal is an all-perovskite tandem solar cell on a radiation-hardened, flexible photonic substrate, targeting 30% efficiency under AM0 (space) illumination for applications including small satellites, active debris removal, and lunar or Martian bases. The flexible single-junction cell reported here is a building block toward that tandem architecture.
The researchers said future work will focus on optimizing the cells' individual layers - including testing and adapting conductive materials to improve current extraction and environmental durability - as well as adapting the fabrication process to new flexible substrates better suited to heat, mechanical stress, and radiation exposure.

title: Researchers achieve high breakdown resistance in 2D perovskite antiferroelectric material
content:
Researchers achieve high breakdown resistance in 2D perovskite antiferroelectric material
Researchers at the Fujian Institute of Research on the Structure of Matter (FJIRSM), Chinese Academy of Sciences, have developed a two-dimensional perovskite antiferroelectric material, (2-MBA)
(2-MBA = 2-methylbutylammonium), with breakdown resistance and cycling stability among the highest reported for molecular antiferroelectrics.
Stable breakdown resistant molecular antiferroelectric triggered by confinement-dependent atomic displacement. (Image by FJIRSM)
Molecular antiferroelectrics, which arrange dipoles in antiparallel configurations between neighboring lattices, are attractive for high-precision digital displacement sensors and energy-storage capacitors. In practice, though, their usefulness has been limited by relatively low maximum applied field strength and poor long-term cycling stability, a gap the field has struggled to close because the atomic-level origin of antiferroelectric ordering itself has not been well understood.
The team's approach centers on cage-confined atomic displacement: rather than relying on the order-disorder dynamics typically invoked to explain antiferroelectric behavior, they found that confining cesium cations within the material's lattice "cages" regulates how the surrounding structural motifs move, and that this confinement is what drives the material's stability. Energy-barrier calculations combined with in situ solid-state NMR spectroscopy showed that displacing the cage-confined Cs
cations requires a notably high energy barrier (2.91 eV) - considerably higher than in order-disorder-type systems - which in turn raises both the material's Curie temperature (~327 K) and its forward coercive field (~56.8 kV/cm).
That combination lets the material switch under stronger external stimuli without breaking down: (2-MBA)
reaches a spontaneous polarization of 5.0 µC/cm², a breakdown field of up to 175 kV/cm, and fatigue endurance beyond 10⁶ cycles, putting it ahead of most molecular antiferroelectrics and, according to the researchers, even some purely inorganic oxide antiferroelectrics on breakdown resistance.
The researchers describe cage-confined dynamics as a general design principle that could extend to other electrically ordered materials beyond this specific composition.

title: A closer look at Marstek's 5 kWh plug-in battery - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Marstek is targeting European markets with its Venus plug-in solution that is scalable to 9kW/15kWh. The Chinese manufacturer confirmed it is working with UK energy management providers on deeper integration to support optimization for home owners.
Matthew Lynas
01 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
Marstek Energy’s VENUS E 4.0 plug-in battery.
Marstek Energy brought its 3 kW, 5 kWh Venus E 4.0 residential storage system to Solar & Storage Live UK, Birmingham, where
pv magazine
took a closer look at the plug-in solution.
The system combines 5,024 Wh of lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery storage with 3 kVA grid-connected charging and discharging capability. It can also provide 3 kVA of off-grid output and deliver up to 3.6 kVA of peak backup power for 10 seconds, allowing homeowners to maintain essential loads during power outages.
Marstek Energy claims a cycle life exceeding 10,000 cycles at 25 C, with an 88% depth of discharge and efficiency above 90% across the battery and AC cycle.
According to Daisy Jiang, key account manager at Marstek Energy, the company believes the 5 kWh model is particularly well suited to British households.
“The Venus E series has already arrived in the UK through our local distribution network. Our initial focus is on the Venus E 5 kWh system, which we believe is a strong fit for the market,” Jiang said.
Designed for outdoor deployment, the Venus E 4.0 carries an IP65 rating and operates in temperatures ranging from -20 C to +60 C. The battery measures 520 mm x 430 mm x 191.2 mm, weighs 47.2 kg and uses natural convection cooling rather than active fans. Protection specifications include DC II and AC III overvoltage protection categories.
The battery supports Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, LAN, RS485, MQTT and cloud-to-cloud communications. According to Marstek Energy, these capabilities are intended to support integration with energy management systems and dynamic tariff platforms, an increasingly important feature in the UK residential storage market.
“We are currently working on deeper integration with Octopus Energy and other energy management providers,” Jiang said. “This allows homeowners to optimize battery charging and discharging around dynamic electricity pricing and maximize the value of flexible tariffs.”
Scalability is another feature of the platform. While the base unit offers 5 kWh of storage, Marstek Energy says the Venus E platform can be expanded through parallel operation to provide up to 15 kWh of storage capacity and 9 kW of power output using its SmartBox solution.
The Venus E range forms part of a wider strategy that has already seen the manufacturer establish positions in several European markets. Jiang said the company has achieved significant penetration in Germany, France, Poland, Ukraine and the Benelux countries through its plug-in storage products.
While plug-and-play batteries have gained traction across mainland Europe, UK regulations for plug-in solar introduced in August did not include plug-in battery products. The UK government has since launched a tender for a
technical risk and safety assessment
of plug-in battery products to inform future regulations.
“The deployment of plug-in battery products is currently influenced by UK regulations, which do not yet fully accommodate this type of solution,” Jiang said.
“While the regulatory environment for plug-in batteries is moving more slowly in the UK than in some European markets, we continue to see strong long-term potential,” she added. “Once UK regulations evolve to accommodate plug-in battery systems more fully, we believe the market will expand rapidly.”
Marstek Energy argues that its vertically integrated manufacturing model helps differentiate it in an increasingly crowded residential storage market. The company manufactures key system components in-house, including battery cells, inverters, battery management systems and software.
“Our biggest differentiator is vertical integration,” Jiang said. “Because we control the entire product stack, we can manage costs effectively while maintaining product quality and performance.”
In addition to the 5 kWh Venus E Gen 4.0, Marstek Energy’s full plug-in battery range includes the 2 kWh Venus E Mini, and 10 kWh Venus E Max.

title: Germany could generate over 600,000 tonnes of PV module waste by 2030 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A Fraunhofer CSP study estimates that Germany’s installed PV modules contain 5.35 million tonnes of materials worth billions of euros, highlighting significant recycling potential. More than 600,000 tonnes of PV waste could arise by 2030, but uncertain return volumes may create temporary overcapacity in Germany’s expanding recycling sector.
Petra Hannen
01 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
A recent
Fraunhofer Center for Silicon Photovoltaics
(Fraunhofer CSP), commissioned by the German Mineral Resources Agency (DERA), has examined the raw material and recycling potential of photovoltaic modules installed in Germany.
The materials contained in the modules represent considerable economic value, particularly aluminum and silver. According to the study, their potential material value amounts to €4.8 billion ($5.4 billion). Silver is particularly significant for the PV industry: In 2023, the sector accounted for 19.3% of global silver production.
Recycling depends on module technology
The recoverability of individual raw materials depends on the module technology and the recycling process used.
For crystalline silicon modules, Germany already has established recycling processes on an industrial scale. Glass, aluminum and copper can be recovered from discarded modules, while silver can be separated through additional refining processes.
Silicon, which accounts for a significant share of the value of some module components, is generally not recovered at present. Plastics are typically thermally treated. According to the study, current processes achieve a material recycling rate of around 85% and an overall recovery rate of more than 95%.
The study also examines thin-film modules. Cadmium telluride (CdTe) modules contain cadmium and tellurium, while CIGS modules contain indium, gallium and selenium. However, the quantities of these materials installed in Germany are comparatively small because thin-film technologies account for a much smaller share of the market than crystalline silicon modules.
Actual return volumes difficult to estimate
More than 600,000 tons of PV module waste could be generated by 2030. However, the volumes that will actually reach recycling companies, and when they will arrive, remain difficult to predict.
According to the study, the recorded volume of end-of-life modules declined between 2022 and 2024, contrary to expectations. The researchers cite several possible reasons, including the export of used modules.
Estimated quantities of end-of-life PV modules in selected EU countries, based on installed capacity (Eurostat, 2025a) and assuming a 20-year service life, an average module output of 250 W, and an average module weight of 20 kg. | Image: Fraunhofer CSP
This creates a significant gap between available recycling capacity and actual return volumes. In 2024, more than 50,000 tonnes of recycling capacity was already available for crystalline silicon modules, while only around 9,300 tonnes of decommissioned modules underwent initial processing. The study projects that recycling capacity will reach approximately 64,000 tonnes in 2026 and 75,000 tonnes by the end of 2027.
The authors therefore recommend aligning further capacity expansion with actual return volumes to avoid temporary overcapacity. Based on a modeled expansion pathway, the study estimates that annual recycling capacity of 300,000 tonnes could be sufficient by 2040. Temporary peaks in return volumes could be managed through measures such as the interim storage of decommissioned modules.

title: Indian PV manufacturer Vishakha Renewables files for IPO - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Vishakha Renewables, jointly promoted by the Vishakha Group and the Adani Group, produces four of the six key components used in solar modules and is the largest solar component manufacturer (non-cell) in India in terms of combined installed production capacity as of March 31, 2026.
Uma Gupta
01 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
solar glass
Vishakha Renewables’ fully automated solar glass manufacturing facility
Vishakha Renewables Limited, a manufacturer of critical solar module components, has filed its Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP) with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) for its proposed initial public offering (IPO).
The IPO comprises a fresh issue of equity shares aggregating up to INR 1,250 crore ($129.9 million) and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 1.82 crore equity shares by the selling shareholders. The company is jointly promoted by the Vishakha Group and the Adani Group, with Adani Properties being a promoter and a promoter selling shareholder in the offer.
Vishakha Renewables said it may also consider a pre-IPO placement of up to INR 250 crore, which, if undertaken, will reduce the size of the fresh issue.
The company proposes to utilise INR 900 crore of the net proceeds towards repayment and/or pre-payment of certain borrowings, with the balance towards general corporate purposes. As of June 30, 2026, the company had consolidated outstanding borrowings of INR 2,700.57 crore.
According to a CRISIL report, as of March 31, 2026, Vishakha Renewables was the second largest solar glass manufacturer in India, with an installed capacity of 660 tonnes per day (tpd), the second largest EVA/EPE encapsulant manufacturer, with capacity of 23.20 million linear metres, and the largest aluminium frame manufacturer in India, with an installed capacity of 14,508.75 tonnes per annum (tpa). It was also among the top 10 backsheet manufacturers in India.
The company produces four of the six key components used in solar modules and, according to the CRISIL report, is the largest solar component manufacturer (non-cell) in India in terms of combined installed production capacity as of March 31, 2026. Its four product categories collectively represent approximately 40–45% of the average cost of a bifacial solar module.
Vishakha Renewables is also expanding its solar glass manufacturing capacity from 660 tpd (equivalent to 4.4 GW of solar module capacity) to 1,920 tpd (12.80 GW), while also ramping up aluminium frame and encapsulant production. Upon completion of the solar glass expansion, the company’s facilities are expected to house the largest operational solar glass furnace in India, as stated in the DRHP.
Vishakha Renewables has entered into long-term offtake arrangements with Mundra Solar PV Ltd and Mundra Solar Energy Ltd. These include a 15-year take-or-pay arrangement for solar glass from its Phase I facility, an 8.5-year arrangement for aluminium frames and a 17-year arrangement for solar glass from its Phase II facility. The arrangements provide for minimum offtake commitments and are intended to provide demand visibility for the company’s products.
The company operates its manufacturing facilities in Mundra, Gujarat, in close proximity to the facilities of its key offtakers and the Mundra Ports and Special Economic Zone. It had 99 customers as of March 31, 2026.
SBI Capital Markets, ICICI Securities and IIFL Capital Services are the book running lead managers to the offer, while MUFG Intime India is the registrar to the offer.

title: Ireland energizes first SRESS solar farm, opening new revenue opportunities for farmers and landowners - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
“This is the beginning of a wave of small-scale energy projects being developed by farmers and communities,” Ken O’Byrne, of Flogas Energy told
pv magazine
. Flogas has a 15-year PPA with the 650 kW Meadhill Solar farm’s developer, Cork farmer Sean Keating.
Blathnaid O’Dea
01 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Power purchase agreements
The 650 kW Meadhill Solar farm in Cork can power around 150 homes in the locality
The first solar farm under the Irish government’s Small-Scale Renewable Energy Support Scheme (
) has been energized in County Cork. SRESS supports projects that produce between 50 kW and 6 MW of electricity.
The 650 kW Meadhill Solar farm was developed by Cork farmer Sean Keating and provides space for sheep grazing around and underneath the solar panels.
The project generates sufficient energy to power around 150 homes in the area and provides a revenue stream for Keating, who began work on it in 2017. The farmer has entered into a 15-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with Flogas, a DCC Energy-owned company that is listed on the London Stock Exchange.
Flogas is actively seeking other farmers, landowners and small enterprises interested in exploring PPAs. Ken O’Byrne, managing director, Flogas told pv magazine he sees plenty of opportunities for further PPAs under the SRESS, adding that there is a lot of capacity yet to be allocated to facilities under the scheme.
“The major benefits to farmers and communities in our opinion is to diversify revenue streams while making a positive carbon reduction impact to the national electricity grid,” O’Byrne said, pointing out that Keating’s flagship Meadhill Solar Farm project demonstrates to farmers what is achievable even on a small parcel of land.
“We think this is the beginning of a wave of small-scale energy projects being developed by farmers and communities. Significant solar deployment is occurring at domestic rooftop scale and at major utility scale. Farmer or community led projects are the scale in between these and now have the opportunity to follow suit and benefit from strong supply chains, proven solar technology and in an unobtrusive way to their farms and communities with relatively small but impactful solar installations. Farmers have been harvesting solar via crops for millennia, this is simply a new medium to harvest solar energy: via PV technology,” said the Flogas head.
Irish company PV Generation Ltd. (PVGEN) took on the installation tasks and assisted Keating throughout the development phase. Edward Carbery, the company’s group marketing lead, told pv magazine that it has been involved since the very early stages and part-funded the project.
“The planning permission and grid connection was already obtained by the client before PVGEN came on board, but we completed lots of design iterations at the pricing stage and supplied the client with production models to bring to the banks to apply for funding,” said Carbery.
PVGEN completed the electrical installation, commissioning and testing of more than 1,000 panels at the site and arranged for testing on the ground conditions, as well as for the mounting array to be designed and procured from Turkey. It also liaised with the Irish distribution systems operator to ensure the design complied with the grid connection agreement and provided the EGIP protection panel and the LV distribution board.
Like O’Byrne from Flogas, Carbery said PVGEN is seeing a lot of interest in microgeneration solar from farmers and landowners. “People are starting to see this as a good opportunity to diversify their income. We would definitely say that there has especially been a bigger interest in farmers exploring all kinds of solar projects as a result of the energy crisis and the recent jump in electricity and diesel prices.”
Besides the SRESS, the Irish government supports renewable energy generation through solar PV grants, for roof top solar on farm buildings, as part of the Targeted Agricultural Modernisation Scheme (TAMS).

title: Shared grid connections concentrate battery insurance risk - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Tokio Marine GX (TMGX) sees exposures of up to billions of dollars building up at co-located battery energy storage system (BESS) sites, and says lenders are only beginning to require cyber cover.
Brian Publicover
01 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Shared grid connections at co-located solar-plus-storage sites are concentrating insured revenue into a growing risk for BESS insurers, said Olly Litterick, head of renewables at TMGX, a green transformation underwriting business that Japan’s Tokio Marine group launched in 2025.
Such projects now carry “hundreds of millions of dollars or even billions of dollars of exposure in a single location where multiple insureds share grid connection points,” he said.
Because TMGX covers loss of revenue resulting from physical damage, a failure at a shared export point can affect several insured projects at once, Litterick told
ESS News
“When the grid goes down due to [a] material damage incident or there’s a
transformer failure
or something of that description, you know, the numbers can be astronomical,” he said. “And that’s one of the many things that we as an industry need to get our heads around to support the green transition.”
TMGX acts as lead underwriter on much of its book.
“We lead, we set the terms on many of these projects and other insurers then follow us and provide additional capacity,” said Litterick. “But it’s about controlling that aggregation because these projects are just becoming bigger and bigger and bigger almost monthly.”
TMGX underwriter James Totton has also described
aggregation risk at single substation connection points
as co-location grows. In a report released in May, TMGX said the renewables insurance market must prepare for the
rising complexity of co-located projects
, with elevated aggregation risk where shared grid infrastructure creates a common point of vulnerability.
Marsh, an insurance broker, says in BESS risk guidance on its website that insurers need sufficient separation between battery modules and critical infrastructure such as site transformers and substations, and that minimizing single points of failure is key to avoiding contingent business interruption. Some insurers, including AXIS, sell contingent business interruption cover for lost income when the first substation a project does not own is damaged.
Fastest-growing line
TMGX builds on 20 to 25 years of renewable energy underwriting at GCube, which Tokio Marine acquired in 2020, covering solar, onshore wind, offshore wind, and now battery storage, mainly for property damage and resulting loss of revenue. Litterick said BESS is TMGX’s fastest-growing technology on a compound annual growth basis. He said TMGX’s figure of about 8 GW of BESS refers to its insured participation and is “probably slightly outdated” because the book is growing so quickly.
Most of that book is still in construction, he said, and utility-scale BESS has only been widespread “for the last three to five years,” so the claims record remains limited. TMGX writes significant BESS business in California but has not experienced earthquake losses. “Again, it is very, very early stage,” said Litterick.
Thermal runaway
remains the main driver of probable maximum loss estimates, and Litterick said “the spacing arrangement is obviously crucial to how we underwrite BESS.” He credited the industry with rapid progress on standardization and certification, borrowing from the solar and wind sectors. GCube reported in 2024 that more than half of BESS failures occur within the first two years of operation.
Cybersecurity gap
TMGX’s standard property cover largely excludes
cyberattacks
. Cybersecurity “is usually excluded, or there are certain perils that are written back into a general property policy,” said Litterick, with broader cyber cover usually bought in a separate specialist market. He said this leaves an uncertain gap in cover that needs to be addressed.
Project-finance lenders have traditionally required property damage, natural catastrophe, and machinery breakdown cover, Litterick said. “We are beginning to see lenders insist that their clients … purchase cyber. But it’s quite rare at the moment,” he said.
Litterick said TMGX has not really declined or repriced BESS risks over cyber exposure, because cyber cover has not been a lender requirement and TMGX has not been providing it. He added that demand from clients and lenders is rising, and that TMGX is developing a broader solution.
The cyber exposure of battery storage has drawn wider scrutiny this year. A December 2025 attack on distributed energy assets in Poland revealed a
cyber-insurance gap for battery storage
, while an EU funding ban on high-risk inverter suppliers extends to
BESS power conversion systems

title: South Korea grid overhaul to connect more than 100 GW of renewables - pv magazine Global
content: South Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (MCEE) has lifted restrictions on new renewable energy connections in the Honam region, which covers Gwangju and the provinces of North and South Jeolla in the country’s southwest. Projects already waiting for connection will get priority for early connection applications, while new projects will apply under a revised framework from January 2027, said the ministry. Parts of the Chungcheong region that were closed to new generation will also reopen, and restrictions on the east coast will be lifted in the first half of 2027, when the first phase of a high-voltage direct current line from the east coast to Singapyeong is completed. Under a new flexible connection regime, projects can connect beyond a grid section’s normal hosting limit and will have output curtailed when generation exceeds what the network can take. The ministry said this raises the solar connection limit on a distribution line from 14 MW to 16 MW and at a substation from 50 MW to 60 MW. It estimates the change will allow 2.6 GW of additional solar in Honam alone without new grid construction. The MCEE also plans to use energy storage as an alternative to new lines. By 2030, it aims to connect 3 GW of additional solar in saturated areas through storage on distribution networks and another 1.6 GW through storage at substations. The ministry did not specify the capacity of the batteries involved. It said it has already recovered 9 GW of grid connection rights by checking solar projects that had reserved capacity but were not viable. It will now also push back the connection rights of long-delayed projects to the date they will actually use the grid. The ministry said it expects to recover more than 10 GW in Honam alone by 2030 as a result, including from delayed offshore wind projects. For capacity entering from 2031, it will allocate connection rights using a 67.2% actual on-time completion rate for renewable projects, instead of assuming every project is built on schedule. Connection studies will also change. Until now, they assumed new renewable generation would run after existing fossil fuel plants. They will now assume renewables are dispatched first, reflecting actual grid operation. The ministry estimates this will allow 20 GW of additional renewable capacity nationwide by 2030, including in the southeastern Yeongnam region and northeastern Gangwon province, where coal and liquefied natural gas plants are concentrated. From January 2027, grid connection rights will be linked to a reformed renewable portfolio standard , with rights going to projects selected through competitive bidding rather than on a first-come, first-served basis. The ministry projects that the measures will raise national transmission-level renewable hosting capacity from 119 GW to 171 GW by 2030, and distribution-level capacity from 84 GW to 110 GW. In Honam, it projects transmission capacity rising from 37 GW to 64 GW and distribution capacity from 18 GW to 30 GW. Separately, the Korea Power Exchange opened a tender on Sept. 22 for 1,100 MW/6,600 MWh of six-hour battery storage under 15-year contracts. Winners are due to be announced in November, with projects to be commissioned by February 2029. Seoul-based think tank Solutions for Our Climate argued in a June 2026 paper that South Korea’s first-come, first-served queue allowed stalled projects to hold scarce grid capacity, and it called for connections to be prioritized by project readiness, with greater disclosure of congestion data. South Korea is forecast to add 3.5 GW of solar this year, according to the Export-Import Bank of Korea. title: Spanish researchers validate 10,000 cycles for iron-lead flow battery - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
A Spanish-developed iron-lead flow battery uses a single electrolyte loop and a fluorine-free membrane to cut costs and reliance on critical raw materials, with kilowatt-scale modules the next development step.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
01 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
Spanish research center CIC energiGUNE has completed 10,000 charge-discharge cycles on an iron-lead redox flow battery, a design built from abundant materials and intended to store electricity for several hours in stationary applications.
The technology was tested at temperatures of 25 C to 30 C and uses iron and lead as active materials. Its single-electrolyte-loop design is intended to simplify the conventional flow battery architecture while reducing system costs and dependence on critical raw materials.
The battery also incorporates a fluorine-free membrane designed to reduce internal resistance and limit unwanted transport of chemical species between the two sides of the battery. CIC energiGUNE said the active materials have established industrial and recycling supply chains, potentially reducing dependence on critical materials.
The development is aimed at applications that require electricity to be stored for several hours, including storing excess renewable generation for later use by the electricity system.
Unlike conventional flow batteries with separate electrolyte circuits, the architecture developed by the Spanish research center uses a single electrolyte loop and fewer components.
Flow batteries store energy in electrolytes held in external tanks. Increasing the volume of electrolyte can therefore increase energy capacity, while power output depends primarily on the size and number of cells and stacks. This separation of power and energy allows systems to be configured for applications requiring several hours of storage without necessarily increasing both parameters proportionally.
CIC energiGUNE said the combination of this characteristic, high cycling capability and safety makes flow batteries suitable for solar and wind integration, grid-scale storage, microgrids and industrial energy management.
The iron-lead battery has progressed from initial laboratory cells to larger stacks. The next step is to develop kilowatt-scale modules through a combination of simulation, system design and experimental validation.
CIC energiGUNE is also researching other redox flow battery technologies, including new electrolytes and organic molecules, membranes adapted to different chemistries, electrodes, bipolar plates and stack components. It is also developing approaches to reduce the cost and vanadium consumption of vanadium-based flow batteries.
The center aims to move its developments from the materials and cell level toward complete systems through modeling, prototyping and cost and sustainability analysis. The 10,000-cycle validation represents a step toward scaling a technology designed for intensive cycling and long operating periods with reduced degradation.

title: Two-stage pyrolysis process turns waste solar panels into silicon carbide - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Russian scientists have developed a process that combines pyrolysis at 500 C with electric arc treatment above 1,800 C. The resulting solid product contained up to 61% silicon carbide, a material used in power electronics and refractory ceramics.
Lior Kahana
01 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Raw Materials
Russian researchers have developed a two-stage process to convert waste solar panels into silicon carbide (SiC), a silicon-carbon compound valued for its hardness, thermal conductivity, and resistance to heat and corrosion. SiC is widely used in applications including power electronics and refractory ceramics.
“The rapid growth in the number of solar panels worldwide is making the issue of their utilization increasingly urgent,” the researchers said. “This paper presents the results of an experimental study on the recycling of spent solar panels using pyrolysis and vacuum-free plasma electric arc conversion methods, to obtain carbon residue, silicon carbide, and synthesis gas that can be used for energy production.”
The researchers used a decommissioned polycrystalline silicon solar panel, which they shredded and pyrolyzed at 500 C under a continuous nitrogen flow to decompose its polymer components and obtain a carbon-containing solid residue.
They then processed batches of approximately 2 g of the material in a graphite crucible using a vacuum-free electric arc reactor. The reactor operated at 200 A for 60 seconds, reaching temperatures above 1,800 C.
The scientists tested different carbon additions, using carbon black to promote the conversion of silicon-containing compounds into SiC. They compared the resulting products with those obtained from panel material treated directly in the electric arc reactor without prior pyrolysis.
The researchers then used electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and thermal analysis to examine the products’ morphology, crystalline composition, and oxidation behavior.
“Pyrolysis helped accomplish several tasks at once: removing polymers that interfere with further processing, obtaining a solid carbon residue, and collecting gaseous products,” said Zhanar Bolatova, one of the researchers involved in the study. “According to our calculations, the average yield of carbon residue was 45.8% of the mass of the material being processed.”
Bolatova said the maximum methane concentration in the gas mixture reached 5% by volume, while carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide concentrations were approximately 0.6%.
“Analysis of the composition also confirmed the advantage of preliminary pyrolysis,” she said. “After this treatment, the iron silicide phase disappeared from the final product. This reduced the amount of unwanted impurities and increased the proportion of the target silicon carbide.”
The results also showed that increasing the carbon content of the starting mixture from 0% to 30% raised the proportion of SiC in the solid product from 46% to 61%. At the same time, the share of free silicon fell from 19.7% to 8.3%, while silicon dioxide declined from 3% to trace levels.
The researchers said the results indicate that the additional carbon promoted the conversion of silicon into SiC.
The researchers described the process in “
Stage Recycling of Solar Panels by Pyrolysis and Vacuum-free Electric Arc Conversion to Produce SiC
,” published in
. The research team included scientists from Russia’s National Research Tomsk Polytechnic University and Sevastopol State University.
